Because in cold spray the powder particles never melt. Metal powders are entrained in a high‑pressure gas and accelerated to very high velocities (typically a few hundred to >1,000 m/s). Particle impact with the substrate (or previously deposited particles) generates extreme, highly localized plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at the interface. That severe deformation produces jetting and removes surface films so intimate metal–metal contact and metallurgical bonding occur while the material remains in the solid state. Temperatures locally rise from deformation but stay well below the bulk melting point, so no large-scale melting/solidification occurs.

Key advantages this solid‑state route gives for metal powders
- No melting/solidification defects: avoids porosity, solidification shrinkage, hot cracking and dendritic microstructures that are common in fusion AM.
- Minimal oxidation and chemistry loss: because there is no molten pool and exposure time at elevated temperature is short, oxidation is much reduced and volatile/low‑boiling alloying elements are not lost.
- Retention of feedstock microstructure: nanostructured, work‑hardened or metastable powder structures and precipitates are largely preserved (grain growth and precipitate dissolution are minimized).
- Reduced thermal damage to substrate: small heat‑affected zone, lower residual thermal stresses and less distortion of parts than fusion processes.
- Ability to join dissimilar materials: limited interdiffusion and suppressed formation of thick intermetallic layers make cold spray useful for depositing dissimilar metals and composites.
- Good deposit density and mechanical properties: solid‑state bonding via severe plastic deformation plus oxide removal yields high cohesive strength and dense deposits without melt‑related inclusions.

(Practical note: materials must deform sufficiently on impact—very brittle powders are difficult to cold‑spray without preheating or special process tuning.)

Short answer: Cold gas dynamic spraying (cold spray) is a solid‑state deposition process: particles remain solid (below their melting point) and bond by extreme high‑velocity plastic deformation and adiabatic‑shear/jetting at the impact interface. Thermal spraying melts or semi‑melts the feedstock so coating forms by flattening and rapid solidification of droplets (splats).

Key distinctions

- Particle state
  - Cold spray: particles stay solid (no bulk melting). They may be preheated but remain below melting temperature.
  - Thermal spray (APS, HVOF, plasma, detonation): particles are molten or partially molten when they reach the substrate.

- Impact velocity and energy
  - Cold spray: very high velocities (typically several hundred up to ~1200 m/s), producing very high strain rates on impact.
  - Thermal spray: lower velocities (typically tens to a few hundred m/s) relative to cold spray.

- Bonding mechanism and coating formation
  - Cold spray: bonding by severe plastic deformation, mechanical interlocking and metallurgical contact produced by adiabatic shear and jetting that removes oxides at the interface → solid‑state metallic bonding.
  - Thermal spray: molten droplet flattening into splats, rapid solidification into a lamellar structure; bonding mainly by mechanical interlocking, some metallurgical bonding/diffusion at splat interfaces; oxide entrapment and interlamellar defects are common.

- Microstructure and defects
  - Cold spray: dense, low‑oxide coatings with low porosity, retained feedstock microstructure but often work‑hardened and ultrafine at interfaces; minimal oxidation/heat‑affected zone.
  - Thermal spray: lamellar/splat structure with interfacial oxides, higher porosity and entrapped gases, stronger substrate heating and more pronounced residual thermal stresses.

- Practical consequences
  - Cold spray: good for ductile metals, repair of parts and coatings on heat‑sensitive substrates; preserves feedstock chemistry; limited for ceramics unless hybrid approaches used.
  - Thermal spray: can deposit ceramics and refractory materials readily; allows tailored splat microstructures but typically more oxidation and brittleness.

In short: cold spray = solid particles + high‑velocity plastic bonding; thermal spray = molten droplets + splat solidification.

Because cold gas (cold spray) deposits particles by high-velocity impact and plastic deformation rather than by melting and solidification. Key reasons for phase conservation are:

- No melting / no solidification: particle temperatures remain well below the melting point of the feedstock, so there is no melt/solidification cycle that would produce new solidification microstructures or metastable phases.  
- Very short thermal exposure and low heat input: any heating is highly localized at the impact interface and transient (micro- to milli-seconds), so there is insufficient time and temperature for long-range diffusion or thermally driven phase transformations.  
- Bonding by plastic deformation and adiabatic shear: bonding occurs through severe, high-strain-rate deformation (and localized adiabatic heating) rather than chemical reactions or liquid-phase wetting, so crystal chemistry and phase composition are largely unchanged.  
- Suppressed high-temperature reactions and oxidation: because bulk temperatures are low and exposure to oxidizing environments at high temperature is avoided, you don’t form oxides, intermetallics or decomposition products typical of high-temperature sprays.  
- Possible microstructural refinement without phase change: severe plastic deformation can produce ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains (dynamic recrystallization) but usually does not change the basic crystalline phases.

In contrast, high-temperature thermal spray processes melt the feedstock and expose it to high temperatures long enough for diffusion, reactions, oxidation and rapid solidification-driven phase changes, so the original crystalline phases are often altered or lost.

Short answer
The self‑lubricating behavior of tribo‑oxides that form on cold‑sprayed amorphous (metallic‑glass) coatings comes from a combination of a particular nanoscale structure (nanogranular / glassy / layered) and dynamic formation mechanisms (tribo‑oxidation + severe plastic deformation + mechanical mixing) that produce a thin, adherent, low‑shear tribofilm which both accommodates shear and seeds a low‑adhesion transfer film on the counterface. The tribolayer is continuously repaired during sliding, so lubrication is sustained.

Key structural characteristics
- Continuous, compact surface tribo‑oxide (typical thickness: tens of nm to a few µm) that is strongly bonded to the subsurface.
- Nanogranular and/or amorphous (glass‑like) morphology of the oxide/crushed debris (grain sizes often <100 nm), sometimes with aligned, shear‑deformed lamellae.
- Compositional grading through the layer (oxide‑rich surface → mixed oxide/metal beneath → undeformed amorphous bulk) that produces strong mechanical and chemical adhesion.
- Embedded oxide nanoparticles and smoothed, plastically consolidated debris that reduce asperity height and give a smooth contact surface.
- Presence of specific low‑shear oxide phases or glassy oxides (examples: B2O3/boric acid, V2O5, MoO3, hydrated glassy borates/silicates, or hydrated oxides) or hydrated layers that have low shear strength and can act as lubricants.
- Residual compressive stress and plasticity support from the underlying amorphous metal that suppress brittle spallation of the film.

Mechanisms that produce low friction and durability
1. Tribo‑oxidation under contact pressure and flash temperature
   - Mechanical action exposes fresh metal and creates local heating; oxygen reacts rapidly with active alloying elements in the metastable amorphous matrix, producing oxide species at the contact.
2. Mechanical mixing, comminution and compaction
   - Wear debris is comminuted to nanoscale and plastically consolidated into a dense tribofilm by the high contact pressures of cold‑sprayed, highly deformable coatings.
3. Selective oxidation and glass formation
   - Elements that form glassy or low‑shear oxides concentrate at the surface (e.g., B/Si → glassy borates/silicates; certain Mo/V oxides form layered low‑shear structures). Glassy oxides and hydrated borates provide low shear strength and accommodate sliding easily.
4. Formation of a cohesive, low‑shear sliding plane
   - Sliding is accommodated within the tribofilm (intragranular shear, intergranular sliding, or shear along layered oxide planes) rather than at high‑adhesion metal–metal asperity contacts, lowering friction and adhesion.
5. Transfer film formation
   - The tribofilm seeds a thin transfer layer on the counterface that further reduces adhesion and stabilizes friction.
6. Self‑healing / renewal
   - Continued wear produces new activated surfaces and debris; oxidative and mechanical processes rebuild the tribofilm, maintaining lubrication.
7. Structural support from amorphous substrate
   - The ductile, high‑free‑volume amorphous bulk beneath the tribofilm accommodates deformation, supplies fresh material, and reduces brittle cracking/delamination of the oxide layer.

Practical implications and control knobs
- Alloy chemistry: including elements that form lubricious glassy oxides or layered oxides (B, Si, Mo, V, some dopants) promotes low friction; iron/nickel alone tend to give less lubricious oxides.
- Environment: humidity and oxygen partial pressure affect formation of hydrated borates or hydroxylated glassy films (often beneficial).
- Contact conditions: enough pressure/temperature to induce tribo‑oxidation and comminution is required; too severe conditions can cause abrasive grinding or oxide breakdown.
- Coating microstructure: the as‑sprayed amorphous state (high free volume, lack of grain boundaries) accelerates oxide formation and supplies ductility to support an adherent tribofilm.

In short, the self‑lubrication arises not from a single chemical species but from a nanostructured, adherent tribo‑oxide/compacted debris film with low internal shear strength, formed and continuously regenerated by tribo‑oxidation and mechanical consolidation of wear debris on the deformable amorphous substrate.

Solid-state supersonic deposition (e.g., cold/kinetic spray) differs fundamentally from fusion thermal spray (plasma, flame, HVOF, detonation) because the feedstock particles remain solid and bond by high‑velocity plastic deformation rather than by melting and re‑solidification. Primary advantages:

- Minimal thermal damage / low heat input  
  - Substrate and powder stay well below melting, so there is a very small heat‑affected zone. Suitable for heat‑sensitive substrates (polymers, composites, thin sections) and for in‑service repair with minimal distortion.

- Preservation of feedstock chemistry and microstructure  
  - No melting means volatile and oxidation‑sensitive elements are retained (e.g., Al, Cu, Ti) and metastable or nanostructured powders are not coarsened or decomposed.

- Low oxidation and low contamination  
  - Limited oxidation during deposition → cleaner metal‑metal interfaces, higher electrical and thermal conductivity, and improved corrosion behavior relative to fusion sprays which form oxide phases in-flight and in the splat layer.

- Dense, high‑cohesion deposits with high mechanical properties  
  - Bonding via severe plastic deformation produces strong particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces, often yielding dense coatings with low porosity and high cohesive and adhesive strength. Resulting coatings commonly exhibit work‑hardening and favorable compressive residual stresses that improve wear and fatigue life.

- Ability to deposit high‑melting or oxidation‑prone materials  
  - Refractory metals and reactive alloys that are difficult to melt or that form deleterious phases on melting can be deposited in the solid state.

- High deposition efficiency and less overspray (for many powders)  
  - Because particles are not required to melt, more of the input powder can be incorporated into the coating, reducing material waste.

- Improved functional properties for specific applications  
  - Examples: near‑bulk electrical conductivity for Cu coatings, retention of ductility for Al repairs, and reduced oxide content for corrosion‑resistant layers.

In short: solid‑state supersonic methods produce dense, mechanically robust, low‑oxidation coatings while minimizing thermal effects on both powder and substrate—advantages that enable coating/repair of sensitive materials and retention of feedstock properties that fusion sprays typically alter.

Short answer
- Increasing carbon content in martensitic steels raises the as‑quenched hardness of the martensite because carbon in supersaturated martensite (a) produces large lattice distortion (increased tetragonality) and (b) strengthens by a solid‑solution / dislocation interaction mechanism.  
- However, higher C also lowers the martensite start (Ms) and finish (Mf) temperatures, increasing the risk of retained austenite (which reduces bulk hardness) and of embrittlement — so the net hardness depends on heat‑treatment/cooling history and carbide formation.

How it works (concise technical points)
1. Lattice and solid‑solution strengthening
   - Carbon occupies octahedral interstices in martensite, increasing c/a tetragonality and producing strong lattice strain fields. That raises yield strength and hardness of the martensitic matrix.

2. Effect on transformation temperatures and retained austenite
   - Carbon strongly depresses Ms/Mf (empirically Ms ≈ 539 − 423·C (wt%) + …), so higher C makes full martensitic transformation harder to achieve on cooling. Any retained austenite softens the bulk material and lowers hardness compared with fully transformed martensite.

3. Morphology and dislocation structure
   - Higher C tends to produce thinner, harder martensite plates (or more highly tetragonal martensite) and can increase dislocation density introduced on transformation, both increasing hardness.

4. Carbide formation and tempering behaviour
   - On tempering, carbon can precipitate as transition carbides or cementite. Higher C gives higher peak hardness in the as‑quenched condition but also greater hardness drop on tempering due to carbide formation and recovery of dislocations. Carbide distribution affects wear/resistance.

5. Practical limits / tradeoffs
   - Below ~0.2–0.3 wt% C you get lower hardness martensite (better ductility). Between ~0.3–0.6 wt% C martensite hardness rises significantly and is useful for many high‑strength steels. Above ~0.6–1.0 wt% C you can achieve very high as‑quenched hardness but you increase retained austenite risk, brittleness, and poor impact/deformation behavior.
   - For powders (atomized, small particles), very high cooling rates can suppress retained austenite so the hardness increase with C may be realized, but high‑C powders are more brittle (particle fracture on impact) and more difficult to cold‑spray deposit.

Practical implication for cold‑spray or powder processing
- Higher carbon powder → higher intrinsic hardness and wear resistance of deposits but reduced plasticity and worse bonding by cold deformation; increased risk of particle cracking. Often a compromise carbon level or post‑deposition heat treatment (to relieve stresses or transform retained phases) is used.

Bottom line
Carbon increases martensitic hardness through lattice distortion and strengthening, but because it lowers Ms/Mf and changes tempering/carbide behaviour, the realized hardness depends strongly on transformation completeness and heat treatment. Choose carbon to balance hardness, retained austenite risk and ductility for your processing route.

Primarily they act as high‑aspect‑ratio, lamellar barrier particles that dramatically increase the tortuosity of diffusion paths for water, oxygen and aggressive ions (Cl–). In practice that means:

- Impermeability of the individual sheets: defect‑free graphene is essentially impermeable to gases/ions; graphene oxide (GO) is less perfect but still blocks direct through‑paths.
- Tortuosity effect: dispersed, plate‑like graphene/GO aligned roughly parallel to the substrate forces corrosive species to follow a long, zig‑zag path around flakes, greatly reducing the effective diffusion coefficient (Nielsen‑type behavior).
- Pore‑filling and reduced free volume: GO’s functional groups improve wetting and bonding to the polymer/ceramic matrix, sealing microvoids and microcracks and lowering water uptake.
- Synergistic mechanical effects: flakes stiffen the matrix and pin crack propagation, which helps keep the barrier intact.

Practical caveats: effectiveness depends on dispersion, orientation, aspect ratio and loading (low loading of well‑dispersed, aligned flakes is most efficient). Also electrically conductive graphene networks can create galvanic risks at the metal interface unless insulated or chemically passivated (GO or rGO treatments are commonly used to manage this).

Archard’s wear law (for adhesive/abrasive sliding) is usually written

V = (K · L · s) / H

where V is wear volume, K is a dimensionless wear coefficient, L is the normal load, s is sliding distance, and H is the hardness of the softer contacting material.  

Thus wear volume is inversely proportional to the softer material’s hardness: increasing H reduces V (e.g., doubling H halves V for the same K, L and s). Note the caveat that K can change with materials, environment and wear mechanism, so real-world behavior may deviate from the ideal 1/H scaling.

Short answer
Cold spray is a solid‑state, high‑velocity impact process. Unlike conventional thermal spray (plasma, HVOF, flame, arc), particles are not melted; they bond by extreme plastic deformation and jetting on impact rather than by splat solidification.

Key distinguishing points
- Energy source and particle state
  - Cold spray: kinetic energy from a supersonic gas jet (De Laval nozzle). Particles remain solid (below melting).
  - Thermal spray: thermal energy melts or partially melts feedstock; molten droplets strike and solidify as splats.

- Bonding mechanism
  - Cold spray: bonding via high‑strain-rate plastic deformation, adiabatic shear, interfacial jetting and metal‑to‑metal contact (cold welding). Requires particle velocity above a material‑dependent critical velocity.
  - Thermal spray: bonding by mechanical interlocking and metallurgical contact after solidification of molten droplets.

- Process parameters (typical)
  - Particle velocities: cold spray ~300–1200 m/s (depends on gas, pressure, nozzle); thermal sprays typically produce lower or comparable velocities but with molten particles (plasma/HVOF droplet speeds vary widely).
  - Gas and temperature: cold spray uses heated/compressed N2 or He (gas temps often 400–1000 °C) but particle temp stays below melting; plasma and HVOF use much higher temperatures that melt the feedstock.

- Thermal input and substrate effects
  - Cold spray: low heat input to substrate — minimal dilution, low metallurgical changes, suitable for heat‑sensitive substrates and for joining dissimilar metals.
  - Thermal spray: high local thermal input, possible oxidation, phase transformations, tensile residual stresses, and substrate heating.

- Microstructure and chemistry
  - Cold spray: retains starting microstructure and chemistry, little oxidation of particles, dense coatings with low porosity and strong bulk‑like properties.
  - Thermal spray: rapid solidification microstructures, oxides, possible phase changes, and higher porosity/interlamellar oxides depending on process.

- Material and application limitations
  - Cold spray: best for ductile metals (Cu, Al, Ni, Ti alloys, some steels); brittle ceramics are difficult to deposit unless as composites with a ductile binder; needs velocity above critical value—hard materials may require He or very high pressures.
  - Thermal spray: can deposit a wider range of materials including ceramics, cermets, and polymers (by melting) but with different tradeoffs.

Practical implications
- Advantages of cold spray: low oxidation, high retained mechanical properties, strong cohesive strength, low thermal damage to substrate, good for repair and additive manufacturing of metals, and for joining dissimilar metals.
- Tradeoffs: equipment cost (especially when using helium/high pressures), sensitivity to particle size/ductility and process parameters, and limited pure‑ceramic deposition.

In short: cold spray replaces melting and splat formation with high‑velocity solid‑state impact bonding — a fundamentally different bonding mechanism that gives low thermal input and different material possibilities and limitations compared with conventional thermal spray.

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) can raise the hardness of ceramic nanocomposites by several complementary nanoscale mechanisms. Key effects are:

- Load transfer and elastic stiffening: stiff, high-modulus CNTs that are well bonded to the ceramic matrix pick up part of the applied load under indentation. This increases the composite effective modulus and local resistance to deformation.

- Crack bridging and arresting: CNTs that span crack faces bridge and carry tensile stress across cracks, reducing crack opening and slowing crack growth beneath an indenter. By impeding the formation and growth of microcracks, the material resists the brittle fracture processes that otherwise reduce apparent hardness.

- Crack deflection and tortuosity: CNTs at grain boundaries or within grains force cracks to change direction (deflect, branch, or bifurcate). This increases fracture surface area and the energy needed to propagate cracks, reducing indent-induced damage.

- Pull-out and frictional energy dissipation: when CNTs debond and pull out during cracking or indentation, frictional sliding dissipates energy and limits crack propagation. The work required for pull-out increases effective resistance to penetration.

- Grain-growth inhibition and microstructure refinement: CNTs located at grain boundaries pin grain growth during sintering, producing finer-grained ceramics. Smaller grains often improve hardness by reducing the size of flaw-prone regions and increasing the constraint against local deformation.

- Residual compressive stresses / CTE mismatch: differences in thermal expansion between CNTs and the ceramic can generate compressive residual stresses in the matrix around CNTs after cooling from sintering. Compressive fields hinder crack opening under load and raise apparent indentation resistance.

- Improved densification (when well dispersed): well-dispersed CNTs and optimized sintering (e.g., spark plasma sintering) can promote more uniform densification and reduce porosity, increasing hardness. Conversely, CNT agglomeration usually introduces pores and weak zones that lower hardness.

Important practical dependencies:
- Interface quality dominates performance: strong but not overly brittle CNT–matrix bonding yields good load transfer and bridging; too-weak bonding gives easy pull-out without load share, too-strong or chemically reacted interfaces can embrittle or destroy CNTs.
- CNT dispersion, aspect ratio and orientation: uniform dispersion and high aspect ratio maximize bridging and grain pinning; alignment can make properties anisotropic.
- Processing temperature/chemistry: high-temperature sintering can damage CNTs or form carbides/graphitic shells, changing the mechanisms.
- Optimal CNT content is low (typically < a few wt%): small additions give benefit; higher loadings risk agglomeration, porosity and reduced hardness.

In short, CNTs enhance ceramic hardness mainly by limiting indentation-induced cracking and microstructural damage through load sharing, crack-bridging/deflection/pull-out, grain refinement and improved densification — provided CNTs are well dispersed and the CNT–matrix interface and processing are properly controlled.

Short answer
- A larger spherical indenter produces a stiffer (steeper) elastic force–displacement response and pushes the elastic-to-plastic transition to larger depths and forces.  
- A smaller radius concentrates stress, produces higher contact pressures for the same depth, and causes plasticity (dislocation nucleation/yield) at smaller depths/forces.

Key continuum scalings (Hertz contact, rigid spherical indenter on elastic half‑space)
- Elastic F–δ relation: F = (4/3) E* √R · δ^(3/2). Thus at fixed δ the elastic force increases with √R; at fixed F the elastic δ decreases with R^(−1/3).  
- Peak contact pressure (center): p0 = (2 E*/π) √(δ/R) ∝ 1/√R (for fixed δ). So smaller R → larger p0.  
- If yielding occurs when p0 reaches a critical p_y, the critical indentation depth scales as δ_y ∝ R (δ_y = (π^2 p_y^2 R)/(4 E*^2)), and the critical force scales as F_y ∝ R^2. So larger R gives proportionally larger δ_y and much larger F_y.

Important caveats for nanoparticles
- Geometry limits: when the indenter radius is comparable to or larger than the particle radius, the effective contact radius is set by the two‑sphere geometry (1/R_eff = 1/R_ind + 1/R_particle) and continuum Hertz solutions must be adjusted. If the indenter is much larger than the particle the contact approaches a “flat punch on a finite object” problem.  
- Finite-size and surface effects: nanoparticles often show higher yield strength (size‑dependent strengthening), surface stresses, adhesive forces (JKR/DMT regimes) and atomistic discreteness — these modify or delay onset of continuum plasticity and can violate the simple Hertz/yield scalings.  
- Boundary/support conditions (supported vs free particle) strongly affect the elastic response and the onset of plasticity.

Practical implication
- Use larger-radius spherical indenters to probe bulk-like elastic stiffness and extend the elastic regime; use small-radius spheres to probe local strength, dislocation nucleation and surface-dominated plasticity, keeping in mind that continuum predictions may break down for very small particles/indenters.

Cold spray is a solid‑state process — particles remain below their melting point — so bonding must come from purely mechanical and metallurgical processes activated by very high‑velocity impact. The key mechanisms are:

- Severe plastic deformation and high contact pressure  
  - Particles hitting the substrate (or previously deposited particles) at supersonic speeds undergo extreme plastic flow. Local pressures well above the yield strength force intimate metal‑to‑metal contact and generate very high strain rates (typically 10^5–10^9 s^-1). This plastic flow creates a large, fresh contact area and local lattice distortion that promotes bonding.

- Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) and jetting  
  - Localized shear at the impact periphery can soften the material adiabatically (strain‑rate heating faster than heat conduction), producing shear instabilities and a lateral “jet” of material. Jetting expels surface oxides/contaminants and produces clean, fresh metal surfaces that collide at high pressure — a necessary condition for metallic bonding.

- Oxide/discontinuity removal and mechanical mixing  
  - Impact stresses fracture, delaminate, and extrude oxide layers or adsorbates out of the interface. The combination of jetting and mechanical mixing yields oxide‑free contact spots and interfacial locking by plastically deformed fragments.

- Dynamic recrystallization, grain refinement and dislocation structures  
  - The severe deformation produces extreme dislocation densities and often dynamic recrystallization in a very thin interfacial layer, producing ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains. This increases boundary area, local diffusivity, and the propensity for metallurgical bonding (lowers the barrier to atomic contact and short‑range diffusion).

- Atomic/metallic bonding under high contact pressure  
  - Once oxides are removed and surfaces are pressed into intimate contact, metallic bonds form across the interface (similar in principle to solid‑state welding). Local temperature rises (from deformation) can accelerate recovery/recrystallization and short‑range diffusion but remain well below melting.

- Mechanical interlocking and residual stresses  
  - Large plastic deformation produces topographical interlocking between particle and substrate, plus residual compressive stresses that help cohesion and coating consolidation.

Practical consequences: successful bonding requires exceeding a material‑specific critical particle velocity (depends on material hardness, temperature, particle size, gas, nozzle, substrate condition). In short, cold spray bonds by extreme, localized plasticity and oxide removal (jetting/ASI) that create clean, highly deformed surfaces which form metallurgical bonds without melting.

Short answer
Dynamic recrystallization (DRX) and the resulting grain refinement are central microstructural processes in solid‑state additive manufacturing (cold spray, friction‑stir deposition/FSAM, high‑strain impact methods). They convert severe, localized plastic deformation and heat into fine, often equiaxed, strain‑free grains at particle interfaces or in the stirred zone. The net effect is stronger, harder, and usually more cohesive deposits with altered ductility, toughness, texture, residual stress state and anisotropy — but the details depend on material, DRX mode, and process conditions.

Key mechanisms
- Driving forces: very high local strain, strain rate and (often) short localized heating during deposition drive dislocation accumulation and recovery, then nucleation/growth (discontinuous DRX, DDRX) or progressive subgrain rotation into high‑angle grains (continuous DRX, CDRX).  
- Process dependence: cold spray produces severe shear/adiabatic heating at particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces that promotes localized DRX and ultrafine/nanocrystalline interfacial layers. Friction‑stir / friction‑based deposition produces bulk DRX in the stirred zone due to combined thermomechanical action.  
- Microstructural signatures: very small grain size (submicron → nanoscale in interfacial layers), high fraction of high‑angle grain boundaries, reduced dislocation density inside recrystallized grains, weakened or randomized texture relative to the starting material.

How microstructure changes influence mechanical properties
- Strength and hardness: primary increase via Hall–Petch grain‑boundary strengthening (σy ≈ σ0 + k d−1/2) plus retained dislocation and interface strengthening. Grain refinement produced by DRX commonly raises yield strength and microhardness substantially versus coarse‑grained or merely cold‑worked material.  
- Ductility and toughness: can go either way. Fine, equiaxed recrystallized grains often improve uniform elongation and toughness because deformation is more homogeneous and large work‑hardening gradients are reduced. However, if strengthening is dominated by very high dislocation density or if grain boundaries are sites for decohesion/oxidic films or porosity, ductility and fatigue resistance can be degraded.  
- Fatigue: fine, well bonded, recrystallized interfaces generally improve fatigue performance by removing weak mechanical bonds and stress concentrators; conversely, residual porosity/oxides at interfaces can still dominate crack initiation.  
- Residual stress & anisotropy: DRX relaxes some work hardening and residual stresses and tends to reduce strong extrusion/rolling textures — lowering anisotropy in mechanical response. But layered deposition can still lead to macro‑scale heterogeneities in grain size and properties.  
- Thermal stability: ultrafine grains from severe DRX may coarsen on subsequent heat exposure; alloy chemistry (solute, precipitates) controls stability.

Practical trade‑offs and controls
- Tuning: the extent of DRX and grain refinement is controlled by impact/strain rate, local temperature, cumulative strain, and base/alloy composition (stacking‑fault energy, precipitates). Optimize for the desired balance of strength vs ductility and to obtain good metallurgical bonding.  
- Limitations: DRX cannot fix defects caused by surface oxides, poorly bonded particles, or trapped porosity — interfacial chemistry still matters. Over‑refinement without cohesion or with unstable grain boundaries can hurt high‑temperature or cyclic properties.  
- Characterization: EBSD (grain size / HAGB fraction / texture), TEM (nanoscale structure), microhardness mapping, tensile and fatigue tests, and residual stress measurements are used to assess DRX effects.

Bottom line
DRX-driven grain refinement in solid‑state AM is a powerful route to produce high‑strength, well‑bonded metallic deposits with modified toughness and reduced texture/anistropy. The net property outcome is set by the balance of Hall‑Petch strengthening, retained/dislocated substructure, interfacial chemistry, and the thermal/mechanical history — so process parameters and alloy design must be tailored to exploit DRX beneficially.

Key XRD pattern features that indicate residual stresses and microstrain in cold‑spray coatings, and their causes:

1. Peak shifts (systematic shift of peak positions)
   - What you see: all Bragg peaks shifted to higher or lower 2θ compared with stress‑free reference.
   - Interpretation: uniform (macro) elastic strain/residual stress. Compressively strained lattice → interplanar spacing d decreases → peaks shift to higher 2θ; tensile strain → d increases → peaks shift to lower 2θ.
   - Cause in cold spray: extensive particle peening and constrained plastic deformation during high‑velocity impact produce macroscopic compressive or tensile residual stresses (often compressive near impact interfaces).

2. Peak broadening (increased FWHM)
   - What you see: peaks are wider than those of the reference material.
   - Interpretation: microstrain (distribution of lattice spacings) and/or reduced coherent domain (crystallite) size. Microstrain broadening increases with angle (roughly ∝ tanθ), whereas size broadening scales like 1/cosθ.
   - Cause in cold spray: very high dislocation densities, severe plastic deformation, subgrain and nanocrystalline formation, and lattice distortion from collisions and adiabatic shear.

3. Anisotropic broadening and hkl‑dependent effects
   - What you see: some reflections broaden or shift more than others; peak shapes vary with hkl.
   - Interpretation: strain anisotropy (directional elastic/plastic strains) and dislocation contrast (different dislocation types/arrays produce different broadening for different lattice planes).
   - Cause in cold spray: preferential deformation directions, crystallographic texture from particle deformation, and non‑uniform dislocation structures.

4. Peak asymmetry, tails, and splitting
   - What you see: asymmetric peaks with low/high 2θ tails, shoulders, or apparent double peaks.
   - Interpretation: strain gradients, coexistence of differently strained regions/phases, or overlapping contributions from coating and substrate.
   - Cause in cold spray: steep strain gradients across the coating thickness (near interface vs surface), mixed populations of heavily deformed and less‑deformed grains, or partial retained/formed phases.

5. Increased diffuse background and loss of intensity
   - What you see: raised background or lower peak intensity.
   - Interpretation: increased defect concentration, amorphous content, or very small crystallites.
   - Cause: severe disorder and possible amorphization at impact sites.

How to distinguish and quantify
- Sin2ψ method (d vs sin2ψ) isolates macrostress (elastic strain) by measuring d‑spacing vs tilt.
- Williamson–Hall or size–strain plots separate size and strain broadening (βcosθ vs sinθ or tanθ).
- Rietveld or whole‑pattern line‑profile analysis (Warren–Averbach, dislocation models) can quantify microstrain, crystallite size and dislocation density, and account for anisotropic broadening and contrast factors.

Summary: In cold spray coatings expect peak shifts (macrostress), increased and anisotropic peak broadening (microstrain, small domains, dislocations), asymmetry/splitting (strain gradients/multiple strain states) and increased background (disorder). These arise from the extreme, high‑rate plastic deformation, high dislocation densities, grain refinement and constrained peening produced during particle impact.

Short answer: because larger PREP droplets are harder for surface tension to fully round and to freeze in as spheres — they cool more slowly, experience larger aerodynamic and collisional stresses, oscillate/ deform for longer, and are more prone to oxide-skin or coalescence effects. Those factors increase with diameter so sphericity falls as powder size increases.

Key physical reasons (with simple scaling/intuition):

- Surface-tension versus aerodynamic forces (Weber number). The Weber number We = ρ_g V^2 d / σ rises linearly with particle diameter d. Larger droplets therefore suffer relatively stronger aerodynamic deformation and breakup/flattening that surface tension cannot fully remove before solidification.

- Solidification (cooling) time grows rapidly with size. Thermal diffusion time τ_c ~ d^2/α (α = thermal diffusivity), so large droplets remain liquid much longer and thus have more time to be deformed, collide, or develop skin layers before freezing.

- Shape relaxation (capillary re-spherization) slows with size. The natural capillary relaxation/oscillation time scales like τ_cap ~ (ρ d^3/σ)1/2 (or otherwise grows strongly with d). For large d the relaxation is slow compared with deformation or the residence time, so perturbations do not damp out before freeze-in.

- Oscillations and viscous damping. Large molten droplets are more susceptible to low-frequency oscillations and their viscous damping is less effective per unit perturbation; that lets lobes and indentations persist.

- Oxide/solid skin and coalescence. HEA chemistry can form surface oxide or oxide/solid skins that locally freeze shape irregularities. Larger droplets have longer exposure and higher probability of partial solidification/skin formation or collisions/coalescence with satellites, producing non-spherical shapes.

In PREP specifically, droplets are ejected at high velocity from a rotating electrode into a gas stream. Increasing d increases We and τ_c while decreasing the ability of capillarity to restore roundness before solidification or further aerodynamic/collision disturbance — hence sphericity decreases with increasing powder size.

Short answer: plastic strain is much higher at particle–particle interfaces than in particle interiors. Interfaces are the zones of severe, highly localized plastic deformation (bonding jets, shear bands, adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization), while particle cores usually undergo little to moderate plasticity.

Why: during impact most deformation is concentrated at the contact/flange region where jetting and intense shear occur. Those regions accumulate very high dislocation densities, grain refinement and strain localization; the particle interior mainly transmits load and is comparatively undeformed.

Evidence and indicators:
- FEM of single‑particle impacts and multi‑particle builds show peak equivalent plastic strains at contact zones far exceeding those in the interior.
- EBSD (high KAM and misorientation) and TEM (very high dislocation density, ultrafine grains) are observed at interfaces but not in particle cores.
- Nanoindentation/hardness maps show hardness peaks at interfaces.

Typical magnitude and scale: exact numbers depend on material, particle size, and impact velocity, but interface strains are commonly an order of magnitude (or more) greater than interior strains. In practical terms interiors often show only modest plastic strains, whereas interface zones exhibit severe plastic strains sufficient to produce ultrafine grains and very high local hardness.

Implication: bonding, mechanical properties (strength, wear, fatigue) and post‑deposit heat treatment behavior are controlled by these highly strained interface regions.

Definition (brief)
- Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) is a dynamic localization phenomenon in which intense, high-rate plastic deformation produces so much heat in a narrow zone that thermal softening outpaces strain hardening and the zone localizes into a thin shear band. “Adiabatic” means heat generated by plastic work cannot be removed fast enough, so the local temperature rises rapidly.

Physical mechanism and instability criterion
- Under very high strain rates the temperature rise per unit strain is large (Ṫ ≈ βσ ε̇/ρc, where β is the Taylor–Quinney factor). If the material’s thermal softening (∂σ/∂T) combined with the temperature rise with strain causes a net drop in flow stress faster than work hardening increases it, localization occurs. A compact form of the instability condition is:
  (∂σ/∂ε)_T + (∂σ/∂T)·(dT/dε) < 0.
- Constitutive laws used in simulations (e.g. Johnson–Cook) capture this competition among strain hardening, strain-rate hardening, and thermal softening.
- Typical localization strain rates in impact problems are very large (often 10^5–10^8 s^-1) and shear-band thicknesses are microns or sub-microns.

Role in cold spray bonding
- Cold spray deposits solid metallic particles onto a substrate by high-velocity impact. Bonding requires intimate metal–metal contact and disruption/removal of surface oxides.
- ASI contributes to bonding by:
  1. Producing highly localized plastic flow and very high local temperatures at the particle–substrate interface, which promotes thermal softening and sometimes dynamic recrystallization or local melting-like behavior in a narrow band.
  2. Driving interfacial jetting: severe localized shear ejects surface material (including oxides) from the impact periphery, exposing fresh metal and creating mechanically interlocked contact.
  3. Creating ultrafine-grained or heavily deformed zones that enhance diffusivity and metallurgical bonding across the interface.
- For many metallic systems (especially harder alloys and high-velocity impacts) the onset of ASI (or at least very strong localized shear and jetting that it facilitates) is a primary mechanism enabling a strong bond. The process has a practical “critical velocity” below which ASI/jetting does not occur and bonding is poor.

Caveats and limits
- ASI is not strictly required for all cold-spray bonding: very ductile, low-strength metals can bond by widespread plastic deformation without a classic adiabatic shear band. Conversely, excessive localization can cause particle fragmentation or brittle failure in some alloys.
- Whether ASI forms depends on impact velocity, particle/substrate material properties (hardness, thermal conductivity, work-hardening, ∂σ/∂T), oxide state, particle size, and initial temperature.

Practical implications
- To promote bonding via ASI and jetting, cold spray parameters are tuned to reach or exceed the material’s critical velocity (gas temperature, pressure, nozzle design, particle size). Preheating or using softer alloys can lower the required impact energy.
- Understanding ASI helps in predicting deposition windows, microstructural evolution (ultrafine grains in shear bands), and avoiding detrimental particle fragmentation.

Summary
- ASI is a high-rate, thermally driven localization of plastic deformation that, in cold spray, facilitates oxide removal, localized softening/flow and jetting at the contact, and formation of metallurgical bonds. It is a dominant bonding mechanism for many materials at sufficiently high impact velocities, but not the only possible bonding route.

Both changes increase hardness in cold‑sprayed metallic coatings, by two complementary strengthening mechanisms:

- Grain/crystallite‑size reduction — grain‑boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch): σy = σ0 + k·d^(−1/2). Smaller crystallites raise the barrier to dislocation motion, so hardness/strength increases as d decreases (until very small nanocrystalline sizes where inverse Hall–Petch behavior can occur).

- Higher dislocation density — forest/Taylor hardening: Δσ ≈ α G b √ρ. A higher ρ produces more dislocation–dislocation interactions and stronger impediment to glide, increasing yield strength and hardness (typical SPD/impact dislocation densities in cold spray can give tens–hundreds of MPa of extra strengthening).

Practical caveats: the net hardening can saturate, and thermal recovery or post‑deposition annealing will reduce dislocation density and grain refinement (thus lowering hardness). But in the as‑sprayed state, reduced crystallite size plus increased dislocation density → higher hardness.

Short answer: because the top of the deposit is the least mechanically confined and least re-compacted by subsequent impacts, so impacting particles there undergo less intense plastic flow, jetting and pore-collapse than particles that hit the substrate or buried layers. That combination leaves more open/connected porosity at the free surface.

Key mechanisms (concise, technical):

- Reduced confinement and lower hydrostatic pressure at the free surface. Impacts on a rigid substrate (or on previously compacted material) generate high reflected stress waves and large compressive hydrostatic pressures that drive severe plastic flow, adiabatic-shear/jetting and collapse of voids. Impacts at the free surface lack that rigid backing, so plastic flow is less effective at closing pores.

- Fewer subsequent “hammering”/peening events. Particles deposited early and in subsurface layers are repeatedly impacted and re-compacted by later particles. The topmost layer receives fewer high-energy re-compaction impacts, so initial porosity is preserved.

- Increased particle rebound, splashing and shadowing. With less confinement and less effective bonding at the unconstrained surface, partial rebounds or splashing of particles are more likely to produce gaps or poorly bonded interfaces near the free surface.

- Surface contamination and oxide films. Oxides, adsorbates or loosely attached debris on the growing free surface reduce local metal-to-metal contact and bonding quality, promoting open pores near the surface.

- Residual stress state. Tensile or lower compressive residual stresses near the free surface can open existing micro-voids that would be closed under compressive conditions nearer the substrate.

Practical consequence: cold-sprayed coatings typically show a densification gradient (densest near the substrate, more porous at the top). Common mitigation measures are higher particle velocity, substrate/preheat, peening or heat-treatment/forging after spraying, or applying additional high-energy over-sprays to recompact the surface.

Short answer: cold spray is a solid‑state, high‑velocity process — particles remain below their melting point and bond by extreme plastic deformation on impact (adiabatic shear, jetting and intimate metallic contact). Conventional thermal sprays heat particles to molten or semi‑molten states and rely on splat formation and solidification (mechanical anchoring plus splat‑to‑splat metallurgical/oxidic bonding).

Key distinctions

- Particle heating
  - Cold spray: particles are accelerated in a supersonic gas jet but remain in the solid state (significantly below melting temperature). Gas temperatures are elevated but not high enough to melt feedstock. Typical particle velocities are high (hundreds to >1,000 m/s).
  - Thermal spray (plasma, HVOF, flame, wire‑arc): feedstock particles are heated to near or above the melting point (fully or partially molten) before impact. Particle temperatures are high and solidification occurs on the substrate; particle velocities are generally lower (process dependent).

- Adhesion/bonding mechanism
  - Cold spray: bonding is mechanical/metallic via severe plastic deformation at impact — localized adiabatic shear, material jetting that removes surface oxides, intimate metal‑to‑metal contact, dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement at the interface. Result: dense, low‑oxide, low thermal‑damage deposits with high cohesive/bond strengths for ductile metals.
  - Thermal spray: molten droplets flatten into splats, then solidify to form a lamellar (splat) microstructure. Adhesion is by splat interlocking, some metallurgical bonding where wetting/chemical reactions allow, and often by mechanical anchoring; splat interfaces commonly contain oxides and pores, and deposits exhibit higher thermal alteration and residual stresses.

Implications: cold spray is preferred for ductile metals when minimal oxidation and low heat input are required; thermal spray is required when depositing ceramics or when metallurgical bonding from melting is acceptable or needed.

Short answer
Surface oxides strongly hinder metallurgical bonding in cold spray because they prevent direct metallic contact and act as hard, brittle interlayers that are difficult to remove at solid-state impact conditions. Successful bonding therefore depends on fracturing/expelling or otherwise eliminating those oxides during the high‑strain, high‑strain‑rate impact event.

Key effects and mechanisms
- Barrier to true metal–metal contact: a continuous oxide film (even a few nanometres thick) prevents intimate atomic contact and metallurgical bonding; cold spray is solid‑state so oxides are not melted away.
- Increased critical velocity: oxides raise the particle critical velocity required for bonding because extra impact energy is needed to fracture/expel the film and produce fresh metal contact.
- Mechanical behavior of the oxide controls outcome:
  - Hard, brittle oxides (Al2O3, TiO2, Cr2O3) tend to crack and fragment; if fragments are not expelled they form an interfacial oxide layer that weakens the bond.
  - Ductile or poorly adherent oxides are easier to disrupt/flow away, so bonding is less impeded.
- Interfacial jetting and adiabatic shear localization: at sufficiently high impact velocity and localized plastic strain, a metal jet forms and can sweep oxide fragments out of the interface exposing fresh metal — this is the primary route to metallurgical bonding in cold spray.
- Entrapment/contamination: if oxides are not fully expelled they become oxide-rich stringers or continuous films at particle–particle or particle–substrate interfaces, increasing porosity, reducing cohesive strength, electrical/thermal conductivity and corrosion resistance.
- Dependence on material and processing: the effect scales with oxide thickness, adhesion and toughness, particle velocity, particle temperature/preheat, particle size and substrate ductility. For example, the native Al2O3 layer on Al (a few nm) significantly increases the required impact velocity; some metals (Cu) with very thin or more reducible oxides bond more readily.

Practical implications and mitigation
- Increase impact energy: higher gas pressure/temperature or gas choice to raise particle velocity and temperature helps fracture/expel oxides.
- Pre-treat powders or substrates: chemical etch, vacuum/controlled-atmosphere storage, reduction treatments, or thin metallic coatings can reduce oxide coverage.
- Use oxide‑tolerant process windows: co-deposit ductile feedstocks, select softer substrates or use peening strategies to promote jetting and oxide removal.
- Engineer powders: gas- or vacuum-atomized powders with minimal oxide, or powders with engineered surface layers that promote bonding.
- Post‑processing: heat treatments or localized plastic deformation can consolidate or heal residual oxide-rich interfaces, but are not a substitute for removing oxide at impact.

Bottom line
Surface oxides are a primary limitation to cold-spray metallurgical bonding. Bond formation requires either fracturing and ejection of the oxide during the impact (via jetting/adiabatic shear) or pre-removal/reduction of the oxide; failure to do so produces weak, oxide‑rich interfaces and poorer mechanical and functional properties.

Key characteristics of metallic glass (amorphous metal) that make it an effective reinforcement in composite coatings — including cold-spray and other solid‑state coating processes — are:

- Extremely high strength and hardness
  - Yield and compressive strengths approach theoretical limits for the alloy class, so small particles provide large load‑bearing and wear‑resistant reinforcement compared with conventional crystalline particles.

- Homogeneous, grain‑boundary‑free structure
  - No grains or grain‑boundary precipitates means isotropic mechanical properties and no micro‑galvanic corrosion sites; improves uniform corrosion and wear resistance of the composite.

- High elastic strain limit and localized shear response
  - Metallic glasses can store high elastic energy and deform by highly localized shear bands rather than conventional dislocation motion. That localized shear/softening can promote particle compaction, mechanical interlocking and adhesion during high‑strain processes (e.g., cold spray).

- High surface reactivity (metastable state / fresh surfaces)
  - Freshly fractured or deformed amorphous particles expose oxide‑poor, high‑energy surfaces that bond well to matrices, improving interfacial strength.

- Ability to produce nanocrystalline/dispersion strengthening by controlled devitrification
  - Under thermal or strain‑induced activation metallic glass reinforcements can partially crystallize to form very fine nanocrystals or hard precipitates, giving additional dispersion strengthening inside the coating.

- Excellent wear and abrasion resistance and good corrosion resistance
  - The combination of high hardness and a chemically homogeneous structure gives superior tribological and corrosive performance relative to many crystalline reinforcements.

- Tailorable chemistry and thermal stability
  - Compositions can be chosen to balance hardness, thermal stability (Tg, Tx), and toughness for the intended deposition/process window.

Practical caveats to consider
- Many bulk metallic glasses have limited macroscopic tensile ductility — for reinforcement use, small particles/flakes or controlled composition (more ductile glass) are preferred.
- Some compositions can devitrify under processing heat or high strain; that can be beneficial (nanocrystals) or detrimental (loss of amorphous properties) depending on goals.
- Particle size, morphology and surface condition are critical for embedding and bonding in cold‑spray or other coating processes.

In short: the combination of very high strength/hardness, homogeneous chemistry/structure, localized shearability and the potential for in‑service/processing nanostructuring are the main reasons metallic glass particles are effective reinforcements in composite coatings.

Because cold spray is a solid‑state, high‑strain, short‑time process rather than a melting/solidification process. The key reasons:

- No melting: particles are accelerated as solids (gas and particle temperatures remain well below the powder’s melting point), so there is no melt/solidification cycle that would cause solute partitioning, segregation, evaporation, or formation of melt‑derived phases.

- Very limited thermal exposure and diffusion: the particle temperatures and the contact time at elevated temperature are short (microseconds–milliseconds), so atomic diffusion distances are negligible. Thermal driving force and time for diffusion‑controlled phase transformations or new phase precipitation are therefore minimal.

- Bonding by severe plastic deformation and jetting: bonding occurs by mechanical interlocking, surface oxide disruption, adiabatic shear and local plastic flow (jetting) at the impact interface rather than by liquid mixing. This produces intimate metallic contact and sometimes dynamic recrystallization/strain‑induced microstructure refinement, but not large‑scale compositional change.

- Low oxidation/chemical reaction overall: removal of oxide films by jetting exposes fresh metal for bonding; because bulk temperatures are low and times short, extensive oxidation or chemical reaction with the substrate is uncommon.

Result: the deposited material usually keeps the original alloy chemistry and the same bulk phases present in the feedstock. (Exceptions can occur if very reactive powders, unusually high gas temperatures, or post‑deposition heat treatments produce reactions or phase changes.)

Short answer
Because effective cold-spray bonding requires the particle to undergo severe, high‑strain plastic deformation and to generate a high interfacial pressure/jet that strips oxides and produces intimate contact. If the substrate is too soft it absorbs the impact energy by indenting instead of forcing the particle to deform and jet, so you get embedding and poor metallurgical bonding. A harder (or at least not much softer) substrate forces the particle to plastically deform and produce the local shear/jetting needed for a sound bond.

Key points (physics)
- Energy partition: particle kinetic energy must be dissipated into plastic work at the particle–substrate interface. A hard substrate resists yielding, directing that energy into deformation of the particle and the interfacial zone. A soft substrate absorbs energy by deep indentation, reducing particle deformation and interfacial shear.
- Jetting and oxide removal: bonding in cold spray depends on a very localized, high‑strain-rate flow ("jetting") at the particle rim that expels surface oxides/contaminants and creates fresh metal–metal contact. Jetting requires strong resistance from the substrate; a soft substrate suppresses jet formation.
- Interfacial pressure and contact: higher local pressure and shear promote intimate contact and metallurgical bonding (adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization). If the substrate yields early, contact pressures are lower and the bond is weaker (mechanical anchoring or voids rather than a metallurgical bond).
- Practical balance: the substrate needn’t be infinitely harder—if it’s too hard relative to the particle, the particle may fracture or rebound. In practice you aim for substrate strength/hardness equal to or greater than the particle’s yield strength (or use preheating, interlayers, or other process adjustments when substrates are soft or particles brittle).

In brief: a harder substrate forces the particle to deform and produce the interfacial jetting and pressure that are central to cold‑spray metallurgical bonding; a too‑soft substrate prevents those mechanisms and gives poor bonding.

Primary challenge
- Graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) strongly agglomerate and restack because of high surface area, strong van der Waals attraction and their high aspect ratio, and they also wet poorly and bond weakly to most oxide ceramic surfaces. The result is inhomogeneous microstructure, porosity and poor load/strain transfer so the expected mechanical or functional benefits are lost.

How it is commonly addressed
- Convert to a more dispersible form (graphene oxide, GO) or chemically functionalize the platelets to add polar groups that improve wetting and surface charge.
- Use colloidal processing: disperse GNP/GO in water or an appropriate solvent with surfactants or polymeric dispersants (e.g., SDBS, sodium cholate, PVP), adjust pH/zeta potential, and apply controlled ultrasonication or three‑roll milling to deagglomerate.
- Mix the stable graphene suspension with the ceramic sol/slurry (or use sol–gel/in‑situ routes), then remove solvent (freeze‑dry, spray‑dry) and densify (SPS, hot pressing) with any required thermal reduction of GO.
- Optionally employ silane coupling agents or covalent grafting to improve interfacial bonding.

Notes/tradeoffs
- GO and aggressive milling give better dispersion but can damage the graphene structure or require reduction steps that may not fully restore pristine properties; processing parameters must balance dispersion versus platelet integrity.

Bulk metallic glasses (BMGs) are metallic alloys that solidify with an amorphous (non‑crystalline) atomic structure. That single fact gives them a set of distinctive and technically useful properties:

- Extremely high strength and hardness: yield strengths often in the 1–2 GPa range and hardness well above equivalent crystalline alloys (high strength-to-weight ratio).  
- Large elastic strain limit: recoverable elastic strains up to ~1–2% (much higher than conventional metals), enabling high elastic energy storage and spring applications.  
- Isotropic mechanical and physical properties: no grain boundaries or texture → uniform properties in all directions.  
- Excellent wear and abrasion resistance: high hardness and homogeneous microstructure reduce adhesive and abrasive wear.  
- Good corrosion resistance: chemical homogeneity and lack of galvanic microcells improve corrosion behavior versus many polycrystalline alloys.  
- Distinct thermoplastic formability: a glass transition and a supercooled liquid region (ΔTx) allow viscous forming, molding and precision replication of complex shapes at elevated temperature (thermoplastic forming similar to polymers).  
- Soft magnetic behavior (for Fe–, Co–, Ni–based BMGs): very low coercivity and high permeability because of absence of magnetocrystalline anisotropy.  
- Elevated electrical resistivity and reduced thermal conductivity relative to crystalline counterparts (useful in some electronic/thermal applications).  
- Size/processing sensitivity: glass formation requires sufficiently fast cooling or favorable composition, so achievable sample thickness (casting size) depends on composition (critical casting thickness).  
- Characteristic deformation mode and limited tensile ductility at room temperature: plasticity tends to localize into narrow shear bands, which can lead to brittle-like failure in many monolithic BMGs unless toughening strategies (composites, notches, structural design) are used.

In short: BMGs combine very high strength and hardness, large recoverable strain, isotropy and moldability (via the supercooled liquid region), plus useful magnetic and corrosion properties, but they require careful composition/processing and often need microstructural design to overcome shear‑band localization and limited macroscopic ductility.

Short answer
- Particle inertia controls how quickly a particle can respond to the accelerating gas. For a fixed gas flow (velocity field, temperature, pressure) heavier and/or larger particles accelerate more slowly, lag the gas flow, and therefore reach a lower velocity in the nozzle/jet than small light particles.

Key physics (equations and scaling)
- Particle motion is set by Newton’s 2nd law with aerodynamic drag:
  m dv_p/dt = F_drag ≈ 1/2 C_d ρ_g A_p (v_g − v_p)^2   (general/high‑Re compressible flow)
  or for very small Re: F_drag ≈ 3π μ d (v_g − v_p)   (Stokes).
- Particle mass m ∝ ρ_p d^3; cross‑section A_p ∝ d^2. That yields strong size dependence:
  - In the quadratic drag regime a characteristic acceleration (relaxation) length L_r ~ m/(C_d ρ_g A_p U_g) ∝ ρ_p d /(ρ_g U_g).
  - In the Stokes regime a characteristic relaxation time τ = ρ_p d^2/(18 μ) and length L_r = τ U_g ∝ ρ_p d^2 U_g/μ.
- Non‑dimensional measure: Stokes number Stk = τ U_g / L_char. If Stk << 1 the particle follows the gas (quickly reaches gas velocity); if Stk >> 1 it does not (large lag).

Consequences for cold spray
- Small particles (low inertia) rapidly approach gas velocity inside the nozzle/jet and so can reach near-gas speeds given sufficient nozzle length/residence time.
- Large/heavier particles retain more lag (lower velocity at nozzle exit) because they require longer acceleration distance/time to pick up gas momentum.
- Since kinetic energy ∝ m v^2, larger particles may still deliver high impact energy even at lower v, but cold spray requires exceeding a material‑dependent critical velocity — particle inertia can prevent some particles from reaching that critical speed.
- Practical levers: decrease particle diameter, increase gas pressure/temperature (raising gas velocity and density), use lighter/higher‑sound‑speed gases (He vs N2), or increase nozzle length/residence time to accelerate high‑inertia particles.

Brief practical rule of thumb
- Particle inertia scales ~ρ_p d^3; drag resisting acceleration scales ~ρ_g d^2 (quadratic) or μ d (Stokes). Therefore particle acceleration capability drops quickly as diameter and density increase — choose particle size, gas conditions, and nozzle geometry accordingly to ensure particles reach the critical impact velocity.

Short answer
Sintering in powder metallurgy (PM) is a thermally driven diffusion process that consolidates a compact by heating it (typically 0.5–0.9 Tm) so atoms migrate, necks grow, porosity closes and the part shrinks. What is often called “sintering” in cold spray is fundamentally different: initial bonding is created mechanically and dynamically at room or modest bulk temperature by high‑velocity impact (severe plastic deformation, adiabatic shear, oxide removal and jetting, dynamic recrystallization). Any true diffusion‑controlled densification in cold spray normally requires a separate heat treatment (or HIP) after deposition. In short: PM sintering = thermal diffusion consolidation; cold spray bonding = impact/strain consolidation + optional post‑heat sintering.

Detailed comparison (mechanisms, kinetics, consequences)

- Driving force
  - PM sintering: reduction of surface/interface energy via atomic diffusion driven by elevated bulk temperature.
  - Cold spray: initial bonding is driven by mechanical energy (kinetic → plastic work), local adiabatic heating and oxide disruption. Subsequent densification (if applied) is driven by diffusion during post‑heat treatment.

- Temperature and time
  - PM: long furnace holds at a significant fraction of melting temperature (0.5–0.9 Tm).
  - Cold spray: deposition at near room temperature to moderately elevated spray temperatures; any diffusion‑type sintering requires a separate anneal or HIP (much shorter or lower temperature sintering may occur locally at impact points, but overall bulk temperature is low).

- Primary bonding/densification mechanisms
  - PM: lattice diffusion, grain‑boundary diffusion, surface diffusion, viscous flow, and (with pressure) plastic flow → neck growth, pore shrinkage, macroscopic shrinkage and grain growth.
  - Cold spray: severe plastic deformation, adiabatic shear, particle jetting and oxide removal, dynamic recrystallization → immediate metallic contact and mechanical/ metallurgical bonding. Post‑anneal diffusion can then heal residual pores and strengthen interfaces.

- Kinetics and scale
  - PM: diffusion‑controlled, predictable neck growth with well‑known sintering stages (initial → intermediate → final).
  - Cold spray: bonding is essentially instantaneous at impact and localized; diffusion kinetics (if used afterward) are enhanced by high defect densities (dislocations, vacancies, ultrafine grains) so post‑anneal densification can be faster or occur at lower temperatures than starting powders, but macroscopic geometry is largely retained during deposition (little shrinkage).

- Microstructure and properties
  - PM: significant grain growth and homogenization during sintering unless controlled; measurable part shrinkage.
  - Cold spray: retains heavily deformed/ultrafine grains in as‑deposited state, high residual stresses; post‑heat treatment reduces defects, may coarsen grains but can close pores and relieve stress. Residual porosity in cold spray typically differs in morphology from PM (interparticle voids vs. sintering pores).

- Practical implications
  - PM is used to make near‑net shaped parts where shrinkage and densification are expected and accounted for.
  - Cold spray is used for coatings, repairs and additive manufacturing where low overall heat input, minimal oxidation, and shape retention are important. To approach PM densities, cold‑sprayed parts are often HIPed or annealed (post‑sintered) to achieve stronger metallurgical continuity and lower porosity.

When the term “sintering” appears in cold‑spray literature it usually refers to:
  - post‑deposition thermal treatments (anneal, HIP) that produce diffusion‑based consolidation, or
  - the localized, impact‑assisted atomic contact and short‑range diffusion enabled by high defect densities created during deposition (sometimes called “in‑situ” or “dynamic sintering” but not the same as classical PM sintering).

Bottom line
Cold spray provides solid‑state, impact‑driven bonding with limited intrinsic diffusion‑based densification; classical PM sintering is a thermal diffusion process that produces densification and shrinkage. To convert cold‑sprayed parts into fully dense, PM‑like components you normally need post‑deposition sintering/HIP or tailored thermal treatments that take advantage of the high defect density left by impact.

Primary bonding mechanisms in cold spray
- Severe plastic deformation / cold welding: High-velocity impacts produce very large plastic strains at the particle/substrate (and particle/particle) interface. Deformation breaks surface films locally, forces intimate metal-to-metal contact, and allows metallic bonding (solid-state cold welding).
- Adiabatic shear and jetting: Very high strain rates produce adiabatic shear at the impact front and a lateral “jet” that ejects oxides/contaminants from the interface, exposing fresh metal and increasing true contact area—essential for metallurgical bonding.
- Mechanical interlocking (micromechanical anchoring): Particles and substrate asperities mechanically engage (particles deform into undercuts, valleys, or around protrusions of previously-deposited particles), providing load-bearing mechanical attachment where metallic contact is incomplete.
- Metallurgical (diffusion/recrystallization) contributions: Localized high strain and temperature can produce ultrafine grains, dynamic recrystallization and short-range diffusion across clean interfaces—strengthening the bond over time even though bulk melting is absent.

How to enhance mechanical interlocking
- Increase substrate surface roughness and create undercut features:
  - Grit blasting (Al2O3, SiC), shot peening or laser/texturing to produce deeper asperities and undercuts that particles can wedge into.
  - Controlled patterned machining or laser ablation to create micro-pockets or grooves for anchoring.
- Use powder morphology and size control:
  - Angular or irregular particles provide better mechanical bite than highly spherical powders.
  - Bimodal or multimodal size distributions (large particles for anchoring, small to fill gaps) improve packing and mechanical interdigitation.
- Optimize particle kinetic energy and impact conditions:
  - Higher particle velocity and appropriate particle temperature increase particle plasticity and penetration into asperities, improving anchoring (but avoid velocities that cause excessive substrate erosion).
  - Normal (near-90°) impact angles maximize penetration into surface topography; oblique impacts tend to slide.
- Apply or tune bond coats / sacrificial interlayers:
  - A soft ductile bond coat (Cu, Al, soft Ni) or an engineered rough bond layer can be sprayed first to create a mechanically receptive surface for the principal material.
- Process sequencing and in-situ tactics:
  - Immediate spraying after surface preparation (to avoid oxide/contaminant re-deposition).
  - Multiple passes with alternating angles or peening passes to seat particles deeper into asperities.
- Powder/substrate material choices and hardness balance:
  - Select particle-substrate hardness combination so particles deform into asperities without simply crushing them away; excessively hard substrates can prevent embedding, excessively soft substrates may smear rather than form interlocks.

Trade-offs and notes
- Mechanical interlocking is most effective when combined with oxide removal and metallurgical contact; roughening alone cannot substitute for adequate impact energy and jetting/cleaning.
- Excessive roughness or overly aggressive blasting can introduce damage, reduce effective contact area, or create weak subsurface cracks—optimize roughness scale relative to particle size.

Cold spray bonds primarily by solid‑state plastic deformation: particles striking the substrate at high supersonic velocities undergo severe, high‑strain‑rate deformation and adiabatic shear that produces a localized jet and fractures/expels surface oxides. That jetting and deformation expose fresh metal, create intimate atomic contact (cold‑welding) and mechanical interlocking. Because there is no bulk melting and contact times are short, diffusion plays little role; the bond is driven by deformation‑induced metallurgical contact (and associated grain refinement) rather than fusion.

Short answer
During moderate-temperature annealing cold-sprayed metallic coatings undergo recovery, partial or full recrystallization and grain growth, interparticle diffusion and interface evolution, reduction of porosity and residual stresses, and alloy-specific precipitation or phase changes. These processes convert the highly strained, nanocrystalline/ultrafine microstructure produced by the high-strain impact into a more equilibrated, lower-energy structure with concomitant changes in mechanical and physical properties.

Key microstructural changes (what and why)
- Recovery (low–moderate T): rapid rearrangement and annihilation of dislocations into cells/subgrains; drop in stored dislocation density and internal strain without formation of new grains. Happens at relatively low homologous temperatures (≈0.2–0.4 Tm).
- Subgrain formation / LAGB development: dislocations reorganize into low-angle grain boundaries (subgrains); typical early-stage structure after recovery.
- Recrystallization (moderate T/time): nucleation of new strain-free grains (often at particle boundaries, triple points or severely deformed zones) and growth into surrounding deformed material; converts LAGBs into HAGBs and produces equiaxed grains. Extent depends on stored energy and temperature-time.
- Grain growth / coarsening: growth of recrystallized grains and consumption of nanoscale/ultrafine regions; further reduces strength from the as-sprayed state.
- Interface healing and interdiffusion: atomic diffusion across particle–particle boundaries and/or substrate–coating interfaces increases metallurgical bonding, reduces distinct particle boundaries, and can eliminate microcracks/open interfaces.
- Porosity closure / densification: creep- and diffusion-assisted shrinkage of pores and relaxation-induced closure of microchannels; aided by plasticity at lower temperatures if present.
- Residual-stress relaxation: reduction of impact-induced compressive/tensile stresses through recovery and creep—affects dimensional stability and fatigue behavior.
- Precipitation, coarsening or dissolution (alloy-specific): annealing can cause formation of fine precipitates (age-hardening), coarsening of existing precipitates, or dissolution depending on temperature/time (e.g., Al alloys: GP zones → precipitates; Cu alloys: secondary phases may coarsen).
- Oxide and intermetallic evolution: oxide fragments at particle boundaries may sinter, thicken, or redistribute; in dissimilar-metal systems intermetallic layers may form or grow (can strengthen or embrittle the interface).
- Texture evolution: reduction/relaxation of impact-induced deformation texture; new textures can develop during recrystallization.

Typical temperature scale
- More useful in homologous temperature: moderate annealing typically lies around 0.3–0.6 Tm (absolute temperature divided by melting temperature in K).
- Examples (approx.): Al alloys ≈150–400 °C; Cu alloys ≈200–600 °C; steels/stainless ≈400–800 °C; Ti alloys higher (≈400–900 °C depending on alloy and desired effect). Exact windows depend on alloy chemistry and desired balance of recovery vs recrystallization.

Typical consequences for properties
- Hardness/strength: usually decreases as dislocation density falls and grains grow (softening). However, precipitation during anneal can temporarily increase hardness in age‑hardening alloys.
- Ductility/toughness: generally increases after recovery/recrystallization.
- Cohesive bond strength and fatigue resistance: often improve because of interface healing and residual-stress relaxation (but brittle intermetallics/oxides can be detrimental).
- Electrical/thermal conductivity: generally improves as scattering from defects decreases.

Controlling factors
- Alloy chemistry (solute and precipitate behavior)
- Initial state: stored energy, grain size, oxide coverage, porosity
- Annealing temperature, time, heating/cooling rates
- Atmosphere (vacuum/inert prevents further oxidation; presence of oxygen may alter oxide behavior)
- Substrate constraint (mechanical restraint can affect recrystallization and stress relaxation)

Practical note
To preserve the high strength from severe plastic deformation while gaining some bond improvement, practitioners often choose low-to-moderate anneals (promote recovery without full recrystallization) or controlled short anneals. For improving adhesion and reducing porosity, longer/higher anneals that enable interdiffusion and recrystallization are used, bearing in mind loss of as-sprayed strength and potential intermetallic/oxide formation.
