- Lower capital and operating cost
  - LP systems use smaller compressors, lower gas flows and lower heating power, so equipment, energy and consumable (gas) costs are significantly reduced.

- Simpler, safer, more portable equipment
  - Lower gas pressures (typ. ~1–6 bar vs HP ~15–40+ bar) reduce stored energy and associated safety requirements, piping/valving complexity and regulatory burden, enabling lighter, portable/field systems.

- Ability to use compressed air or nitrogen instead of helium
  - LP commonly runs on compressed air or N2, avoiding expensive/limited helium and lowering running costs.

- Gentler treatment of substrates and parts
  - Lower particle impact velocities produce less erosion, peening, plastic deformation and thermal input, so thin, delicate or heat‑sensitive substrates (thin sheets, electronics, coated/templated parts) are easier to coat without distortion or damage.

- Reduced nozzle and part wear
  - Lower velocities and temperatures reduce abrasive wear on nozzles and fixtures, lowering maintenance and consumable replacement.

- Easier process setup and operation
  - Fewer safety/engineering controls and simpler gas handling make setup, operator training and in-field repairs simpler.

- Lower residual stresses and less distortion in coatings
  - The reduced kinetic/peening effects often give coatings with lower compressive stresses and less risk of substrate distortion.

Brief caveat: LP‑CS trades reduced kinetic energy for these benefits — it is best for soft/ductile metals (Al, Cu, Zn, Ni, some alloys) and for repair/field work. Hard, high‑strength materials or thick, high‑performance deposits often require HP‑CS to reach the critical particle velocities and higher deposition efficiencies.

Typical cold‑spray metallic deposits are not recrystallized cast microstructures but strongly deformed, strain‑hardened assemblies of plastically flattened particles with ultrafine/nanocrystalline grain refinement concentrated at the particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces.

Why this forms
- High‑velocity particle impact (hundreds to >1,000 m/s) produces extremely large plastic strains at very high strain rates (roughly 10^5–10^7 s−1). That generates very high dislocation densities, dislocation cells/subgrain structures and severe grain subdivision.  
- Localized adiabatic heating at the impact zone and intense dislocation activity can drive dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallization in the near‑surface region of particles, producing an ultrafine or nanocrystalline layer (typically tens of nm to a few microns thick) at interfaces.  
- Impact jetting and shear localization help remove surface contamination/oxides and produce clean metallic contact and mechanical interlocking, so bonding is achieved without bulk melting.  
- Away from interfaces the particle interiors are often only partially deformed and remain work‑hardened/coarser, so the overall deposit is a laminated, heterogeneous microstructure of highly refined interfacial zones and less‑refined cores.

Consequences: high hardness and strength at interfaces, residual compressive stresses, and generally good cohesion without melting. (Brittle or very hard powders can fracture rather than plastically deform, giving different microstructures.)

Short answer
- Order-of-magnitude ranges encountered in cold spray:
  - Bulk/overall particle deformation: roughly 10^6 – 10^9 s^-1.
  - Localized interfacial/shear-band/jetting zones: roughly 10^7 – 10^11 s^-1 (can reach 10^10–10^11 s^-1 in the thinnest shear bands).

How these numbers are obtained (simple estimate)
- A useful back-of-envelope relation is strain rate ≈ velocity / characteristic deformation length.
  - Use v ≈ 300–1,200 m/s (typical particle impact speeds).
  - Characteristic lengths:
    - particle diameter or plastic zone size: ~1–100 μm → v/d gives ~10^6–10^9 s^-1.
    - shear-band or jet thickness at the interface: ~1–100 nm (often reported 10–100 nm) → v/δ gives ~10^8–10^11 s^-1.
- Example: 50 μm particle at 800 m/s → v/d ≈ 800 / 50e‑6 ≈ 1.6×10^7 s^-1 (bulk); if a 100 nm shear band forms locally, v/δ ≈ 800 / 1e‑7 ≈ 8×10^9 s^-1 (local).

Notes and caveats
- These are order-of-magnitude estimates; direct experimental measurement is difficult. Most published values come from FEM/SPH/MD simulations and microstructural inference (e.g., extreme grain refinement, adiabatic heating patterns).
- Actual strain rates depend strongly on particle size, impact velocity, material properties, impact angle, substrate stiffness, and the thickness of the dynamically formed shear band/plastic zone.

Face-centered cubic (FCC) metals.  

FCC crystals (e.g. Al, Cu, Ag, Ni) have the lowest resistance to plastic deformation for cold‑spray impacts because they offer many active slip systems (12 {111}<110> systems), close‑packed planes and directions, low critical resolved shear stress/Peierls stress and facile dislocation motion.  By contrast BCC behaviour is more temperature/strain‑rate sensitive and HCP has far fewer easily activated slip systems at room temperature, so both tend to resist deformation more.  

(Caveat: alloying, stacking‑fault energy, grain size, oxide films and high strain‑rate/temperature effects can modify real depositability.)

Ceramic particles strengthen cold‑sprayed metal matrix composite coatings by several complementary micromechanical and microstructural mechanisms. Key mechanisms are:

- Load transfer / stress partitioning  
  Hard, stiff ceramic particles carry a portion of the externally applied stress so the metal matrix sees reduced effective stress. Efficiency scales with particle stiffness, aspect ratio, volume fraction and, critically, particle–matrix interfacial strength.

- Dispersion (particle) strengthening / Orowan looping  
  Non‑shearable particles act as obstacles to dislocation glide. Dislocations bow between particles and leave loops (Orowan mechanism); the strengthening increment rises as interparticle spacing decreases (most effective for fine, well‑dispersed particles).

- Dislocation generation and work hardening  
  Impact and subsequent deformation produce high local dislocation densities around particles. Dislocation pileups at particle/matrix interfaces increase flow stress (forest strengthening).

- Grain refinement / Hall–Petch strengthening  
  Particles stimulate severe local plastic deformation and act as sites for nucleation of fine grains (particle‑stimulated nucleation and dynamic recrystallization). Reduced matrix grain size increases strength via the Hall–Petch relation (σ = σ0 + k d−1/2).

- Zener pinning (grain‑boundary stabilization)  
  Particles at grain boundaries inhibit boundary motion and grain growth, stabilizing the refined microstructure and maintaining higher strength at elevated temperature.

- Crack deflection, bridging and blunting  
  Particles force crack paths to deviate, bridge cracks, or blunt crack tips, increasing the energy required for crack propagation and improving apparent toughness and fatigue resistance (provided particles are well bonded).

- Residual stresses and constraint effects  
  Solid‑state impact plus thermal mismatch between ceramic and metal generate residual stresses and constrain plastic flow; mild compressive residual stresses near the surface can improve resistance to crack initiation and fatigue.

- Mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding effects  
  Surface roughness, particle morphology and any metallurgical interaction at the interface improve load transfer and long‑term stability of the reinforcement.

Practical caveats: effectiveness depends strongly on particle size (micro vs nano), morphology, volume fraction and spatial distribution, and on interfacial bonding produced by the cold spray parameters. Excessive particle content, poor bonding or large brittle particles can instead create porosity, weak interfaces and embrittlement, reducing coating strength.

Briefly: both welding and laser glazing produce thermo-mechanically induced residual stresses with the same basic pattern — tensile near the heated surface/centerline and balancing compressive stresses deeper or further from the heat source — but details depend strongly on geometry, constraint and phase changes.

Typical features

- Peak tensile stresses at or near the weld/glaze surface and along the weld centerline (longitudinal direction). These arise because the heated molten/softened zone contracts on cooling but is constrained by the colder surrounding material.
- Transverse tensile stresses are usually present but smaller than the longitudinal component for typical butt- or fillet-welded plates.
- Through-thickness profile: a surface (or near-surface) tensile peak, then a subsurface layer of reduced tensile or compressive stress, and finally opposite-sign balancing stresses at greater depth so the net force/moment = 0.
- Magnitudes: for restrained structural welds tensile residuals commonly reach a few 100 MPa (often comparable to yield in common steels). Laser glazing (surface remelt) typically gives tens to a few 100 MPa tensile stresses at the surface unless other effects intervene.
- Exceptions: phase-transformation strains (e.g., martensitic transformation in steels) or deliberate peening/shock-peening can generate compressive surface stresses. Laser shock peening (not glazing) deliberately produces compressive surface stresses.

Factors that change the distribution: joint geometry and restraint, heat input and cooling rate, preheat/interpass temperature, weld sequence, filler metallurgy and phase transformations, and post‑weld treatments.

Common measurement methods: X-ray diffraction (surface), hole-drilling (near-surface), neutron or synchrotron diffraction and the contour method (through-thickness).

Because cold spray is a solid‑state, high‑velocity consolidation process rather than a melt‑and‑solidify process, the physical/chemical situations that create porosity and oxides in thermal spray are largely avoided. Key reasons:

- No melting → low oxidation and no splat solidification
  - Thermal spray melts or partially melts feedstock; molten droplets oxidize in flight and at the substrate, and rapid solidification traps oxides and gas. Cold spray particles remain solid (only very localized adiabatic heating), so there is little in‑flight oxidation and no oxide‑rich splat boundaries from resolidification.

- Severe plastic deformation and jetting
  - Impact velocities exceed a critical value, producing extreme plastic flow and a high‑velocity jet at the particle/substrate interface. That jet mechanically scrubs and ejects surface oxides/contaminants to the periphery and fragments oxide films, exposing fresh metal for intimate metallic contact and bonding.

- Mechanical bonding and pore closure
  - The intense plastic deformation produces intimate particle–particle contact, work‑hardening, dynamic recrystallization and mechanical interlocking that close voids. Thermal sprays form lamellae with intersplat gaps and solidification shrinkage that produce higher porosity.

- Controlled atmosphere and short high‑temperature exposure
  - Cold spray uses compressed inert or low‑reactivity gases and the metal spends negligible time at elevated temperature, so oxygen uptake is minimal compared with the high temperatures and long thermal exposure of plasma/HVOF processes.

Net effect: far fewer continuous oxide films and entrapped oxides, and much denser consolidation (porosity typically much lower than in conventional thermally sprayed coatings).

Short answer
- Raising tool rotational speed generally increases heat input. That tends to increase the fraction of material that undergoes dynamic recrystallization (DRX) but also promotes post‑DRX grain growth, so the final grains are often coarser.  
- Lower rotational speed reduces thermal input (and for a fixed travel speed often increases effective strain rate/strain per pass), which favors finer recrystallized grains but can reduce the completeness of DRX — very low speeds can leave a mixed microstructure of deformed and partially recrystallized regions.

Why (mechanisms)
- Temperature vs. strain/strain‑rate balance: rotation changes both local strain and heat. Higher rotation → higher heat and lower Zener‑Hollomon effective Z (because T up), which makes boundary migration and grain growth easier. Lower rotation → lower T and higher Z (if strain is high), promoting formation and retention of very fine DRX grains (especially by continuous DRX in high‑SFE FCC metals) but possibly incomplete transformation if T is too low.
- DRX mode: many FCC alloys undergo continuous dynamic recrystallization (CDRX) under FSP (subgrain formation and progressive misorientation). CDRX is sensitive to both accumulated strain and temperature — enough strain is needed to generate high dislocation density/subgrains; enough temperature is needed to rotate and transform those into high‑angle boundaries.
- Material dependence: the exact response depends on stacking‑fault energy and thermal properties. High‑SFE FCC metals (Al alloys, Cu) more readily form fine CDRX grains; low‑SFE FCC (some stainless steels) may show twinning and different DRX kinetics.

Practical implications and tuning
- If you want the finest, fully recrystallized grains: aim for a processing window that supplies large plastic strain with moderate heat — e.g., moderate-to-low rotation combined with increased traverse speed (so strain per unit time is high but peak temperature is limited), or active cooling.  
- If rotation is too high: you may get full recrystallization but subsequent grain growth (coarser grains), softening and loss of strengthening.  
- If rotation is too low: you may get very fine zones where DRX occurred but also wide bands of unrecrystallized, work‑hardened material.

Typical experimental observation (qualitative)
- Increasing rotation from low → moderate: recrystallized fraction rises and grain size initially refines as strain increases.  
- Increasing rotation further → recrystallized fraction approaches 100% but grain size increases due to thermal growth.

Summary
Control of final grain size and recrystallization extent is a competition between imposed deformation (strain/strain rate) and thermal exposure. Rotational speed is one of the main levers: higher rotation tends to increase recrystallization fraction but also promotes grain coarsening; lower rotation tends to produce finer grains but risks incomplete DRX unless compensated by other changes (tool geometry, traverse speed, cooling, multi‑pass).

Short answer
- Individual cold-sprayed splats are highly microstructurally heterogeneous: the region that experienced the highest impact strain and shear (the contact/interface and peripheral “jet” zones) is severely refined (ultrafine / nanocrystalline, high dislocation density, many high‑angle boundaries), while the interior (rear) of the original particle is comparatively coarse-grained and less-worked. This graded grain structure produces strong local mechanical property gradients (hardness, yield strength, residual stress, ductility) inside each splat.

Why the grain structure is non‑uniform
- Impact kinematics create large spatial gradients in strain, strain‑rate and temperature within a particle. The face contacting the substrate and the splat rim undergo the largest plastic flow, shear bands and adiabatic heating; the particle core sees much less deformation.
- High local strains and strain‑rates promote dislocation accumulation, subgrain formation and continuous/dynamic recrystallization in the heavily deformed zones, producing ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains (tens of nm to submicron, depending on material and conditions).
- Less-deformed cores retain original (or only moderately refined) grain sizes and lower dislocation density. Flow produces elongated grains in the impact direction in intermediate regions.

Typical microstructural features (reported by TEM/EBSD)
- A thin interfacial layer (hundreds of nm to a few microns) of very fine equiaxed grains and high-angle boundaries at the substrate/particle interface.
- Peripheral “jet” or shear-band regions with extreme refinement and high misorientation.
- Interior cores with coarser, often elongated grains and lower stored energy.
- Sharp or gradual transitions between these zones depending on impact energy and material.

Mechanical heterogeneity this causes
- Hardness/Strength gradients: refined interfacial and rim regions show much higher hardness and yield strength (Hall–Petch + dislocation strengthening) than the coarse particle cores. Nanoindentation maps commonly show hardness increases toward interfaces.
- Local residual stresses: high deformation regions contain large compressive/tensile residual stresses that vary spatially.
- Heterogeneous plasticity: under load, the softer cores or weaker interfaces can localize deformation, while the hard interface layers carry higher stresses—this leads to load partitioning, nonuniform deformation and early localization or fatigue crack initiation at boundaries between zones.
- Fracture/toughness consequences: the interfaces between refined and coarse regions (or along oxide films) can be preferred crack paths; brittle behavior can appear locally where severe work hardening / microcracking occurred.
- Macroscopic anisotropy and scatter: because each splat is heterogeneous and splat-to-splat bonding is variable, coatings show spatial scatter in hardness, tensile/fatigue behavior and wear resistance.

Practical implications
- Coating performance depends on the volume fraction and connectivity of the refined, well-bonded interfacial zones. Process control (particle velocity, temperature, feedstock microstructure) and post‑treatments (annealing, peening) are used to reduce intraparticle heterogeneity or to tailor a useful gradient (e.g., hard interface for wear, tougher interior for toughness).
- Characterization tools: TEM, EBSD (grain-size/misorientation maps), nanoindentation mapping and micro‑Raman/XRD residual stress mapping are typically used to quantify the intra‑splat structural and mechanical gradients.

In short: splats are internally graded from highly refined, hard, highly‑strained interfacial/shear regions to relatively coarse, softer cores — and that graded grain structure drives local property gradients that control bonding, deformation, fracture and overall coating performance.

Short answer
- Because the layers are perfectly bonded, the circumferential (tangential) strain field is common to all layers (strain compatibility). In pure bending the strain varies linearly with radial position measured from the neutral surface.
- The tangential stress in each layer is the layer Young’s modulus times that common strain, so stress jumps at material interfaces in proportion to the modulus difference.
- The neutral radius and curvature are fixed by force and moment equilibrium; the bending stiffness is the stiffness-weighted integral over the cross‑section.

Assumptions: linear elastic, plane sections remain plane (small curvature change), bending about the beam center of curvature, no net axial load.

Key formulas (r measured from center of curvature)
1) Tangential (circumferential) strain
  εθ(r) = (r_n − r) · κ
  where r_n is the neutral radius (εθ(r_n)=0) and κ = 1/ρ is the curvature (signed).

2) Tangential stress in layer i
  σθ,i(r) = E_i · εθ(r) = E_i (r_n − r) κ.

3) Neutral radius (force equilibrium, no resultant axial force)
  0 = ∑_i ∫_{A_i} σθ,i dA  ⇒
  r_n = [∑_i E_i ∫_{A_i} r dA] / [∑_i E_i A_i]
  (i.e. stiffness-weighted centroid in the radial coordinate).

4) Curvature from bending moment M (moment equilibrium)
  M = ∑_i ∫_{A_i} σθ,i r dA = κ · D,  where
  D = ∑_i E_i ∫_{A_i} (r_n − r) r dA  (effective bending stiffness).
  Hence κ = M / D and
  σθ,i(r) = E_i (r_n − r) M / D.

Remarks
- Strain is continuous across interfaces; stress is generally discontinuous where E changes.
- If the cross‑section is thin relative to its radius, the curved-beam formulas reduce to the straight-beam form ε ≈ −y κ and the usual E·ε linear stress distribution.
- There will also be interfacial shear stresses required to enforce perfect bonding; these are determined from transverse equilibrium but are typically small in classical pure‑bending solutions.

Short answer: bonding in cold spray is a solid‑state, high‑strain‑rate phenomenon controlled by (1) extreme plastic deformation at the particle/substrate interface, (2) localized adiabatic shear/jetting that cleans and intermixes surfaces, and (3) microstructural evolution (severe grain refinement/dynamic recrystallization) that produces metallurgical continuity. A threshold particle kinetic energy/velocity (the “critical velocity”) must be exceeded for these mechanisms to occur.

Key mechanisms (concise):

- Plastic deformation and mechanical interlocking
  - Impact converts particle kinetic energy to intense, very high strain‑rate plastic flow in the particle and often the near‑surface substrate. Particles flatten into splats and can mechanically interlock with surface asperities, increasing contact area and normal pressure necessary for bonding.

- Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) and interfacial jetting
  - At sufficiently high strains and strain rates, adiabatic heating localizes into shear bands. ASI produces a peripheral jet of material at the impact interface that expels oxides/contaminants and creates intimate metal–metal contact and hydrodynamic mixing at the rim—this jetting is widely regarded as critical for good bonding.

- Oxide/contaminant disruption and fresh‑surface formation
  - The jetting and severe deformation fracture or eject oxide films and surface contamination, exposing fresh metal surfaces that can contact and bond without needing bulk melting.

- Dynamic recrystallization / severe plastic deformation (SPD)
  - Very high strains and strain rates produce nanograined/deformed interfacial zones through dynamic recrystallization and dislocation processes. This ultrafine microstructure aids metallurgical bonding (increased diffusion, higher boundary area) even though bulk temperatures remain below melting.

- Critical velocity and energy balance
  - A minimum particle velocity (and thus kinetic energy) is required to produce the deformation/ASI/jetting cascade; v_critical depends on particle and substrate mechanical properties (yield strength, hardness, density), particle size/temperature, and impact conditions. Below this threshold particles rebound; above it bonding probability increases rapidly.

- Material and process dependencies
  - Ductile particles/substrates bond more readily than brittle ones. Harder substrates can prevent embedding (raising v_critical), while soft substrates promote embedding. Process variables — gas species and pressure, particle temperature, nozzle design, standoff distance, particle size/shape, and impact angle — control particle velocity/temperature and therefore bonding outcome.

- Resulting interface features and residuals
  - Bonded interfaces typically show a thin (~submicron to few microns) highly deformed or nanocrystalline layer, possible interfacial oxides remaining if not fully removed, and residual compressive/tensile stresses depending on impact sequence and subsequent peening.

Modeling and experimental notes:
- Bonding is typically modeled with high‑rate constitutive laws (e.g., Johnson‑Cook), explicit FEM or SPH, and criteria for ASI/dynamic recrystallization. Empirical critical‑velocity maps exist for many material pairs.
- For materials with stable surface oxides or ceramic coatings, bonding is much harder because oxide removal and ductile flow are limited.

Practical implication: to achieve reliable bonding increase particle velocity and temperature (within material limits), choose ductile particle/substrate combinations, optimize spray gas/nozzle/standoff to exceed critical velocity, and pre‑treat the substrate to reduce oxides/contamination or provide favorable roughness for mechanical interlocking.

The single most useful parameter is the particle kinetic energy density (specific kinetic energy) normalized by the temperature‑dependent flow stress. In practice this is written and used in two equivalent forms:

- particle kinetic energy: E = ½ m v^2  
- kinetic energy density (per unit volume): e = ½ ρ_p v^2

To include temperature effects you normalize by the material’s temperature‑dependent yield/flow stress σ_y(T), e.g.

Normalized impact parameter = (½ ρ_p v^2) / σ_y(T)

When this normalized energy exceeds a threshold (or when E exceeds the energy required to produce the necessary plastic work at the softened σ_y(T)) deposition and good coating microstructure occur. This is the basis for critical‑velocity and deposition models used in cold spray (Johnson–Cook type constitutive models are commonly used to evaluate σ_y(T)).

Short answer
- Cold spray is a very high‑strain, high‑strain‑rate, solid‑state impact process: particles undergo severe plastic deformation on impact (adiabatic shear, jetting, intense compressive/tensile strains), so the as‑deposited material contains extremely large numbers of dislocations (dislocation tangles, cells and dense networks at particle–particle boundaries and shear bands). Typical dislocation densities are in the severe plastic deformation range (∼10^14–10^16 m−2), much higher than in annealed metal.
- Heat treatment lowers that stored defect population by thermally activated processes: recovery (dislocation rearrangement and annihilation), static recrystallization (nucleation and growth of new, low‑dislocation grains) and subsequent grain growth. The result is reduced dislocation density, lower hardness and internal stress, and usually increased ductility and electrical conductivity. The extent depends strongly on temperature, time, material chemistry and second‑phase/oxide particles (which can pin boundaries and retard recovery/recrystallization).

Mechanistic detail
- Why the high dislocation density initially:
  - Impact imposes extremely large, localized plastic strains at very high strain rates (10^4–10^7 s−1). Dislocation multiplication (Frank–Read sources) and generation in shear bands is enormous.
  - Plastic flow is highly non‑homogeneous (particle deformation, jets, particle–particle interfaces), producing tangled dislocation structures, high immobile dislocation fractions and small subgrain/nanograin domains.
  - Little time for dynamic recovery during impact (solid‑state, very fast), so defects are frozen in.
- How heat treatment modifies it:
  - Recovery: at relatively low homologous temperatures dislocations glide and climb to annihilate, form low‑energy configurations and subgrains; dislocation density falls rapidly without large grain boundary motion.
  - Recrystallization: if driving force is sufficient, new strain‑free grains nucleate (often at particle interfaces, defects) and grow, wiping out dislocation networks and strongly reducing dislocation density.
  - Grain growth: at higher T or long times grains coarsen, further reducing boundary area and residual dislocations.
  - Alloying/oxides/precipitates: second‑phase features can pin dislocations and grain boundaries (Zener pinning), slowing reduction of dislocation density and stabilizing the fine microstructure.

Practical consequences
- Softening (drop in hardness/strength) and stress relief follow typical anneals; conductivity and ductility increase.
- Choice of anneal temperature/time must balance defect reduction (to relax stress, improve conductivity) and retention of a fine, strong microstructure (avoid over‑recrystallization/grain growth).

Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) in cold spray is a localized mechanical/thermal instability that develops at the particle–substrate or particle–particle interface during the very high strain‑rate impact of particles. Because impact durations are extremely short (~micro- to sub‑microseconds), most of the plastic work is converted to heat in the deforming zone (high Taylor–Quinney factor) and there is negligible heat conduction away from that zone — hence “adiabatic.” The local temperature rise causes thermal softening that can outpace strain hardening, so a small perturbation in strain grows rapidly into a narrow shear band (adiabatic shear band).

Why this matters for bonding:
- The shear band produces extreme local deformation and can trigger material jetting at the interface, which mechanically removes oxides/contamination and exposes clean metal surfaces.  
- The localized high temperature and strain promote dynamic recovery/recrystallization and grain refinement, enabling intimate atomic contact and metallurgical welding across the interface.  
- ASI therefore enables the transition from mere plastic flattening/rebound to true bonding; achieving it is closely related to the process’s critical velocity.  

Practical implications: ASI depends on particle velocity, mass, temperature, material yield/strain‑rate sensitivity, and oxide layers. If impact energy is too low no ASI (and no bond) occurs; if too high it can cause erosion or particle fragmentation. Experimental evidence of ASI includes narrow shear bands, jetting features, high local temperatures inferred from microstructure, and nanocrystalline zones at interfaces.

Short answer
Adding ceramic nanoparticles to a polymer feedstock usually reduces cold-spray deposition efficiency and slows coating build-up unless carefully controlled. Rigid nanoparticles make the feedstock less able to plastically deform/flow on impact, raise the effective critical velocity for bonding, increase rebound/fragmentation and porosity, and thereby reduce mass gain per pass. At low loadings and with good dispersion/surface treatment, nanoparticles can be incorporated with only a modest loss in DE and can improve final coating properties; at higher loadings the negative effects dominate.

Why (mechanism)
- Cold spray bonding of polymers relies on particle impact deformation/viscous/viscoelastic flow, intimate contact and interdiffusion/adhesion. Ceramic nanoparticles are non‑deforming inclusions that:
  - Increase stiffness, yield strength and brittle response of particles → reduce ability to flatten and form intimate contact on impact.
  - Produce stress concentrations and promote fragmentation or particle rebound.
  - If agglomerated, create hard asperities that prevent good contact and increase porosity.
- Net effect: higher required critical velocity (v_c) and higher kinetic energy needed for deposition, so at fixed spray parameters DE ↓ and coating build-up rate ↓.
- Possible counter-effect: well‑dispersed low concentrations of nanoparticles can enhance mechanical interlocking and local shear heating (adiabatic shear) at impact sites, which under some conditions can assist bonding.

Practical dependencies
- Particle loading: small additions (single-digit to low tens wt% or a few vol%) may be tolerable; high loadings (>~20–30 wt% or high vol%) typically cause severe DE loss.
- Nanoparticle size and dispersion: well-dispersed, sub-100 nm particles are less damaging than agglomerates; agglomeration dramatically worsens DE.
- Surface chemistry: treated/functionalized nanoparticles that wet the polymer matrix better reduce interfacial debonding and improve DE.
- Spray conditions: increasing gas pressure/temperature (higher particle velocity and more thermal softening) and preheating substrate or using core–shell feedstock help counteract the loss in DE.

Mitigation strategies
- Limit nanoparticle loading or use graded feedstock (polymer-rich outer layers).
- Improve nanoparticle dispersion and surface functionalization/bonding to the polymer.
- Increase particle velocity/temperature (higher gas pressure, preheat) to meet the higher critical velocity.
- Use composite particles (polymer binder around nanoparticle agglomerates) or post-deposition consolidation (thermal/pressure) to densify coatings.

Bottom line
Ceramic nanoparticles improve final coating mechanical and functional properties but make cold spray deposition more difficult. Success requires keeping loadings modest, eliminating agglomerates, and adapting spray parameters or feedstock design to overcome the higher critical velocity and reduced deformability.

Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) in cold spray is the rapid, highly localized loss of load-carrying capacity in the particle/substrate contact zone caused by very fast plastic deformation and the accompanying adiabatic temperature rise. It produces narrow shear bands (micron-scale) where material softens and deforms intensely on microsecond timescales. ASI is important in cold spray because it governs jetting, interfacial mixing, and in some cases local melting or fracture — all of which strongly affect bonding quality.

Mechanism (concise):
- During high-velocity particle impact the contact region experiences extreme strain rates (10^4–10^7 s^-1). Mechanical work is converted to heat faster than it can diffuse away, so the deformation is effectively adiabatic.
- The local temperature rise ΔT ≈ (β/(ρ Cp)) ∫ σ dε (β ≈ fraction of plastic work → heat). If thermal softening of the material (reduction of flow stress with increasing T) outpaces strain hardening and any strain-rate hardening, a small perturbation in strain grows and localizes into a shear band.
- Stability condition (qualitative): thermal softening term > (strain hardening + strain-rate hardening). In constitutive models (e.g., Johnson–Cook) ASI occurs when the 1 − (T*)^m thermal-softening factor reduces flow stress faster than the other factors increase it.

Key features and consequences:
- Shear bands are very narrow (microns), form in microseconds, and often show ultrafine grains or evidence of dynamic recrystallization; local temperatures can approach or reach melting in extreme cases.
- Positive for bonding: ASI-driven jetting and extreme shear can strip oxides and create intimate metal-to-metal contact and severe plastic deformation that enhances bonding.
- Detrimental effects: excessive localization can cause particle fragmentation, porosity, or brittle failure at the interface.

Factors that promote ASI:
- Higher impact velocity (higher strain rate and work per impact).
- Low thermal conductivity, high fraction of plastic work converted to heat, low strain-rate sensitivity, materials with strong thermal softening.
- Large particles (longer contact times and larger energy) and high initial particle temperature can also influence localization.

Detection/analysis:
- Observed via SEM/EBSD/TEM as narrow bands of ultrafine grains, local phase changes, or melt-like features; modeled using high-strain-rate constitutive laws (e.g., Johnson–Cook) coupled with adiabatic heating and stability analyses.

Practical implication:
Control of ASI (via impact velocity, particle size, temperature, material selection or feedstock condition) is a key part of optimizing cold spray parameter windows to maximize bonding while minimizing deleterious defects.

Dynamic recovery (DRV) during severe plastic deformation (SPD) is the in‑process, thermally‑ and stress‑assisted reduction and rearrangement of dislocations that competes with their generation. In high stacking‑fault‑energy (SFE) FCC metals (e.g., Al, Cu, Ni) DRV is especially active because screw dislocations can cross‑slip readily and climb is relatively facile; as a result dislocations annihilate and reorganize even at modest temperatures and high strains.

Key mechanisms
- Cross‑slip of screw segments and climb of edge segments, enabling annihilation of opposite‑sign dislocations.
- Polygonization/pile‑up relaxation: rearrangement of remaining dislocations into low‑energy walls and cells (subgrains), reducing long‑range internal stresses.
- Progressive increase of subgrain misorientation (continuous dynamic recrystallization, CDRX) as strain accumulates.

Effect on dislocation density
- DRV reduces the net accumulation rate of dislocations during SPD by annihilating pairs and by converting disordered dislocation populations into lower‑energy structures (cell walls/subgrains). Practically this produces a strain‑dependent steady‑state (saturation) dislocation density rather than indefinite growth.
- The balance can be represented simply as dρ/dt = G(ė) − A·ρ^2 (generation minus annihilation), so annihilation scales roughly with ρ^2; higher temperature and greater mobility increase A and lower the steady‑state ρ.
- Consequences: lower peak dislocation densities and pronounced subgrain/low‑angle boundary structures (instead of extremely dense, random dislocation networks or extensive twinning). This limits work‑hardening but facilitates ductility and enables CDRX to produce fine grains with high‑angle boundaries at very large strains.

Practical implication: in high‑SFE FCC metals DRV is a dominant softening mechanism during SPD, setting the achievable dislocation density and influencing the final grain size, texture, and mechanical response.

Short answer
Preheating (of the spray gas/particles and/or the substrate) promotes bonding in cold spray primarily by thermally softening material at the impact site so that higher plastic deformation, interfacial jetting/oxide removal, and dynamic recrystallization occur at a given particle velocity. That reduces the process “critical velocity,” increases deposition efficiency and adhesion, and modifies residual stresses and microstructure — but excessive heating increases oxidation, changes phase/toughness for some alloys, and can degrade some advantages of cold spray.

Key mechanisms (why preheating helps)
- Thermal softening: increased temperature reduces yield strength/flow stress (Johnson–Cook style behavior), so particles and substrate deform more readily on impact for the same kinetic energy. More deformation increases contact area and metallurgical bonding.
- Enhanced jetting and oxide disruption: softer material promotes the high-strain-rate shear flow at the interface (the “jet”), which mechanically cleans oxides/contaminants and exposes fresh metal for bonding.
- Local temperature rise and dynamic recrystallization: preheating makes it easier for plastic work at the interface to raise local temperatures into regimes that promote ultrafine-grain dynamic recrystallization and stronger metallurgical bonds.
- Reduced critical velocity: because of the above, the minimum particle velocity required to obtain bonding (critical velocity) is lowered when particles and/or substrate are warmer.
- Improved cohesion and lower porosity: generally yields denser coatings with higher interfacial strength and fewer unbonded particles.

Differences between particle (gas) preheating and substrate preheating
- Particle (gas) preheating
  - Most common in cold spray — heated carrier gas raises particle temperature in-flight and increases gas sound speed (can increase particle exit velocity).
  - Benefits: lowers particle flow stress, raises impact deformability, reduces critical velocity, often increases deposition efficiency and layer buildup rate.
  - Risks: higher in‑flight temperatures can accelerate oxidation (especially for Al, Ti), cause particle sintering/agglomeration in the feed path, and for reactive alloys can produce brittle surface layers.
- Substrate preheating
  - Heats the target surface (plate/heater/laser) before or during spraying.
  - Benefits: softens substrate, makes interface easier to plastically deform, reduces rebound, can improve bonding to hard or low‑ductility substrates and reduce thermal mismatch stresses in multilayer builds.
  - Risks/limits: excessive substrate temperature can affect substrate microstructure or cause phase changes, and it does not mitigate particle surface oxides unless combined with particle/jet effects.

Practical effects on properties
- Deposition efficiency: typically increases with moderate preheating (lower critical velocity → more particles bond).
- Adhesion/cohesion: improved interfacial strength and cohesion within the coating due to better plastic bonding and dynamic recrystallization.
- Microstructure and hardness: more plastic deformation may increase work hardening and refined grain structure at the interface, but bulk hardness can decrease if thermal softening of large volumes occurs.
- Residual stress: preheating generally reduces thermal gradients and can reduce tensile residual stresses, but final stress state depends on process specifics.
- Oxidation/contamination: higher temperatures favor oxide growth — use inert carrier gas or controlled atmospheres for oxidation-prone alloys.

Guidelines and trade-offs
- Use particle/gas preheat to reduce required particle velocities or to enable deposition of harder alloys; typically control temperature to avoid excessive oxidation and feed system problems.
- Use substrate preheat when bonding to hard or brittle substrates or to reduce substrate work hardening and cracking — but keep below temperatures that alter substrate properties undesirably.
- For reactive metals (Ti, Ni, some Al alloys) favor inert gases, minimize in‑flight residence time at high T, and carefully balance temperature so you gain ductility but avoid surface embrittlement or increased oxide thickness.
- Optimize experimentally: preheat temperature, gas composition, pressure, nozzle parameters and stand-off distance interact; monitor deposition efficiency, coating porosity, interfacial shear strength and microstructure.

Bottom line
Moderate preheating is a powerful lever in cold spray: it lowers critical velocity and promotes the plasticity-driven bonding mechanisms that produce dense, strongly adhered coatings. But benefits depend on material chemistry and process control — excessive heating increases oxidation, phase changes or agglomeration and can harm final properties.

Short answer
Oxygen that diffuses into a cold‑sprayed Ti coating during thermal oxidation almost always raises near‑surface hardness, but by two distinct mechanisms with different depth scales and tradeoffs: (1) interstitial oxygen dissolved in the Ti lattice (solid‑solution strengthening) increases strength/hardness over a diffusion‑controlled depth; (2) formation of titanium oxides (TiOx) produces a very hard, brittle surface layer. Excessive oxidation, thick oxide growth, or oxide spallation can, however, degrade the functional mechanical integrity.

How it works (mechanisms)
- Solid‑solution strengthening: Oxygen is a small interstitial in hcp α‑Ti and produces strong lattice distortions that pin dislocations. Even modest O concentrations (at.% levels) markedly raise yield strength and hardness. This is the principal source of increased hardness below the external oxide.
- Oxide formation: At the surface oxygen reacts to form TiOx (commonly TiO2/rutile and lower oxides depending on conditions). These oxides are much harder and stiffer than metallic Ti but also brittle; they dominate surface hardness measurements if the oxide thickness is comparable to the indentation depth.
- Microstructural effects: Cold‑sprayed Ti has very high dislocation density, ultrafine grains and many interfaces/porosity. That defect structure raises fast diffusion pathways (pipe/grain‑boundary diffusion), so oxygen penetrates faster and gives steeper hardness gradients than in wrought Ti. Oxidation can also close pores by oxide filling (local densification) or produce internal stresses that cause cracking/spallation.
- Residual stresses and embrittlement: Oxygen uptake causes lattice expansion and can generate compressive/tensile stresses and embrittlement (reduced toughness), so increased hardness often comes with reduced ductility and risk of delamination.

Diffusion and depth dependence (quantitative framework)
- Oxygen transport is diffusion‑controlled: Fick’s law applies. For a constant surface concentration you can use the complementary‑error‑function solution
  C(x,t) = C_s − (C_s − C_0) erf( x / (2√(Dt)) )
  where D is the oxygen diffusivity in Ti at the oxidation temperature.
- Oxide thickness often follows parabolic kinetics (growth ∝ √t) once a continuous oxide forms.
- The hardness profile reflects the interstitial O concentration profile: hardness increases from H0 to Hsurface over the same characteristic diffusion length ≈√(Dt).

Practical consequences for cold‑sprayed coatings
- Surface nanoindentation will often read very high hardness if the oxide is present; deeper indentation or cross‑section mapping will show a gradient controlled by oxygen penetration.
- Because cold‑sprayed microstructures enhance diffusion, oxidation at a given temperature/time penetrates farther than in bulk Ti — expect stronger, shallower hardening but also higher embrittlement risk.
- For desired hardening without embrittlement, oxidize at lower temperature/shorter time to achieve moderate oxygen uptake (solid‑solution strengthening) but avoid thick oxide growth that can spall.

Measurement and control
- Characterize O profiles by SIMS, GD‑OES, XPS depth profiling or EDS/WDS on cross sections and correlate with micro/nano‑hardness mapping.
- Control by adjusting oxidation temperature/time, atmosphere (partial pressure of O2), or pre‑/post‑treatments (sealants, aluminizing, nitriding alternatives) to tailor oxide thickness and subsurface O concentration.

Bottom line
Oxygen diffusion raises hardness of cold‑sprayed Ti primarily by interstitial solid‑solution strengthening below the surface and by forming a hard oxide at the surface. The coating’s high defect density accelerates O uptake, producing a steep hardness gradient; but excessive oxidation produces brittle oxides and stress that can reduce functional performance.

Cold spray is a solid‑state process, so particle adhesion is produced primarily by extreme plastic deformation and the resulting intimate metal‑metal contact — not by melting. The key bonding mechanisms are:

- Severe plastic deformation / mechanical interlocking
  - High‑velocity impact (high strain rates) flattens particles and increases real contact area, producing geometrical interlocking and frictional anchoring on the substrate and neighboring particles.

- Oxide disruption and material jetting (interfacial cleaning)
  - Impact induces adiabatic shear at the particle rim that produces a high‑velocity lateral jet. The jet strips oxides and adsorbates from the interface and ejects them, exposing fresh metal surfaces and enabling direct metal‑metal contact.

- Adiabatic heating and flow stress reduction
  - Localized, rapid temperature rise at the impact zone (adiabatic heating) lowers the yield strength and facilitates plastic flow and contact formation, even though bulk melting does not occur.

- Dynamic recrystallization / ultrafine grain formation
  - Very large strains and strain rates produce severe plastic deformation, high dislocation densities and dynamic (often continuous) recrystallization in a thin interfacial layer. The resulting nanocrystalline/subgrain structure promotes atomic contact, subgrain rotation, and formation of metallurgical bonds across the interface (solid‑state bonding or cold welding).

- Interfacial metallurgical continuity (solid‑state bonding)
  - Where conditions (impact energy, oxide removal, intimate contact, and deformation) are sufficient, atomic bonding or grain‑boundary continuity forms across the particle/substrate interface. Long‑term diffusion or post‑heat can further strengthen these links, but bulk diffusion is not required for initial bonding.

Practical implications: there is a material‑specific critical particle velocity (and energy) window — below it particles rebound or only plastically deform without bonding; above it good bonding and dense deposits form. Particle size, hardness, temperature, substrate condition, and surface oxides all control which mechanisms dominate.

Why hard materials are difficult to deposit by cold spray
- Cold spray bonds particles by extreme, localized plastic deformation at impact (jetting, adiabatic shear, intimate metal–metal contact). That requires the particle and/or substrate to plastically flow at the impact strain rates.
- Hard or brittle materials (high yield strength, low ductility, low fracture toughness — e.g., ceramics, cemented carbides, some intermetallics and heavily cold‑worked alloys) do not plastically deform readily at room temperature and high strain rate. Instead they fracture or rebound, so they do not produce the jetting/metallic contact needed for bonding.
- The result is a very high critical velocity for bonding (often beyond practical gas/nozzle limits), high particle rebound, powder fracture, poor cohesion, and oxide/contaminant layers that further impede cold welding.

General strategy to expand the processable materials
- Reduce the effective requirement for particle plasticity by supplying a ductile phase or increasing particle ductility during deposition. Concretely:
  - Use a ductile carrier/matrix: co‑spray hard particles with a ductile metal (Al, Cu, Ni, Co) so the ductile phase bonds and mechanically traps/encapsulates the hard phase.
  - Use core–shell or coated powders: a soft metal core or ductile coating around a hard particle lets the powder deform and form a bond while retaining the hard phase in the deposited structure.
  - Preheat (warm spray) and/or increase gas pressure/nozzle performance so particles reach higher velocity and have lower flow stress at impact (adiabatic heating lowers effective strength).
  - Reduce particle size or tailor particle morphology to improve acceleration and reduce fracture propensity.
  - Post‑spray consolidation or heat treatment: sinter, react, or alloy deposited layers to form the desired hard phase after bonding (e.g., deposit ductile precursor then convert to hard intermetallic/ceramic by heat/reactive treatment).
  - Surface cleaning/activation and optimized substrate roughness to improve mechanical anchoring and contact.

Examples/typical implementations
- WC or ceramic particles embedded in a Ni or Co matrix deposited by cold spray (or co‑spray) and optionally heat treated.
- Ductile metal shells on ceramic particles (core–shell) so the shell cold‑welds to the substrate while the core provides hardness in the final coating.

In short: hard materials are limited by their inability to plastically deform at the impact conditions cold spray provides. The practical remedy is to introduce or retain a ductile phase (or raise particle ductility/velocity) so bonding can occur, and then produce the final hard microstructure by design (composite, core–shell, or post‑deposition treatment).

Definition (short)
- Cold spray is a solid‑state thermal spray/additive process in which micron‑sized powder particles are accelerated to very high velocities (typically ~300–1200 m/s) in a high‑pressure gas jet and impact a substrate at temperatures well below the powder melting point. Bonding is achieved by extreme plastic deformation (adiabatic shear, mechanical interlocking and dynamic recrystallization) rather than by melting.

Key process facts
- Carrier gases: nitrogen or helium (helium gives higher particle velocity for low‑density powders).
- Gas temperatures: from near ambient up to several hundred °C (warm spray variants go higher but still below melting).
- Particle sizes: typically ~5–100 µm.
- No significant bulk melting — minimal oxidation, low thermal distortion and retained feedstock microstructure.

What materials can be deposited
- Ductile metals and alloys (best results):
  - Aluminum and Al alloys (widely used).
  - Copper and copper alloys.
  - Nickel and nickel‑based alloys.
  - Cobalt and Co‑based alloys.
  - Stainless steels and carbon steels.
  - Titanium and some Ti alloys (requires higher velocity/energy).
  - Some refractory metals (W, Mo, Ta) are possible but more challenging—require high energy/helium or substrate preconditioning.

- Metal matrix composites (MMC) / cermets:
  - Ductile metal matrices loaded with ceramic reinforcement particles (e.g., Al + SiC, Al2O3, TiC). Ceramic particles are typically embedded in a metallic matrix; coatings combine wear resistance of ceramics with ductile support of metal.

- Functionally graded materials and multi‑material builds:
  - Layered or mixed powder feeds allow graded composition (e.g., corrosion‑resistant outer layer over structural metal).

- Polymers and polymer/metal composites:
  - Thermoplastic powders and some polymer blends can be deposited in specialized cold/warm spray setups; adhesion mechanisms differ (softening/plastic flow). Less common than metal cold spray.

Materials generally not deposited or difficult
- Bulk ceramics and highly brittle powders (pure Al2O3, SiC, glass): they do not plastically deform on impact and thus do not form coherent dense coatings by cold spray alone. They can be incorporated as dispersed phases in a ductile metallic matrix, but not usually deposited as pure ceramic layers.
- Materials requiring molten‑state reactions or phase formation that depend on melting.

Practical considerations / limitations
- Best for ductile, highly deformable powders; powder morphology and substrate condition strongly influence bonding.
- Gas choice, pressure, nozzle design and particle velocity/temperature must be optimized per material.
- Cold spray is excellent for repairing, coating, and additive manufacture where low heat input, low oxidation and retained feedstock properties are important.

In short: cold spray deposits a wide range of metals, metal alloys, and metal‑matrix composites very effectively; pure brittle ceramics are generally not directly depositable except when embedded in a ductile matrix or processed with hybrid approaches.

Short answer
- The critical velocity ratio Vr = Vimpact / Vc compares the actual particle impact speed to the material’s critical velocity Vc for bonding.
- If Vr < 1 most particles rebound (insufficient plastic deformation/oxide removal); if Vr ≈ 1 you reach the onset of severe plastic deformation and jetting (bonding starts); as Vr increases above 1 the probability of metallurgical bonding rises rapidly. Very high Vr can cause particle fracture or substrate erosion.

Definitions and physical meaning
- Critical velocity Vc is the minimum particle impact speed required to produce the amount and mode of plastic deformation (adiabatic shear, jetting, oxide disruption) necessary for intimate metal-to-metal contact and bonding. Vc is material- and condition-dependent (particle/substrate materials, particle size, temperature, oxide, gas, nozzle geometry, spray angle).
- The critical velocity ratio Vr = Vimpact / Vc is a convenient normalized measure of how “far above” or “below” you are relative to that threshold.

How Vr relates to deformation and bonding probability
- Vr < 1: Impact energy is too low. Deformation is elastic or limited plastic — no sustained jetting or oxide break‑up. Particles tend to rebound; bonding probability ≈ 0.
- Vr ≈ 1: Onset of severe plastic flow and localized adiabatic heating. Material jetting from the periphery can expel oxides and produce fresh metal-to-metal contact. Bonding probability begins to increase from zero.
- 1 < Vr < ~1.2–1.5: Increasing plastic strain, larger jetting region, rapidly rising bonding probability. This is the practical deposition window for many materials.
- Vr >> 1: High strain rates and damage; possible particle fragmentation, excessive substrate erosion, and degraded coating quality. Bonding probability may plateau or drop for some systems.

Typical behavior and modeling
- Bonding probability vs. Vr is typically sigmoidal: near zero below Vr=1, then steeply increasing around Vr≈1, approaching unity at some higher Vr. Many experimental and Monte‑Carlo deposition-efficiency models use logistic-type curves to represent this.
- Vc scales approximately with material strength and density: higher-strength or higher-melting-point materials have higher Vc. A simple dimensional scaling is Vc ∝ sqrt(Y/ρ) (Y = representative flow strength, ρ = density), but the true Vc depends strongly on strain-rate sensitivity, temperature-softening, oxide films, particle size and temperature, and substrate compliance.

Practical numbers (order of magnitude)
- Typical Vc ranges (very approximate): Al alloys ~300–700 m/s, Cu ~600–900 m/s, steels/Ti/SS ~800–1200+ m/s. These values change with particle preheating, smaller particles often require higher Vc, and softer substrates lower the Vc.

How to use Vr in practice
- Measure or estimate Vc for your particle/substrate/temperature; then control gas pressure, temperature, nozzle geometry to achieve Vimpact such that Vr is just above 1–1.3 to maximize bonding probability while minimizing erosion.
- Empirically determine the bond-probability curve for your system (single-particle impact tests or deposition-efficiency vs. speed) because material‑ and process-dependence is strong.

Summary
- The critical velocity ratio Vr = Vimpact/Vc is a normalized indicator of whether particles will plastically deform and bond. Vr < 1 → rebound/no bond; Vr ≈ 1 → onset of bonding via jetting; Vr > 1 → rapidly increasing probability of metallurgical bonding, with practical upper limits beyond which damage or erosion appears.

Typical microstructural features of metallic coatings produced by cold spray, and why they form:

1. Layered, particle-based morphology
   - Coatings are built from impacted solid particles—individual particles (or “splats”) remain visible as stacked layers. Bonding is mechanical/metallic (no melting) so the original particle shapes and boundaries are often preserved to some extent.

2. Heavily deformed peripheral zones and wavy particle–particle interfaces
   - High-velocity impact causes extreme, localized plastic flow at particle edges. That flow produces wavy, interpenetrating interfaces and “jetting” of surface material that cleans oxide/contaminant layers and enables intimate metal–metal contact.

3. Ultrafine / nanocrystalline grain structure at interfaces
   - The severe plastic deformation and very high strain rates induce dynamic recrystallization or continuous grain subdivision near the impacted surfaces. TEM/EBSD typically show submicron to nanometer-scale grains concentrated in a layer (hundreds nm to many µm) adjacent to particle boundaries.

4. High dislocation density and subgrain structures
   - Away from the dynamically recrystallized region but still within deformed zones, grains are heavily work‑hardened with high dislocation densities and pronounced orientation gradients (low-angle boundaries, elongated grains).

5. Shear bands and adiabatic shear features
   - Narrow localized shear bands or adiabatic shear instabilities occur at contact zones where strain rate and local heating are highest. These are often nucleation sites for dynamic recrystallization and bonding.

6. Oxide fragmentation and oxide-rich interfacial remnants
   - Surface oxide films are broken up and entrained into the interface during impact/jetting. This produces oxide fragments or thin oxide networks at some particle–particle contacts; the extent depends on oxide toughness/adhesion and process parameters.

7. Residual porosity and interparticle voids (usually low)
   - Cold-sprayed coatings tend to be dense relative to other thermal spray methods but can still have interparticle pores, lack-of-bond regions, or incomplete deformation-derived contacts where impact conditions were subcritical.

8. Hardness/strength and residual stress gradients
   - Coatings show increased hardness and tensile/compressive residual stresses near impacted surfaces because of severe cold work; gradients correspond to the deformation/DRX depth.

Why these features arise (mechanistic summary)
- Bonding in cold spray is driven by very high-velocity impact producing extreme, high-strain-rate plastic deformation concentrated at particle peripheries. This causes metal jetting that removes surface films, intense dislocation generation, localized adiabatic heating and shear, and often strain-induced (dynamic) recrystallization. The result is a composite microstructure: relatively undeformed particle interiors, surrounded by a thin, highly refined, work‑hardened and frequently recrystallized interfacial layer where the actual bonding occurs.

Implications
- These microstructural features give cold-sprayed coatings high cohesion and wear strength but can produce anisotropy, oxide-enriched interfaces, and high residual stresses; post-spray heat treatments can reduce dislocations/porosity and alter properties.

Short answer
Induction heating raises a metallic substrate’s temperature by generating a time-varying magnetic field from an AC current in a coil. That field induces circulating electrical currents (eddy currents) inside the conductive substrate; the eddy currents dissipate energy as heat by the material’s electrical resistance (Joule heating). In ferromagnetic metals there is additional heating from magnetic hysteresis. The heating is contactless, rapid, and can be localized by coil geometry and frequency.

Key physics (concise)
- Faraday induction: a changing magnetic flux Φ through the metal induces an electric field E that drives eddy current density J.  
- Joule (Ohmic) heating: volumetric heat generation q˙ = J^2/σ (W/m^3), where σ is electrical conductivity.  
- Hysteresis losses: in ferromagnetic metals, alternating magnetization causes additional energy loss per cycle ∝ area of the B–H loop; these disappear above the Curie temperature.  
- Skin effect: induced currents concentrate near the surface. Skin depth δ = sqrt(2/(ω μ σ)), where ω = 2πf, μ = μ0 μr, σ is conductivity. δ controls how deeply energy is deposited.

Practical consequences and control knobs
- Frequency: higher f → shallower skin depth → more surface heating; lower f → deeper bulk heating. Choose f to match desired penetration (surface vs bulk preheat).  
- Coil design and positioning: coil shape (solenoid, pancake, helical), number of turns, and proximity to the part determine magnetic coupling and heating uniformity. Flux concentrators or ferromagnetic susceptor pieces can focus heating.  
- Power and time: heating rate ∝ delivered power density and coupling efficiency; temperature rise also governed by thermal mass and thermal conductivity (heat diffuses from heated layer inward).  
- Material properties: conductivity, relative permeability, and thickness set heating efficiency; ferromagnetic steels heat very efficiently at low–mid frequencies until they pass the Curie point.  
- Thermal losses and control: convection, radiation and conduction to fixtures limit achievable temperature; closed-loop control (pyrometer/thermocouple) and matching networks for the RF source are used.

Simple numerical sense
- Example skin depths at f = 100 kHz: copper (μr≈1, σ≈5.8×10^7 S/m) δ ≈ 0.6–0.7 mm; a steel with high μr (~100) would have δ roughly 10× smaller (≈0.06–0.1 mm). This shows how frequency and permeability strongly affect energy penetration.

Relevance to additive manufacturing
- In cold spray and other AM, induction is used to preheat substrates (reduce thermal gradients and residual stress, increase ductility, improve particle deformation and bonding) or locally post-heat builds. Because it is fast, localized, and non-contact, induction integrates well into AM heads or fixturing; frequency and coil design are chosen to deliver the required temperature profile without overheating surrounding structures.
