Improper cold-spray settings mainly cause insufficient particle impact energy or inadequate consolidation, leaving voids and weak interfaces. Those pores increase ultrasonic attenuation through enhanced scattering, impedance mismatches, and dissipative losses; the effect is strongly dependent on pore volume fraction, pore size relative to the ultrasonic wavelength, and pore connectivity.

Short answer
Porosity in cold‑sprayed coatings almost always makes the electrical conductivity worse than a simple bulk-material-area scaling would predict. The degree of degradation depends not only on porosity volume fraction but strongly on pore morphology, size, orientation, connectivity, and whether the metallic particles are metallurgically bonded or only in point contact (contact/constriction resistance). Isolated spherical pores cause a relatively modest, near‑proportional drop in conductivity; elongated, aligned or interconnected pores and interparticle gaps/oxide films produce much larger (often non‑linear or power‑law) reductions and strong anisotropy.

Why (mechanisms)
- Reduced effective cross section and tortuosity: pores remove conductive material and force current to take longer, more tortuous paths -> higher effective resistivity. For isolated, randomly distributed pores this is approximately monotonic with porosity.
- Pore shape & orientation: high‑aspect‑ratio pores (cracks, lamellae at particle boundaries) block paths more efficiently than spherical pores of the same volume; pores aligned normal to current flow are especially harmful.
- Connectivity (percolation): when pores are connected into networks, the insulating phase can break up continuous metallic pathways. Near the pore‑connectivity threshold conductivity follows percolation power laws (sigma_eff ∝ (metal fraction − p_c)^t) and can collapse much faster than linear with porosity.
- Interparticle contact/constriction resistance: incomplete metallurgical bonding, thin oxide films at particle–particle interfaces, or tiny real contact areas create additional resistance that often dominates over bulk resistivity. Constriction resistance for a single circular microcontact scales as Rc ≈ rho/(2a) (Holm model), so very small contact radii give very large local resistances.
- Anisotropy & heterogeneity: cold‑sprayed coatings commonly show higher in‑plane conductivity than through‑thickness conductivity because pores and weak interfaces are often oriented normal to the coating plane.
- Local heating/inhomogeneous current density: nonuniform porosity and contact spots concentrate current and can cause local Joule heating and further property degradation.

Modeling & scaling
- Effective‑medium models (Maxwell–Garnett, Bruggeman) reasonably predict conductivity for low to moderate porosity with isolated pores (gives a sublinear reduction). These assume particular inclusion shapes and random distribution.
- Percolation/network models or explicit finite‑element models that include pore geometry and interparticle contact resistances are required when pores are elongated, connected, or when contact resistance is significant.
- Contact resistance can dominate even at low porosity; adding series contact resistances to network models is often necessary.

Typical magnitudes (practical guidance)
- Low, isolated porosity (a few percent): conductivity ≈ bulk × (1 − small fraction). Degradation often on the order of a few to a few tens of percent.
- Moderate porosity or significant interfacial gaps/oxides: conductivity can be several× worse than bulk (measured cold‑sprayed metals commonly show resistivities from ~1.2× to multiple times bulk depending on quality).
- Connected/lamellar porosity or poor bonding: conductivity can drop by orders of magnitude relative to bulk (percolation or contact‑limited behavior).

How to assess and mitigate
- Characterize morphology: cross‑section SEM, X‑ray microtomography to quantify pore size, shape, connectivity and spatial distribution; four‑probe measurements in different orientations to detect anisotropy; impedance spectroscopy to separate bulk vs contact resistance.
- Mitigate: optimize spray parameters for better particle deformation and bonding, reduce oxide content (feedstock handling or reducing atmosphere), post‑deposition heat treatment or hot isostatic pressing to close pores and heal interfaces, or apply a conductive interlayer/anneal to lower contact resistance.

Bottom line
Porosity morphology and distribution control whether conductivity degradation is roughly proportional to lost metal or whether it becomes much worse because of percolation, tortuosity and interparticle contact resistances. Predicting performance requires going beyond bulk resistivity × (1 − porosity) and explicitly accounting for pore geometry, connectivity and contact quality.

Short answer
The dominant bonding mechanism in cold spray is set by which body (particle or substrate) sustains the extreme, highly localized plastic deformation and shear at impact. That in turn is controlled by their relative yield strength/hardness, strain‑rate/thermal response, and the impact energy. The material that deforms most severely generates the interface jet, fractures oxide, produces fresh metal contacts, and therefore drives metallurgical bonding (adiabatic shear, severe plastic deformation, dynamic recrystallization). If neither deforms sufficiently you get poor bonding (mechanical contact only); if one is much harder you can get erosion or particle fracture instead of bonding.

Key points (technical)
- Relative hardness/strength governs deformation partitioning. Lower yield strength (softer) material takes most plastic strain at the same impact conditions and is therefore more likely to be the site of adiabatic shear, jetting and formation of fresh metallic surfaces required for metallurgical bonding.
- Jetting/adiabatic shear instability (ASI) occurs where shear heating overcomes strain‑hardening and heat dissipation. Which side undergoes ASI depends on relative strain‑rate sensitivity, thermal softening and strength — not hardness alone, but hardness is a good first indicator.
- Typical regimes:
  - Softer particle onto harder substrate (Hp < Hs): the particle plastically flattens and often forms the peripheral jet; oxide rupture and dynamic recrystallization occur in the particle → strong metallurgical bonding if kinetic energy (velocity, mass) is sufficient.
  - Harder particle onto softer substrate (Hp > Hs): deformation is concentrated in the substrate. The substrate may flow and produce the jet/fresh surface, but hard particles can also penetrate, embed or fracture. If impact energy is too high, erosion/indentation rather than adhesion may occur.
  - Similar hardness: both bodies deform strongly at the interface, often giving the most favorable conditions for metallurgical bonding.
- Critical velocity and process windows shift with hardness: higher hardness/strength (either particle or substrate) raises the required impact velocity/energy to achieve the ASI/jetting and oxide disruption necessary for bonding. Very hard or brittle particles may require interlayers, pre‑heating, or higher velocities and can fail by fracture rather than bonding.
- Other modifiers: particle temperature, size, oxide film properties, and microstructure (grain size, work‑hardening) all influence which side yields and whether bonding is metallurgical or mainly mechanical.

Practical implication
To get metallurgical bonding you want sufficient impact energy to localize plastic work in at least one of the contacting materials so that oxide rupture and jetting occur. If you’re spraying hard particles onto hard substrates, increase velocity/temperature or use a ductile interlayer; if soft particles onto hard substrates, ensure particle energy is high enough to drive their severe deformation.

Short answer
- Increasing processing-gas temperature and/or pressure raises particle exit and in‑flight velocities and therefore particle kinetic energy on impact. That generally increases particle plastic deformation, interparticle bonding and deposition efficiency and so reduces deposit porosity / increases density — up to an optimum.  
- Below the material’s critical velocity you get poor deformation, many non‑bonded particles and high porosity; above it you get progressive pore closure and near‑fully dense layers. Too much temperature/pressure, however, can cause rebound, substrate damage, powder softening/oxidation, or nozzle/wear issues.

Why (mechanisms, technical)
- Particle kinetic energy (KE ∝ m v^2) controls the amount of plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at impact that produces metallurgical bonding and closes interparticle voids. Gas stagnation pressure and temperature determine the nozzle flowfield and gas exit velocity; that gas accelerates particles.  
- Stagnation pressure: higher pressure increases mass flow and the pressure ratio through the nozzle → higher gas velocities and greater drag/acceleration on particles → higher particle velocity and momentum. This improves deposition efficiency and reduces porosity, especially for larger/heavier particles and harder materials that need more momentum to reach critical velocity.  
- Stagnation temperature: higher gas temperature increases sound speed (a ∝ sqrt(T)), so for the same nozzle geometry and Mach number the absolute gas and particle velocities rise roughly with sqrt(T). Higher T also reduces gas density and viscosity changes, which influences acceleration and drag; net effect in typical cold‑spray nozzles is higher particle velocity and modestly greater particle surface heating (but still below melting).  
- The important threshold is the material’s critical velocity (Vc). For most ductile metals Vc is in the few hundred to ~1,200 m/s range; dense deposits are typically obtained when particle velocity ≈1.1–1.4 × Vc. Below Vc porosity and lack of bonding rise sharply.

Typical quantitative behavior (rules of thumb)
- Particle velocity scales roughly with sqrt(T0) and increases with increasing stagnation pressure and pressure ratio; helium gives higher velocities than nitrogen/air for the same P and T because of its lower molecular weight and higher sound speed.  
- Typical cold‑spray operating windows (approximate): low‑pressure systems ~0.5–1.0 MPa; high‑pressure systems ~1.5–4.0 MPa (10–40 bar). Gas temperatures commonly 200–900 °C depending on material and system. Particle impact velocities typically range ~300–1,200 m/s depending on gas, pressure, temperature and particle size.  
- Porosity: poorly optimized conditions (v << Vc) can give porosities of many percent to tens of percent; well‑optimized cold spray deposits of ductile metals can reach <1% porosity and near‑bulk density.

Trade‑offs and limits
- Excessive pressure/temperature risks: increased particle rebound or erosion of already‑deposited material, substrate damage, increased oxidation or microstructural changes in sensitive materials, powder sintering or feed clogging, higher nozzle wear, and higher operating cost (especially with He).  
- Particle size and material matter: larger/heavier particles require higher P/T to reach Vc; harder materials (Cu, Ni, stainless) have higher Vc than Al/Mg and need more aggressive gas conditions. Nozzle geometry and standoff distance also strongly affect achieved particle velocity and porosity.

Practical guidance
1. Measure or estimate in‑flight particle velocity (Doppler or optical) and compare to literature Vc for your powder. Aim for ~1.1–1.4×Vc for dense layers.  
2. Increase stagnation pressure and/or temperature if velocities are below the target. Prefer raising pressure first for heavier particles; raise temperature when using nitrogen to approach helium-like velocities or when nozzle choking/flow limits are reached.  
3. Watch for signs of overheating (oxidation, powder agglomeration), rebound/erosion, and substrate damage; if seen, reduce energy or change gas/nozzle/particle size.  
4. Use helium or mixed gases when very high particle velocities are required for hard alloys, accepting higher cost.

Bottom line
Gas temperature and pressure control particle velocity and thus kinetic energy on impact — the dominant levers for closing pores and increasing deposit density. Increasing either reduces porosity until you exceed practical/physical limits (oxidation, erosion, rebound, cost), so tune P/T to reach and slightly exceed the material’s critical velocity while monitoring powder, nozzle and substrate behavior.

Short answer
The tamping effect is the mechanical confinement of a striking particle (or of the already-deposited layer) by the surrounding/overlapping particles and substrate. That confinement suppresses particle rebound and lateral escape of material and energy, so a larger fraction of the particle’s incoming kinetic energy is forced into plastic deformation and then into internal energy (heat) at the interface. The result is higher local pressure, larger plastic strain and strain-rate, greater adiabatic heating and more effective jetting/oxide-disruption — all of which strongly improve inter‑splat metallurgical bonding.

How it works (energy picture)
- Energy partition on impact: KEinitial = KErebound + Eelastic + Eplastic + Eother (sound, substrate waves, heat conduction).
- Tamping reduces KErebound and energy radiated away, increasing Eplastic. Most plastic work at cold‑spray strain rates is rapidly converted into heat (Taylor–Quinney coefficient β ≈ 0.8–0.95), so the local temperature rise ΔT ≈ β·W/(ρcp) increases as plastic work W increases.
- Confinement also increases local hydrostatic/compressive stress and shear stresses, so plastic flow is more constrained, strain localization (adiabatic shear) and jet formation at the particle–substrate/splat interface are promoted.

Why that matters for inter‑splat bonding
- Higher pressure + higher temperature + larger shear strain: facilitate oxide fracture and ejection (clean metal-to-metal contact), dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement, and enhanced atomic transport — all of which are necessary for strong metallurgical bonding in a process that operates below the melting point.
- Longer effective contact time and reduced cooling into free space (because surrounding material acts as a thermal/mechanical blanket) increase the window for bonding mechanisms to act.
- Practically, tamping yields better splat flattening, reduced porosity, stronger adhesion and cohesion of the deposit.

In short: tamping increases the proportion of kinetic energy that becomes plastic work and heat at the interface, which is the key driver enabling oxide removal, adiabatic shear/jetting, and metallurgical bonding between splats in cold spray.

Short answer
Mesh resolution in Eulerian cold‑spray simulations strongly controls whether you see localized plastic flow and very high, sharply‑peaked temperature rises at the impact interface or instead a smeared, low‑amplitude field. Coarse grids artificially diffuse momentum and energy (and broaden shocks and interfaces) so they underpredict peak plastic strain and peak temperature while spreading deformation and heating over a larger volume. Fine grids (or targeted refinement) are required to capture the narrow shear/jetting zones, shock thickness and adiabatic heating that govern bonding.

Why this happens (mechanisms)
- Numerical diffusion / advection error: Eulerian advection and interface-capture algorithms smear material/velocity and heat across cells. Smearing reduces local strain rates and dissipative heating, lowering predicted peaks.
- Shock and wave resolution: Shock thickness in shock-capturing schemes is several grid cells. Coarse meshes make shocks artificially thick, reducing local pressure/strain rates and shock‑induced heating.
- Localization sensitivity: Plastic flow localizes into thin zones (shear bands, jets). If the cell size is comparable to or larger than the localization width, the simulation cannot form the narrow bands and instead distributes plastic work, yielding smaller peak strains and temperatures.
- Constitutive/model issues: Rate/temperature‑dependent plasticity and thermal softening promote localization; without a physical regularization (viscoplasticity, gradient or nonlocal damage) results remain mesh dependent.
- Time step and CFL: Coarse cells usually give larger time steps but that does not correct spatial smearing; conversely, very fine meshes require small time steps to properly follow wave dynamics.

Practical consequences in predicted fields
- Coarse mesh: lower peak plastic strain and temperature, larger affected volume, smoother gradients, delayed/absent jetting or shear band formation, possible misprediction of bonding/no‑bonding threshold.
- Fine mesh: higher and sharper peaks, correct shock/adiabatic heating capture, resolved shear bands/jetting and narrow neck regions—closer to experimental observations (assuming constitutive model is adequate).
- No mesh convergence: if the model allows pathological localization (no regularization), refining mesh may continuously increase peak values (mesh dependence).

Guidelines and best practices
- Do a mesh convergence study: monitor peak plastic strain, peak temperature, residual particle/substrate velocity, and bonded area vs cell size.
- Resolve key physical lengths: make cell size small compared to the expected localization width or thermal diffusion length scale. Rule of thumb: aim for O(10–100) cells across the particle diameter for overall impact resolution and at least several cells (5–10 or more) across the expected localization/shear band thickness. If thermal diffusion length L_th ≈ sqrt(α t_impact) is a few micrometers, cell sizes should be a few micrometers or less to resolve temperature gradients.
  - Example estimate: for metals with thermal diffusivity between ~1e‑5 and 1e‑4 m²/s and impact durations ~1e‑6 s, L_th is on the order of a few to a few tens of micrometers; cell sizes should be smaller than L_th to capture adiabatic heating gradients.
- Use local refinement / AMR: concentrate resolution at the impact interface and predicted jet/shear regions to keep cost manageable.
- Improve numerics: use higher‑order advection, sharper multi‑material interface methods, and minimize artificial viscosity consistent with stability to reduce numerical smearing.
- Regularize physics: include strain‑rate dependence, thermal softening with physically motivated heat partition and diffusion, or nonlocal/gradient plasticity if you need mesh‑insensitive localization predictions.
- Validate: compare with experiments (microstructure, temperature measurements if available, deposition threshold velocities) to pick an appropriate mesh/resolution.

Summary
Mesh resolution in Eulerian cold‑spray models is a primary control on predicted localization of plastic strain and associated adiabatic heating. Coarse grids smear shocks and interfaces and underpredict peaks; fine, targeted refinement (plus appropriate numerical methods and physical regularization) is required to capture the narrow, high‑strain/high‑temperature regions that determine bonding. Always perform convergence tests and focus refinement where localization and thermal gradients are expected.

Short answer: all three knobs raise the particle impact energy and enhance particle deformability while delivering particles in a focused, high-flux jet. That combination increases splat flattening, fracture of surface oxides, adiabatic-shear/metallic bonding and impact peening — and therefore closes inter-splat voids and produces low-porosity coatings.

How each contributes (and why they act together):

- Carrier-gas heating
  - Raises gas (and to a lesser extent particle) temperature so particles are softer at impact (lowered yield strength), which reduces the critical velocity required for metallurgical bonding and lets particles undergo greater plastic deformation and interlocking on impact.
  - Increases speed of sound and the gas’s enthalpy, which for a given nozzle expansion allows higher gas exit velocities (particle velocity scales roughly with √T0 for similar expansion).
  - Thermal softening plus increased local ductility reduces brittle fracture and pore-producing rebound.

- High stagnation pressure
  - Increases pressure ratio across the nozzle and mass flow, producing higher gas velocities and higher momentum transfer to particles. Kinetic energy per particle ~ 1/2 m v^2 rises steeply with velocity, so small velocity gains greatly increase impact energy.
  - Higher particle flux and momentum increase deposition efficiency (fewer particles rebound or erode) and give stronger impact peening and filling of void spaces between splats.

- Nozzle design (geometry, throat/expansion ratio, length, injection port)
  - A properly designed converging–diverging (De Laval) or optimized supersonic nozzle accelerates the hot pressurized gas to high Mach numbers with stable expansion, maximizing particle acceleration and delivering a focused core flow.
  - Nozzle throat and expansion ratio control the pressure and velocity profile, and length/residence time affect how much acceleration/heat the particles experience before leaving the nozzle.
  - Particle injection location and nozzle exit diameter determine how many particles are in the nozzle core (uniform acceleration vs wall losses) and the jet’s focus — a tight, well-centered jet gives higher local impact density and better mechanical interlocking between splats.

Why these together reduce porosity
- Higher particle velocity + higher particle ductility = greater flattening/splat area and larger contact/metallic bonding area per impact, reducing inter-splat gaps.
- Increased impact energy promotes oxide fracture, fresh metal-to-metal contact and adiabatic shear bonding rather than brittle fracture or rebound, so fewer unbonded pores form.
- Higher mass flux and focused jet geometry produce more overlapping splats and impact peening that plastically closes residual voids and traps compressive residual stress — densifying the deposit.
- Heating lowers the velocity threshold for bonding, so for a given nozzle and pressure you can achieve dense deposits at lower stagnation pressure or with larger particles.

Practical note (trade-offs)
- Too much temperature or pressure can cause substrate erosion, excessive particle heating or unwanted microstructures; nozzle geometry must be matched to particle size and gas conditions to avoid particle-wall collisions or shock-related scattering. Properly tuned heating, pressure and nozzle geometry produce the high-velocity, high-deformability impacts that yield low-porosity cold spray coatings.

Short answer
- Replacing special (low-diffusivity) grain boundaries with random (high-diffusivity) boundaries increases the effective hydrogen diffusivity of the polycrystal, smooths and flattens local concentration peaks, and speeds equilibration (shorter diffusion times).  
- Practically this means less hydrogen buildup immediately adjacent to grains that used to be “blocked”, more rapid transport along the GB network to sinks (surfaces, dislocations, voids), and therefore higher hydrogen flux to remote critical sites (larger penetration depth and faster arrival times).

Why (mechanism)
- Special boundaries act as resistive barriers for hydrogen transport; they generate large local concentration gradients across the boundary and isolate grains. Random high-angle boundaries are faster diffusion paths (and often higher trap densities), so converting low-D boundaries into high-D ones opens up connected, low-resistance channels. That increases transport along the grain-boundary network and reduces intra-granular concentration contrasts.
- Two competing effects matter: diffusivity (D) and trapping/solubility at the boundary. If the random boundary has both higher D and similar or higher trap capacity, net transport into/through the network increases; if it has higher solubility but low D, it could localize hydrogen — but your statement specifies higher diffusivity, so the transport effect dominates.

Quantitative picture (simple models)
- For thin GB layers of thickness δ and grain size d, a volume-fraction-weighted effective diffusivity is a first approximation:
  D_eff ≈ (1 − f)·D_bulk + f·D_gb,  with f ≈ δ/d.
  Thus ΔD_eff ≈ f·(D_gb_random − D_gb_special).
- Characteristic diffusion time scales like τ ~ L^2 / D_eff, so increasing D_eff shortens τ and accelerates equilibration.
- Note: because f is small (δ ≪ d), the bulk-weighted estimate can underpredict the effect of an interconnected GB network. If the high-D boundaries percolate, they can dominate transport much more than their volume fraction suggests (network-limited or tortuosity effects); percolation leads to orders-of-magnitude faster long-range transport along boundaries.

Predicted changes in concentration profiles
- Near-surface hydrogen ingress: shallower but faster transient gradients into depth (faster penetration).  
- At former barrier locations: reduced step-like jumps in concentration; boundaries are no longer strong concentration discontinuities.  
- Along GB network: concentration becomes more continuous and uniform; peaks at isolated grain faces are reduced, while regions beyond the former barriers receive higher concentrations.  
- Time dependence: faster approach to steady state; shorter lag time for hydrogen to reach sinks behind former special boundaries.

Implications
- Increased embrittlement risk at deeper or remote traps because hydrogen reaches those locations faster and in greater quantity.  
- For modeling, use coupled trap–diffusion or network simulations (finite-element or lattice network) to capture percolation and trap-site effects — the simple volume-fraction rule is only a first estimate.
