Short answer
- Cold-sprayed coatings are commonly harder than the starting bulk/feedstock material. Typical increases are on the order of ~20–200% depending on material and spray conditions, but results vary widely.
- The hardness rise is mainly due to severe plastic deformation at particle impact (high strain rate) that produces grain refinement, very high dislocation densities and work hardening, and often residual compressive stresses at/near particle interfaces.

Why the coating is harder (mechanisms)
- Severe plastic deformation/dynamic recrystallization: impact generates very high local strains and strain rates that produce ultrafine- or nanocrystalline microstructures at particle boundaries and inside particles, which raises hardness (Hall–Petch effect).
- Dislocation accumulation and work hardening: large density of dislocations and sub-grain structures increase yield and hardness.
- Adiabatic shear/ localized bonding zones: intense local deformation can form very hard, highly-deformed interfacial zones (sometimes with localized heating) that strengthen the coating.
- Residual compressive stresses: impact-induced compressive stresses raise measured hardness and resistance to indentation.

When coatings can be softer or show lower effective hardness
- Porosity, poor inter-particle bonding or weak adhesion to substrate reduces effective load-bearing area and measured hardness.
- If the bulk/feedstock is already heavily alloyed/precipitation‑hardened, cold spray may not increase hardness much (and subsequent heat exposure can soften the coating).
- Coating hardness is sensitive to spray parameters (particle velocity, temperature, particle size, substrate condition) and material crystallography (fcc metals typically deform differently than hcp or BCC steels).

Measurement caveats
- Hardness depends on scale: microhardness near interfaces is often higher than bulk-average hardness. Indenter size, location (interior of particles, interfaces, near pores), and substrate influence can change readings.
- Post-spray heat treatments can reduce the as-sprayed hardness by relieving dislocations and coarsening grains.

Practical implication
- You can expect cold-sprayed coatings to be harder than as‑received bulk for many ductile metals (e.g., Al, Cu, Ni, some steels) primarily because of SPD-induced microstructural refinement and work hardening—but verify for your alloy and spray parameters, and account for porosity and measurement method.

Short answer
Graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) almost always reduce the dry sliding friction coefficient of cold‑sprayed metal coatings, typically by a substantial fraction (commonly 20–60% in reported studies). The best results are obtained at low-to-moderate GNP loadings (roughly 0.1–2 wt.% in many reports) and with good dispersion and interfacial bonding.

Why (mechanisms)
- Solid lubrication: GNPs are layered, easily shearable platelets that form a low‑shear transfer film at the contact, lowering interfacial shear strength.  
- Third‑body film formation: GNPs migrate to the sliding surface and create a continuous/patchy lubricating layer that separates asperities and reduces adhesive wear.  
- Reduced adhesion and plowing: The presence of GNPs lowers metal‑to‑metal adhesion and the frictional component due to plowing.  
- Microstructure effects: Small amounts of well‑dispersed GNPs can also refine particle contacts, limit cold welds, and sometimes increase hardness (thus changing contact mechanics), further altering friction/wear behavior.

Quantitative trends and limits
- Typical reductions in coefficient of friction: ~20–60% versus the same metal without GNPs (exact numbers depend on metal matrix, test load/speed, environment and GNP content). For example, some Cu or Al cold‑sprayed coatings with optimized GNP additions report COF drops from ~0.5–0.8 down to ~0.15–0.4 under laboratory sliding tests.  
- Optimal content: often low (≤2 wt.%). Above a threshold (varies by system) further additions tend to produce agglomeration, increased porosity, poorer cohesion and can negate benefits or even raise COF and wear.  
- Processing sensitivity: benefits require good GNP dispersion in feedstock and retention of platelet integrity during spraying. Excessive substrate heating or aggressive mechanical treatment that damages platelets will reduce lubrication effectiveness.

Practical guidance
- Use controlled powder mixing (e.g., ultrasonic, surfactants, spray granulation) to avoid GNP agglomerates.  
- Target small platelet thickness (few-layer platelets) and moderate lateral size for effective transfer films.  
- Optimize cold‑spray parameters and consider mild post‑spray heat treatment to improve bonding without degrading GNPs.  
- Validate with representative tribological tests (load, speed, counterface material, environment) because numerical COF changes depend strongly on test conditions.

Bottom line: properly incorporated GNPs act as effective solid lubricants in cold‑sprayed metal coatings and usually give substantial COF reductions, but the degree of improvement depends strongly on loading, dispersion, platelet quality, and spray/post‑processing.

Short answer
- Ceramic particle content (volume fraction and distribution) is one of the primary controls on the hardness of a cold‑sprayed cermet. Increasing ceramic content generally raises hardness because hard particles carry load and block matrix plasticity, but only up to a point — too much ceramic worsens deposition, bonding and porosity and can reduce the effective hardness and toughness.

How it works (mechanisms)
- Load sharing: Hard ceramic particles (Al2O3, SiC, WC, TiC, etc.) take most of the compressive load under an indenter, raising composite hardness roughly according to a particulate‑composite rule of mixtures modified by particle geometry and bonding.
- Constraint of matrix plasticity: Particles impede dislocation motion and local plastic flow in the ductile metal binder (particle strengthening and Orowan/hindrance effects), and the severely deformed metallic matrix around embedded particles is also work‑hardened.
- Particle network/percolation: At low–moderate ceramic content particles are isolated and act as discrete reinforcements; above a percolation threshold particles can form load‑bearing networks that strongly increase stiffness/hardness (but also brittleness).
- Interfacial quality and consolidation: Because cold spray is a solid‑state process, ceramic particles rarely plastically deform; matrix deformation and metallurgical/mechanical bonding at particle/matrix interfaces control effective load transfer. Poor bonding or unembedded particles lead to pull‑out and lower measured hardness.
- Porosity and defects: High ceramic loadings reduce deposition efficiency, increase porosity and interparticle voids, and promote microcracks — all of which lower effective hardness despite the intrinsic hardness of the ceramic.
- Residual stress and microstructure: Thermal and impact‑induced residual stresses, and matrix grain refinement from severe plastic deformation around particles, also affect hardness (often increasing it), and these effects scale with ceramic content and impact conditions.

Practical implications and trade‑offs
- Increasing ceramic content raises hardness but with diminishing returns and an optimum that depends on materials and spray parameters. Typical workable ranges reported for cold‑sprayed cermets are often in the 10–40 vol% ceramic region for a good balance of hardness, cohesion and deposition efficiency; much above ~40–50 vol% becomes difficult to consolidate well.
- Particle size and morphology matter: finer, well‑dispersed particles give higher effective hardness (better interface area and obstruction of plasticity) but are harder to accelerate/embed. Agglomerates or very angular particles increase porosity and reduce effective hardness.
- Process control matters: impact velocity, powder preheat, binder ductility, and bimodal particle distributions can all raise the attainable ceramic fraction while preserving bonding and therefore hardness.

Measurement caveats
- Indentation results depend on indentation size relative to particle size and location (matrix vs particle). Reported hardness must be interpreted with microstructure in mind.

Design guidance (concise)
- For higher hardness while maintaining adhesion/toughness: aim for moderate ceramic volume fractions (often 10–30 vol%), use fine, well‑dispersed ceramics, choose a ductile, high strain‑hardening binder, and optimize spray parameters to maximize particle embedding and minimize porosity.

Short answer
Annealing changes the tensile strength of cold‑sprayed deposits by two opposing routes: it softens the heavily work‑hardened, high‑dislocation, ultrafine‑grained spray microstructure (reducing strength) while at the same time it can improve interparticle bonding and close porosity/voids (increasing strength). Which effect dominates depends on alloy chemistry, the as‑sprayed defect state, and the annealing temperature/time.

Mechanisms (what actually happens)
- Softening (strength ↓)
  - Recovery and annihilation of dislocations reduces strain‑hardening (lower yield and ultimate tensile strength).
  - Recrystallization and subsequent grain growth reduce grain‑boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch).
  - Residual stress relief removes work‑stress contributions to apparent strength.

- Healing/strengthening (strength ↑)
  - Diffusion across particle boundaries and creep at elevated T improves bonding and load transfer, reducing weak interparticle decohesion.
  - Closure of pores/voids and elimination of interfacial defects reduces stress concentrators.
  - For precipitation‑hardening alloys, appropriate solution + aging sequences after anneal can restore or increase strength versus as‑sprayed.

Practical dependence on temperature/time
- Low‑T anneal (recovery): modest softening, big gains in ductility and toughness; interparticle bonding change limited.
- Intermediate T (enough for interdiffusion but below rapid grain growth): can increase net tensile strength if interfaces/porosity dominated failure.
- High T (recrystallization & grain growth): generally net strength loss, large ductility increase.
- Rule of thumb: many microstructural changes occur in the range 0.25–0.6 Tm (absolute), but exact temps/times depend on the alloy.

Examples (typical observations)
- Pure Cu: annealing usually reduces hardness and tensile strength (recovery/recrystallization) while improving ductility; if interparticle bonding was poor, modest heat treatment can improve tensile performance.
- Al alloys: annealing can soften, but a controlled solution/aging sequence can restore or improve tensile strength in age‑hardening alloys.
- Steels/titanium: effects vary with phase changes and oxygen/oxide behavior; can either lower or modify strength.

Practical recommendations
- Characterize as‑sprayed failure mode (interparticle decohesion vs matrix failure) first.
- Select anneal temperature/time to target interfacial diffusion without excessive grain growth.
- Use controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation at interfaces.
- If alloy is age‑hardening, plan solution/aging schedules post‑anneal to recover strength.

In short: annealing trades dislocation/grain‑boundary strengthening for improved bonding and reduced defects; whether tensile strength rises or falls depends on which effect dominates for the specific material and heat‑treatment used.

Short answer
Surface skewness (Ssk) — the sign and magnitude of the third moment of the height distribution — strongly controls how asperities interact with each other, lubricant and debris, therefore shifting friction behavior. In broad terms:
- Positive skew (Ssk > 0): peak-dominated surfaces → higher local contact pressures, more asperity contact/ploughing and adhesive junctions → higher friction in dry and boundary regimes (unless peaks quickly plastically deform or break off).
- Negative skew (Ssk < 0): valley-dominated surfaces → more lubricant/debris storage, gentler load-bearing plateaus → reduced boundary/mixed-lubrication friction and lower wear; helps film formation/entrainment in lubricated sliding.

Why (mechanics)
- Geometry: Ssk describes whether most of the material is below (positive) or above (negative) the mean plane. Positive-skew surfaces expose sharp summits early under light load, concentrating pressure and increasing adhesive and ploughing contributions to friction. Negative-skew surfaces have extended plateaus and deep valleys so the load is carried more by flatter contact regions and valleys act as lubricant reservoirs / debris traps.
- Bearing-area / material-ratio: skewness changes the Abbott–Firestone curve slope near initial contact. Positive skew → steep initial slope (small bearing area, high local pressure); negative skew → broad plateau (larger bearing area at the same approach).
- Lubrication regime dependence: in boundary and mixed regimes skewness dominates friction behavior. In full hydrodynamic/EHL regimes, film thickness and texture geometry matter more; negative skew assists film building and stable entrainment, positive skew is more likely to break film and cause boundary contact.
- Interaction with kurtosis and roughness: the effect of Ssk depends on RMS roughness (Rq/Ra) and kurtosis (Sku). High kurtosis amplifies peak effects; the same Ssk behaves differently for very rough vs very smooth surfaces.

Implications for engineered textures
- Textures designed for low friction in lubricated sliding generally aim for net negative skew (valley-dominated texture plus plateau-bearing zones) so dimples/grooves act as lubricant reservoirs and reduce boundary contact.
- For dry contact where traction is required, controlled positive skew can increase micro-scale interlocking/traction.
- Run-in changes: asperity flattening during run-in tends to reduce positive skew (peaks wear off) and can lower friction over time; design should account for intended lifetime/run-in behavior.
- Design rules of thumb: ensure valley volume (texture depth × area density) is sufficient relative to expected film thickness and debris generation; match dimple depths/widths so that valleys remain below the load-bearing plateau rather than becoming new asperity peaks.

Practical measurement and modeling
- Ssk is computed from the height distribution: Ssk = (1/Nσ^3) Σ (z_i − z̄)^3 (σ = rms height). Use optical profilometry and evaluate together with Abbott–Firestone curves.
- Predict frictional effect by combining contact models (GW-type / numerical contact) with elastohydrodynamic or mixed-lubrication simulations; include valley storage and cavitation for textured surfaces.

Summary guidance
- If your goal is low friction and wear under lubricated sliding, bias textures toward negative skew (valley-dominated with adequate valley volume and a plateau-bearing area).
- If you need high traction or controlled micro-contact behavior in dry/boundary sliding, consider engineered positive-skew features, but expect higher local pressures and wear unless controlled by materials or sacrificial layers.
- Always evaluate skewness together with roughness amplitude, kurtosis, texture geometry and the expected lubrication regime; isolated control of Ssk without those considerations is not sufficient.

Short answer
Surface roughness strongly affects both friction and wear of coatings by changing how surfaces make contact, how debris and lubricant behave in the contact, and where stresses concentrate. Rougher surfaces generally increase ploughing and local contact pressures (raising wear and often friction), but can also reduce adhesive friction or trap third‑body debris/lubricant and thereby sometimes lower wear or steady‑state friction. The net effect depends on scale of roughness, material properties (hardness, ductility), contact load, sliding regime, and environment.

Key mechanisms (concise)
- Real area of contact: Only asperity summits carry load. For plastically deforming asperities, models (Greenwood–Williamson, or simple load/area arguments) predict real contact area ~ load / hardness. Rougher surfaces reduce nominal real area at low loads, changing adhesive contribution to friction.
- Adhesion vs ploughing: Total friction μ ≈ μadhesion + μploughing. As roughness increases, ploughing (mechanical deformation/cutting of asperities) becomes larger and raises μ; for very smooth surfaces adhesion can dominate and μ may rise as well.
- Abrasive third‑body formation: Higher roughness → more asperity fracture and detached particles → three‑body abrasion and higher wear rates.
- Stress concentrations and fatigue: Tall, sharp asperities create local stress risers, accelerating crack initiation, spallation or delamination of coatings.
- Lubricant/third‑body retention: Controlled roughness (valleys) can store lubricant or trap loose debris, lowering contact temperature and wear in lubricated or steady‑state three‑body regimes.
- Directionality and scale: Anisotropic roughness (lay) affects friction directionally. Micro‑scale asperities influence microscale ploughing and adhesion; nano‑scale roughness may change tribochemical films and adhesive bonding.

Quantitative context
- Archard wear law: V = k·W·s / H (V wear volume, k wear coefficient). Roughness mainly changes k (increasing k with damaging roughness) and influences local H through work hardening or thermal effects.
- Ploughing contribution scales with asperity height/shape and penetration depth; adhesive contribution scales with real contact area (which depends on roughness and load).

Cold‑spray coating specifics
- As‑sprayed cold‑spray surfaces are typically relatively rough (Ra often several µm), which helps mechanical interlocking and bond strength but can increase friction and initial wear.
- Rough as‑sprayed surfaces are prone to third‑body abrasion (loose splats, unmelted particles) until a wear‑dependent transfer film forms or the surface is run in.
- Post‑process finishing (grinding, polishing, peening) reduces surface peaks, lowers ploughing and fatigue crack initiation, and is commonly required for sliding applications.

Practical guidance
- For sliding components where low friction/wear is critical, reduce Ra (typical targets depend on application: Ra <0.2–0.6 µm is common for many metal-on-metal sliding pairs; exact target depends on load and lubrication).
- For coatings intended for load transfer/adhesion, a moderate roughness may be desirable (optimize between adhesion and tribological needs).
- Use post‑processing (grinding, lapping, polishing, shot peening) or compliant/solid‑lubricant topcoats (MoS2, graphite, PTFE) if roughness cannot be eliminated.
- Test under representative loads, speeds and environments (pin‑on‑disk or reciprocating wear tests) because roughness effects are contact‑condition dependent.

Takeaway
Roughness is a controlling parameter of friction and wear but not in a single monotonic way — it changes the balance between adhesion, ploughing, abrasion, third‑body effects and lubrication. Minimize sharp peaks and control valley geometry to reduce ploughing and fatigue, and choose finishing or lubrication strategies appropriate to the service condition.

Short answer
- Increasing particle velocity (v) in cold spray raises particle impact kinetic energy (~½mv^2), which generally increases deposition efficiency, reduces porosity (higher deposit density), and improves mechanical properties (hardness, cohesion, tensile and bond strength) — up to an optimum.  
- Beyond a material- and process-dependent optimum velocity you get diminishing returns and possible negatives (particle rebound/erosion, substrate damage, excessive residual stresses).

Why (mechanisms)
- Higher impact velocity → higher impact pressure and strain rate at the particle/substrate interface. That produces:
  - Severe plastic deformation (SPD) in the particle and substrate surface.
  - Adiabatic shear and jetting that expels surface oxides/contaminants and creates fresh metal-to-metal contact.
  - Increased contact area and intimate metallurgical bonding between particles (and to substrate).
- These effects close interparticle voids and eliminate weak interfaces, yielding a denser, better-bonded deposit.

Effects on density and porosity
- Below the critical velocity: most particles rebound or deposit poorly → high porosity / low mass buildup.  
- At and above critical velocity: deposition efficiency increases sharply; porosity and interparticle void fraction drop as velocity increases further.  
- Very high velocities typically approach a near-full-density deposit for ductile metals, but absolute density also depends on particle size, morphology, oxide films, and process gas.

Effects on mechanical properties
- Hardness: rises because of work hardening and high dislocation density introduced by SPD; grain refinement (subgrain/ultrafine structure at interfaces) also contributes.  
- Tensile/yield strength and cohesive strength: increase as interparticle bonds become metallurgical rather than mechanical.  
- Adhesion to substrate: improves with higher velocity due to stronger interfacial bonding.  
- Fatigue: often improved (compressive residual stresses and fewer defect sites), but details depend on residual stress state and surface condition.  
- Ductility/fracture toughness: can be preserved for ductile metals, but excessive work hardening or brittle splat interfaces (or incorporated oxides/particles) can reduce toughness in some cases.

Limits and trade-offs
- Critical velocity is material-dependent (and varies with particle size, temperature, gas). Typical cold-spray particle speeds are hundreds to >1000 m/s; critical velocities for common ductile metals are often in the few 100s of m/s range.  
- Too low a velocity → no/poor bonding. Too high a velocity → particle erosion of the previously-deposited layer or substrate, increased particle fragmentation, excessive residual stresses, and higher equipment/gas costs.  
- Some materials (brittle ceramics, highly oxidized powders) require elevated temperature or hybrid approaches because sheer velocity alone won’t produce good bonding.

Practical implication
- Optimize particle velocity for the specific powder, particle size, substrate, and gun/gas conditions to reach just above the material’s effective critical velocity to maximize density and mechanical properties while avoiding erosion or damage.

It means the substrate immediately beneath the coating did not experience significant plastic deformation, work‑hardening, or thermally‑driven phase changes during spraying. In other words:

- No measurable strain hardening or peening of the substrate up to the interface.  
- No detectable heat‑affected or transformed zone in the substrate.  
- The dominant deformation during impact was confined to the particles rather than the substrate (or the substrate was too hard to deform).  
- Interfacial bonding therefore relied on particle deformation/metallic contact (and any oxide disruption) rather than extensive substrate plastic anchoring; residual stresses near the interface are likely low.

Short answer: as-sprayed cold‑spray AM deposits typically show higher strength/hardness but reduced ductility (lower tensile elongation) compared with conventionally processed/wrought material. In other words, you commonly see a strength–ductility trade‑off: strength goes up while ductility goes down.

Why (brief):
- Strength increases because of severe plastic deformation during impact: high dislocation density, work‑hardening and grain refinement at particle interfaces, and beneficial residual compressive stresses.  
- Ductility decreases because of microstructural heterogeneity: remaining interparticle boundaries/defects, trapped porosity, weak bonding at some particle–particle interfaces and localized strain concentrations that promote early crack initiation and brittle/interfacial fracture.  

Consequence and mitigation (short):
- As‑sprayed parts are often strong but brittle or limited in elongation; ductility is commonly recovered by post‑spray heat treatment (recrystallization, diffusion bonding), warm/hot spraying, or process optimization to improve particle bonding and reduce defects.

Short answer
Solution + aging (solution‑anneal to dissolve strains/precipitates, then aging to nucleate intermetallics) converts a cold‑sprayed maraging deposit from a highly strained, interface‑controlled, low‑ductility structure into a consolidated, precipitation‑strengthened material with much improved cohesive strength. In practice solutionizing lowers hardness and raises ductility by recovery/recrystallization and healing of particle boundaries; subsequent aging raises yield/UTS (precipitation hardening) while reducing ductility relative to the solutionized state but usually leaving better toughness and much more stable, bulk‑like tensile behavior than the as‑sprayed condition.

Mechanisms (what happens microstructurally)
- As‑sprayed: extremely high dislocation density, heavily deformed particle interiors, limited metallurgical bonding at some interfaces, oxide/pores at some boundaries. Fracture often occurs along interparticle boundaries (cohesion poor), giving low elongation and variable strength.
- Solution anneal (typical: ≈820–900 °C, minutes to an hour, then rapid cool): dissolves any existing precipitates, promotes recovery and recrystallization, eliminates many cold‑spray defects (improves interparticle bonding by metallurgical diffusion and pore closure), relieves residual stresses. Result: lower hardness, lower yield stress than as‑sprayed, but substantially higher uniform elongation and more ductile failure mode.
- Aging (typical: ≈450–520 °C for a few hours for 18Ni maraging grades): precipitation of coherent/semi‑coherent intermetallics (Ni‑rich, Mo/Ti/Al containing phases) on dislocations and within grains → strong precipitation hardening. Dislocation mobility is reduced and strength/ hardness increase markedly; ductility drops compared with the solutionized state but usually remains better than the brittle as‑sprayed interfacial fracture case.

Typical tensile/property trends (qualitative)
- Hardness: as‑sprayed high → solutionized drops significantly → aged increases to a peak that often exceeds as‑sprayed hardness.
- Yield strength / UTS: as‑sprayed can be moderate to high (but limited by weak interfaces) → solutionized decreases (softening) → aged increases strongly (precipitation strengthening), often reaching or exceeding wrought/heat‑treated wrought values.
- Elongation/toughness: as‑sprayed low (interfacial failure) → solutionized increases substantially (bulk ductile failure) → aged decreases from the solutionized peak but usually remains acceptable; fracture mode shifts to more bulk/ductile behavior when interfaces are healed.

Practical outcome and notes
- Proper solution + aging can make cold‑sprayed maraging steel achieve near‑wrought heat‑treated mechanical performance because the heat treatment repairs spray defects and then provides the characteristic maraging precipitation strengthening.
- Exact numeric changes depend on alloy (18Ni‑300 vs other maraging grades), powder condition, spray parameters, solution/aging times and temperatures. Typical solution temps ~820–900 °C; aging ~480–520 °C for 3–8 h (adjust to grade).
- Over‑aging or insufficient solutionizing can either drop strength (coarsened precipitates) or leave residual interfacial weaknesses.

Short answer
Cold spray does not melt the powder, but particle impact at high velocity produces extreme plastic deformation and localized adiabatic heating that strongly alters particle microstructure and mechanical properties. Typical effects are severe work‑hardening, very high dislocation densities, grain subdivision/refinement (often ultrafine/nanocrystalline in the impacted zones), texture/shape changes, and formation of bonded interfaces with residual stresses. Net mechanical effects are higher hardness and strength, lower ductility, and improved near‑surface wear and fatigue performance — all strongly dependent on material and process conditions.

Details

Microstructural changes
- Severe plastic deformation at particle peripheries and interfaces:
  - Elongated and flattened particle shapes, formation of jets at the impact front.
  - Massive dislocation generation and subgrain formation; development of high dislocation density cell structures.
- Grain refinement/dynamic recrystallization in heavily deformed zones:
  - Submicron or nanocrystalline grains often form at the particle/substrate and particle/particle interfaces (a gradient from ultrafine at the interface to less‑deformed core).
  - In some alloys (depending on strain and local temperature) dynamic recrystallization produces equiaxed ultrafine grains.
- Localization phenomena:
  - Adiabatic shear bands and shear instabilities can occur locally and contribute to bonding and microstructural change.
- Surface/oxide modification:
  - Oxide films are fractured/fragmented and displaced by jetting, exposing fresh metal and enabling metallurgical contact.
- For brittle/ceramic powders:
  - Particles may fracture or crush instead of plastically deforming; ceramics remain largely unchanged except for fragmentation and embedding in ductile matrix.

Mechanical property changes
- Hardness and strength:
  - Substantially increased hardness and yield/tensile strength in the deformed regions and in the deposited coating versus the original powder (work hardening + grain‑refinement strengthening).
- Ductility/toughness:
  - Reduced ductility locally due to work hardening and high dislocation density; coating may be less ductile than wrought material.
- Residual stresses:
  - Compressive residual stresses are common near the surface or at interfaces (beneficial for fatigue/crack resistance).
- Wear/fatigue behavior:
  - Wear resistance and some fatigue performance often improve because of harder surface and compressive residual stresses; interparticle interfaces and any remaining oxides can still affect performance.
- Anisotropy and heterogeneity:
  - Properties vary through the coating thickness and across particle boundaries (highly deformed outer shells vs less‑deformed cores).

Factors that control the extent of change
- Material ductility and stacking fault energy (SFE): low‑SFE metals behave differently (more twinning/less cross‑slip).
- Particle velocity and impact energy: higher velocities increase deformation, jetting, and grain refinement.
- Particle size and morphology: smaller particles deform more uniformly; large particles retain a larger undeformed core.
- Gas temperature/composition, nozzle design, stand‑off distance, substrate hardness/roughness.
- Post‑treatments: annealing can reduce dislocation density, coarsen ultrafine grains, recover ductility and modify strength.

Practical notes
- The deposited coating is a mechanically and microstructurally graded assembly of plastically deformed particle shells bonded together; intact powder cores may remain in large particles.
- Because cold spray preserves bulk phases (no melting), phase transformations are limited to those driven by severe plastic deformation or local adiabatic heating rather than solidification.
- If you need specific numbers (hardness increase, grain sizes) for a given alloy (e.g., Al6061, Cu, Ni, Ti), tell me the alloy and process conditions and I can cite typical reported values.

Short answer
- Heat treatment usually increases the effective (macroscopic) elastic modulus of cold‑sprayed metal coatings, primarily by removing porosity and improving metallic continuity at particle–particle boundaries. The intrinsic elastic modulus of the base metal changes little unless a phase transformation or stiff second phase forms.

Mechanisms (what actually changes)
- Porosity and microcracks: annealing, diffusion bonding and transient softening can close pores and microcracks and densify the coating. Reduced porosity increases the effective modulus (often the dominant effect).
- Interparticle bonding and diffusion: heat promotes metallurgical bonding across oxide/contaminant layers and atomic diffusion at interfaces, turning a mechanically‑contacted particulate aggregate into a more continuous metal — this raises stiffness toward the bulk value.
- Residual stress relaxation: cold spray generates large compressive/tensile residual stresses and locked elastic strains. Heat treatment relaxes those stresses and may change the apparent measured stiffness (especially in local tests). Relaxation usually produces a more reproducible, intrinsic modulus.
- Microstructure (recovery, recrystallization, grain growth): these mostly affect strength and hardness; elastic modulus is relatively insensitive to dislocation density and grain size, so recovery/recrystallization have only small direct effects on modulus.
- Phase transformations and precipitates: if heat treatment produces new phases (intermetallics, oxides, or transforms crystal structure, e.g., α→β in Ti), the intrinsic elastic modulus can change substantially (up or down) because different phases have different stiffnesses.
- Precipitates/ceramic formation: formation or growth of stiff precipitates or intermetallics at boundaries can increase modulus locally but may embrittle the coating.

Quantitative behavior and models
- Effective modulus depends strongly on porosity and pore morphology. Simple empirical models give E_effective ≈ E_bulk × (1 − p)^n with n typically between ~1 and 3 depending on pore shape and connectivity. More rigorous bounds (Hashin–Shtrikman) and foam models (Gibson–Ashby) can be used for estimates.
- Typical practical changes: for coatings with significant initial porosity/weak interfaces, annealing can raise effective modulus by a noticeable amount (single‑digit to tens of percent) toward the bulk metal value. If porosity is already low, changes are small. If heat treatment causes new stiff phases, changes can be larger but are alloy‑specific.

Measurement caveats
- Method matters: nanoindentation gives local modulus that is sensitive to near‑surface porosity, residual stress and substrate influence (for thin coatings). Resonant frequency, bending, or ultrasonic techniques probe a more global effective modulus.
- Heat treatment also alters substrate/coating stress state and thickness; correct for these when interpreting measurements.

Practical guidance
- If the goal is to increase stiffness: aim to reduce porosity and improve interparticle bonding without forming brittle intermetallics — moderate temperature anneals or solid‑state diffusion bonding cycles are commonly used.
- If the alloy has phase transformations or strong precipitation behavior, design the thermal cycle to avoid unwanted stiff/brittle phases (or to intentionally form them, if appropriate).
- Characterize density/porosity, phases (XRD), microstructure (SEM/TEM), and residual stress before/after heat treatment, and use an appropriate mechanical test for the desired scale (nanoindentation vs. macroscopic).

Summary
Heat treatment mainly increases the effective elastic modulus of cold‑sprayed coatings by reducing porosity and creating stronger metallurgical bonds between particles; intrinsic modulus changes are small unless phase changes or stiff precipitates/intermetallics form. The magnitude of change depends on initial porosity, alloy chemistry and the specific heat‑treatment path.

Short answer
Cold spray generally raises the hardness of ductile metallic coatings relative to the original feedstock (and often relative to conventionally cast/wrought material) because particles impact at high velocity and undergo severe plastic deformation. That deformation produces very high dislocation densities, strong work‑hardening, grain/subgrain refinement and beneficial residual compressive stress. How the cold‑sprayed hardness compares with other coating methods (HVOF, plasma, thermal spray, sintering) depends on the material and the competing thermal/chemical effects in the other process — thermal sprays that form hard oxides/cermets or that melt-and-solidify can give higher hardness for some systems, while cold spray gives high-strength, low‑oxide, tough coatings for ductile metals.

Why cold spray changes hardness (mechanisms)
- Severe plastic deformation at particle impact → high dislocation density and strain hardening.
- Grain/subgrain refinement and dynamic recrystallization at particle interfaces (ultrafine/nanocrystalline zones) → increased hardness via Hall–Petch effect.
- Strong metallurgical/metallic bonding with compact microstructure and low porosity → higher load support and apparent hardness.
- Residual compressive stresses from impact can raise indentation hardness.
- Minimal thermal exposure preserves feedstock chemistry (no oxide scale formation, no extensive precipitate coarsening) so thermal softening is avoided; however, no new hard phases are formed by melting/solidification (unless you deliberately co-deposit hard particles).
- For composite or cermet cold-sprayed coatings, hardness depends on hard particle content embedded in the ductile matrix rather than on formation of fully sintered hard phases.

Typical outcomes (qualitative)
- Ductile metals (Al, Cu, Ti, Ni): cold‑sprayed coatings are usually harder than the starting powder/annealed bulk because of work hardening and grain refinement. Reported increases are commonly tens of percent up to several× depending on process severity and feedstock condition.
- Precipitation‑hardened alloys: because cold spray is solid‑state, initial precipitate distributions can be largely retained, so hardness is not lost by overheating (unlike some thermal-spray routes).
- Hard ceramics and WC‑Co: cold spray cannot create fully sintered ceramic phases, so single‑phase ceramic hardnesses are not achievable. Instead you embed hard particles in a ductile matrix; overall hardness scales with volume fraction and bonding quality.
- Compared with thermal spray (HVOF, plasma): thermal spray may produce higher hardness when it generates hard oxides, cermets, or melted/refrozen microstructures (e.g., HVOF WC‑Co). For ductile metals, cold spray can match or exceed thermal spray hardness because it avoids oxidation while producing severe plastic deformation.

Practical factors that control/alter hardness
- Particle velocity, temperature, gas type (He vs N2), standoff distance — higher kinetic energy → more deformation → greater hardening.
- Powder size and initial microstructure — finer powders and softer initial microstructure promote stronger deformation and finer final microstructure.
- Substrate hardness and temperature — affect flattening and bonding.
- Post‑spray heat treatments or mechanical post‑processing — can increase hardness for precipitation‑hardening alloys (via ageing) or reduce it by recovery/anneal; mechanical post‑treatments (peening, friction stir) can further refine grains and increase hardness.
- Coating thickness and indentation size effect — thin coatings may show substrate influence in hardness tests; residual stresses affect indentation readings.

Measurement caveats
- Indentation hardness of thin coatings is influenced by substrate and by residual stresses; microhardness mapping across particle interiors and interfaces usually shows a gradient (harder at particle boundaries/impact zones).
- Reported numerical values vary widely with alloy, powder condition, and process parameters — so compare only like‑for‑like tests.

Bottom line
Cold spray tends to produce harder metallic coatings than the original bulk feedstock mainly through severe plastic deformation and grain refinement, while avoiding thermal damage and oxidation. Whether a cold‑sprayed coating is harder than a conventionally processed (thermal spray, sintered, or heat‑treated) coating depends on the materials and whether the competing process generates hard phases or microstructures that cold spray cannot produce. To maximize hardness in cold spray, maximize particle kinetic energy, tailor powder size and feedstock microstructure, and consider appropriate post‑process mechanical or thermal treatments.

Short answer
The "shot‑peening effect" in cold spray is the repeated high‑velocity impact of solid spray particles on the substrate and previously deposited material, which mechanically peens (plastic‑deforms) the surface. That repeated impact produces severe localized plastic deformation, surface cleaning and jetting, compressive residual stresses and grain refinement at and near the interface — all of which increase real contact area, mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding between deposit and substrate.

How it works (mechanisms)
- Severe plastic deformation (SPD): Each particle impact plastically strains a small volume of substrate and deposit, generating very high dislocation densities and often producing ultrafine or dynamically recrystallized grains at the interface. The high defect energy promotes bonding and diffusion-like processes at room temperature.
- Microjetting / oxide disruption: Impact induces high strain rates and transient jetting that locally removes or fractures surface oxides/contaminants, exposing fresh metal for intimate contact and cold welding.
- Increased real contact area / mechanical interlocking: Impact roughens and plastically indents the substrate, creating micro‑asperities and undercuts that anchor subsequent particles mechanically.
- Compressive residual stresses: Repeated impacts generate compressive stress fields near the interface that clamp the coating, close interfacial flaws, reduce tensile driving forces for delamination and improve fatigue resistance.
- Densification and pore closure: Peening of early deposited particles consolidates the near‑interface region, reducing porosity and improving cohesive strength of the deposit.

Practical consequences and limits
- The effect is strongly dependent on particle velocity, size, impact angle, hardness ratio, number of impacts (exposure), and substrate temperature. Higher velocity and more impacts increase peening but excessive peening can over‑work the substrate (embrittlement, cracking) or erode material.
- Typical benefits: higher bond strength, lower interfacial porosity, improved adhesion and fatigue life. Excessive work hardening or brittle phase formation can be detrimental if not controlled.

Takeaway
Shot peening in cold spray is an intrinsic benefit of high‑velocity particle impacts: it creates a highly deformed, cleaned, and compressed interface that promotes mechanical anchorage and metallurgical bonding, improving adhesion and performance of the deposit when process parameters are optimized.

Short answer
Particle impact velocity is one of the single most important process variables in cold spray. Raising velocity (above the material’s critical velocity) generally increases particle deformation, interparticle and particle–substrate bonding, densification and work/strain-rate hardening → higher coating hardness and improved wear resistance. However there is an optimum velocity window: below the critical velocity particles rebound and produce porous, soft deposits; above an upper threshold particles can fracture, erode the deposit/substrate or generate detrimental defects so hardness and wear performance can stagnate or fall.

Key mechanisms (why velocity matters)
- Bonding and densification: velocity controls whether impact energy exceeds the critical energy for plastic jetting/adiabatic shear at the interface. Above the critical velocity you get intimate metal–metal contact (oxide disruption and jetting), strong cold welding and low porosity; below it you get poor bonding and high porosity.
- Severe plastic deformation and strain-rate hardening: higher impact velocities produce extremely high strain rates at the deformation front. This raises dislocation density, produces severe work hardening and often dynamic recrystallization / grain refinement to ultrafine/nanocrystalline structures → hardness increases (Hall–Petch + dislocation strengthening).
- Oxide disruption and clean contact: higher velocities promote oxide break-up and ejection via jetting, enabling actual metallic bonding and improving load transfer and wear resistance.
- Residual stress and damage: increased impact energy increases compressive residual stresses (beneficial up to a point) but excessive energy induces fragmentation, porosity from rebounding particles, microcracks, or substrate erosion that degrade mechanical integrity and tribological behavior.

How hardness changes with velocity (typical trend)
- Sub-critical region: low particle deformation, high porosity, poor bonding → low hardness.
- Just above critical: rapid rise in coating hardness due to bonding, densification and strong work hardening.
- Intermediate/high velocity: hardness continues to increase or plateaus as more densification and nanostructuring accumulate.
- Excessively high velocity: hardness may level off or decrease locally because of particle fracture, inter-splat damage, increased brittleness or delamination and more defects.

How wear resistance changes with velocity
- In most ductile metals (Al, Cu, Ni alloys, stainless steels): wear resistance improves as velocity increases past critical because of higher hardness, lower porosity, and stronger cohesion. Improvements are pronounced for adhesive and abrasive wear modes.
- For hard/brittle feedstocks (tungsten, WC, ceramics): higher velocities can help embed hard particles and increase mechanical interlocking, but high velocities also increase fragmentation and cracking of particles—so the effect is more complex and often material-dependent.
- Excessive velocity can increase erosive wear (substrate/coat removal by high-energy impacts) or create brittle deposits that delaminate under sliding — net wear resistance can fall.

Practical numbers and notes (guidance, material-dependent)
- Critical velocities and optimum windows are highly dependent on material, particle size, temperature and gas. Typical particle velocities in gas-driven cold spray range roughly from ~300 to >1,200 m/s depending on gas (N2, He), pressure and temperature.
- For common ductile metals the useful window is often above ~400–600 m/s; for lighter Al alloys the critical velocity is lower than for Cu or Ni. But always determine experimentally for your feedstock and substrate.
- To optimize: raise velocity (or temperature) until you see good deposition efficiency, minimal porosity and rising hardness, then stop before signs of particle fracture, substrate erosion or coating delamination appear.

Recommended characterization to correlate velocity with performance
- Microhardness mapping (cross-section) to see hardness gradients and peak values.
- Porosity/SEM of inter-splat interfaces to verify bonding quality.
- XRD or TEM for grain refinement and dislocation structure.
- Wear tests (pin-on-disk, reciprocating, erosion) under representative conditions.
- Adhesion and residual stress measurements.

Bottom line
Increase particle velocity until you reliably exceed the material’s critical velocity: this produces stronger bonding, greater strain‑rate hardening and grain refinement, and thus higher coating hardness and better wear resistance. But avoid excessively high velocities that cause particle fracture, erosion or coating damage—the result can be worse hardness and poorer wear performance. Optimization must be done empirically for each material/system.

Short answer
Post-deposition heat treatment (annealing, tempering, hot isostatic pressing, etc.) generally increases interparticle metallurgical bonding and coating cohesion, reduces porosity and residual stresses, and therefore raises tensile/cohesive and adhesive strengths and often improves fatigue and electrical/thermal conductivity. At the same time heat treatment changes microstructure (recovery, recrystallization, grain growth, precipitation, intermetallic formation) so hardness, ductility and toughness can either increase or decrease depending on alloy and treatment conditions.

Key mechanisms
- Enhanced atomic diffusion across particle–particle contacts → formation/enlargement of metallurgical necks and elimination of weak mechanical contacts.  
- Recovery and recrystallization → reduction in dislocation density and residual stresses introduced by cold spray.  
- Grain growth and coarsening → reduced strength/hardness from loss of strain hardening but improved ductility.  
- Precipitation or transformation reactions and intermetallic formation (particularly for dissimilar material systems) → can strengthen or embrittle depending on phases formed.  
- Oxidation or oxygen pickup if not performed in controlled atmosphere → degraded bonding and embrittlement for reactive metals (Ti, Al).

Typical effects on properties (general trends)
- Cohesive/adhesive strength: increases (better interparticle bonding and substrate adhesion).  
- Porosity and open defects: decrease (improved density).  
- Hardness: often decreases because of recovery/recrystallization, but can increase if precipitation hardening/intermetallics occur.  
- Ductility/toughness: generally increases after relieving work hardening, unless brittle phases form.  
- Fatigue life and conductivity: typically improve with defect reduction and densification.  
- Residual stresses: reduced.

Practical considerations and trade-offs
- Temperature/time must be chosen to promote diffusion and bonding without excessive grain growth or unwanted phase formation.  
- Use inert gas, vacuum, or reducing atmosphere (or HIP) to avoid oxidation for reactive alloys.  
- For Al/Cu alloys modest anneals (hundreds of °C) often give beneficial bonding with moderate softening. For steels/Ni-based systems higher temperatures are needed but risk substrate tempering or intermetallics if dissimilar materials are present. HIP can produce near-bulk density but is costly.  
- Monitor for brittle intermetallics (e.g., Al–Fe) that can reduce toughness and fatigue performance.

Bottom line
Heat treatment is a powerful tool to convert the mechanically adhered, highly strained cold-sprayed microstructure into a more metallurgically bonded, denser coating with higher cohesion and often better fatigue and functional properties—but it must be tailored (temperature, time, atmosphere, and sometimes pressure) to each material system to avoid softening or embrittling reactions.

Short answer
Particle impact velocity is the single most important cold-spray parameter controlling whether particles bond at all and, if they do, how severely they deform. As velocity increases (below → near → well above the material’s critical velocity) you move from no-bonding or bouncing to partial bonding to full metallurgical/peening bonding. That transition produces progressively greater plastic deformation, interface jetting, adiabatic shear/Dynamic Recrystallization (DRX), dislocation accumulation and grain refinement — which in turn raise hardness and generate larger compressive residual stresses in the deposit. Beyond an optimum range, however, excessive velocity can cause substrate erosion, particle fragmentation, increased defect formation, or coating damage.

Mechanisms (brief, technical)
- Kinetic energy and contact pressure scale strongly with v (KE ∝ v^2), so higher velocity increases impact pressure and strain rate at the particle/substrate and particle/particle contact.
- At/above the critical velocity you get severe plastic deformation and jetting at the interface that expels oxides and enables intimate metallic contact (mechanical/metallurgical bonding).
- High strain rates and adiabatic heating at the impact zone produce very large dislocation densities and often dynamic recrystallization or subgrain formation, producing ultrafine/nanocrystalline structure in the near-surface portions of particles.
- Accumulated plastic strain from repeated impacts creates peening-like compressive residual stresses and work-hardening.

How microstructure changes with increasing velocity
- Below critical velocity: particles largely retain original microstructure, weak mechanical contact, high porosity, unbonded or lightly adhered particles.
- Near critical velocity: localized severe deformation at particle edges and interfaces, formation of a highly deformed/ultrafine grained layer at interfaces, partial bonding, reduced porosity.
- Above critical/optimum velocity: widespread severe deformation, continuous metallurgical bonds, thin (~microns to tens of microns) heavily-deformed, nanostructured layers within particles, low porosity and oxide-free interfaces.
- Very high velocity (beyond optimum): particle fragmentation, substrate erosion or embedding of brittle debris, possible defect formation (interfacial cracks, voids) depending on material mismatch.

Effects on hardness
- Hardness generally increases with impact velocity (once you exceed the critical velocity) because of:
  - Work hardening (high dislocation density).
  - Grain-size refinement (Hall–Petch strengthening) in the impacted layer.
  - Better load transfer across stronger particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces.
- The hardness increase tends to be largest at the deposit surface and interfaces (gradient hardness), and often plateaus once a steady-state deformed microstructure is reached.
- Magnitude depends on material: ductile metals (Al, Cu, Ni) show clear, often large hardness increases; harder/brittle powders respond differently and may fracture instead of plastically deforming.

Effects on residual stress
- Cold spray typically produces compressive residual stresses in the deposit and near-surface substrate because of impact-induced plasticity and peening. Compressive stress magnitude generally increases with impact velocity (more plastic strain and higher contact pressures).
- The depth and magnitude of compressive stress increase with velocity and number of impacts, creating a compressive near-surface layer that is beneficial for fatigue and crack resistance.
- Extremely high velocities or mismatched conditions can induce tensile stresses locally (e.g., from cracking, delamination, or restrained thermal/elastic recovery after very large plastic strains), or promote substrate erosion that reduces adhesion and creates stress concentrators.

Practical consequences and optimization
- There is a process window: keep velocity above the material-specific critical velocity but below velocities that cause excessive erosion or brittle fracture. Critical velocities vary strongly with material (e.g., Al alloys lower than steels/oxides).
- To increase deposit density, hardness and compressive stress: raise velocity (or temperature/helium fraction) until you reach good bonding and steady-state deformation.
- Monitor for negative effects at very high velocities: substrate damage, particle fragmentation, increased entrapped defects, or coating delamination.
- Particle size, temperature, nozzle geometry, and substrate hardness all shift the effective critical and optimum velocities.

Characterization notes (how this is observed)
- Microstructure: SEM, EBSD (grain refinement, subgrain structure), TEM (dislocation structure, nanograins).
- Hardness: micro-/nanoindentation maps show surface and interfacial hardening.
- Residual stress: XRD sin2ψ, incremental hole-drilling, or curvature measurements demonstrate compressive near-surface stresses that increase with impact energy.

Summary
Increasing particle impact velocity past the critical velocity increases particle flattening, metallurgical bonding, dislocation density and grain refinement, which raises coating hardness and produces larger compressive residual stresses. However, there is an optimal velocity window specific to the powder/substrate system: below it you get poor bonding and low hardness; above it you risk erosion, fragmentation and defect generation that can degrade coating integrity and adhesion.

Ceramic particles (Al2O3, SiC, TiC, WC, etc.) improve wear resistance of cold‑sprayed metal matrix composite (MMC) coatings by a combination of mechanical, microstructural and tribological effects. Key mechanisms:

- Hard‑phase abrasion resistance and load bearing  
  - Hard ceramics present at the contact surface take the brunt of abrasive and contact stresses, preventing the softer metal matrix from plowing and cutting. This reduces volume loss under abrasive and erosive conditions.

- Increased composite hardness and strength (dispersion strengthening)  
  - Well‑dispersed hard particles raise the effective hardness and yield strength of the near‑surface region, reducing plastic deformation and forming resistance to adhesive wear and fatigue initiation.

- Load transfer and stress partitioning  
  - Under contact, stresses are shared between matrix and particles. Particles impede shear localization in the metal, delaying crack initiation and propagation.

- Crack deflection, bridging and energy dissipation  
  - Particles act as obstacles to crack propagation (deflection, branching, bridging), increasing fracture toughness of the composite layer and reducing fatigue/impact wear.

- Mechanical interlocking and work‑hardened matrix around particles (cold spray specific)  
  - Cold spray imparts severe plastic deformation to the metal matrix, producing a work‑hardened, refined matrix that clamps particles mechanically. This strong mechanical bonding improves particle retention during sliding/impact compared with powder metallurgy coatings made at high temperature.

- Modification of contact mechanics and reduced real area of contact  
  - Exposed ceramic asperities reduce the real metallic contact area and adhesive junctions, lowering adhesive wear and material transfer.

- Formation of protective tribo‑layers / third‑body behavior  
  - In some systems, detached fine ceramic fragments or oxides form a hard third body that protects the substrate and reduces further metal‑metal contact.

Important practical considerations and tradeoffs
- Particle size, shape, volume fraction and spatial distribution strongly control effectiveness: too few or poorly bonded particles give limited benefit or act as crack initiators; too many or large particles reduce ductility and increase brittleness/pull‑out.  
- Particle/matrix interface quality matters: cold spray tends to produce primarily mechanical bonding; where metallurgical bonding is needed, post‑heat treatment or interlayers can help. Weak interfaces lead to particle pull‑out and increased wear.  
- Hardness mismatch and residual stresses can cause microcracking around particles if not optimized.  
- Cold spray’s low temperature preserves ceramic integrity and avoids undesirable interfacial reactions, but also limits in‑situ wetting that could improve bonding.

In short: ceramic particles increase wear resistance by providing hard load‑bearing phases, raising surface hardness and strength, blocking plastic flow and crack growth, and modifying surface contact mechanics—provided particle size, fraction and bonding are properly engineered for the cold‑spray process.

Summary
Post‑cold‑spray heat treatment (HT) strongly changes the microstructure produced by the severe plastic deformation of cold spray and therefore alters strength, ductility, residual stresses, porosity/interparticle bonding, wear and fatigue behavior. The net effects depend on temperature, time, atmosphere and the alloy (CP‑Ti vs Ti‑6Al‑4V). In practice HT is used to (1) improve interparticle and substrate bonding and reduce porosity, (2) relieve stored strain energy and residual stresses, and (3) tailor phase constitution — but excessive HT can coarsen grains, relieve beneficial compressive stresses, and cause oxygen pick‑up/oxidation.

Microstructural effects (mechanisms and regimes)
- As‑sprayed baseline: particles plastically deform and weld in the solid state producing very high dislocation densities, ultrafine/subgrain structures near particle boundaries, strong microstructural heterogeneity (deformed rims vs less‑deformed cores), retained oxide fragments at some interfaces and some interconnected porosity.
- Low‑temperature anneal / stress relief (roughly a few 100 °C, dependent on stored energy): recovery dominates — dislocation annihilation and rearrangement, reduction of internal stresses, partial softening, little grain growth. This improves ductility and reduces residual stresses without completely removing the refined microstructure.
- Moderate temperature / recrystallization (typically higher hundreds of °C; depends on alloy and stored energy): recrystallization of heavily deformed zones produces new, often equiaxed grains and removes much of the subgrain/dislocation structure. Grain growth occurs with increasing temperature/time. Recrystallization also enhances diffusion across particle boundaries, tending to eliminate visible particle boundaries and reduce porosity (solid‑state sintering effect).
- High temperature / phase transformation (temperatures near or above the α–β transus: CP‑Ti ~882 °C, Ti‑6Al‑4V ~~990–1000 °C): the alloy can enter the β field and on cooling will transform, producing new phase morphologies (coarse α, lamellar structures, or martensitic/alpha' depending on cooling). Solution + aging treatments for Ti‑6Al‑4V can be used to re‑establish strengthening precipitate distributions after cold spray.
- Atmosphere effects: HT in air produces surface oxidation (thickening of TiO2/“α‑case”) and interstitial oxygen uptake; oxidized interfaces can remain brittle and oxygen hardening increases surface hardness and embrittlement. Inert or vacuum HT minimizes these deleterious effects and promotes better metallurgical bonding.

Mechanical property consequences
- Strength and hardness: as‑sprayed deposits are often relatively hard/strong because of work hardening and ultrafine microstructure. Recovery and recrystallization reduce dislocation density and thus reduce hardness and yield strength. Depending on processing, appropriate solution/aging can re‑strengthen Ti alloys.
- Ductility and toughness: HT generally increases ductility and fracture toughness by removing brittle, highly strained microstructure and improving interparticle cohesion. That is beneficial for tensile elongation and fracture resistance.
- Adhesion/cohesive strength and porosity: diffusion and recrystallization during HT increase interparticle necking and reduce open porosity, improving cohesive tensile strength and the bond to the substrate.
- Fatigue and residual stresses: cold‑sprayed components often exhibit beneficial compressive residual stresses that improve fatigue life. HT relieves residual stresses and can therefore reduce fatigue performance; the net fatigue behavior depends on whether improved bonding/porosity reduction outweighs loss of compressive stresses.
- Wear and surface behavior: HT softening may reduce wear resistance, while oxygen pickup or α‑case formation can increase surface hardness but embrittle the surface.

Practical guidelines
- Choose HT temperature/time to balance interparticle bonding and recovery versus undesirable grain growth and stress relaxation. Short higher‑temperature excursions can improve bonding with less grain growth than long anneals.
- Avoid HT in air if oxidation or oxygen pickup is a concern—use vacuum or inert atmospheres (Ar) or protective coatings if possible.
- For CP‑Ti perform HT below the β‑transus when you want to avoid phase changes; for Ti‑6Al‑4V you can use solution + aging schedules if you intend to re‑establish strength, but parameters will differ from wrought material because of the cold‑sprayed starting microstructure.
- Characterize by SEM/EBSD/TEM (grain size, interface integrity), hardness mapping, and mechanical testing (tensile, fatigue) to confirm the trade‑offs.

Bottom line
Post‑cold‑spray heat treatment converts a highly strained, particle‑based, and heterogeneous microstructure into a more continuous, lower‑dislocation, and better‑bonded material. That generally increases ductility and bond integrity and reduces porosity, but lowers as‑sprayed hardness and can relieve beneficial compressive stresses. Atmosphere control and careful selection of time/temperature are critical for titanium to avoid oxidation and adverse phase/oxygen effects.

Short answer
Moderate-temperature annealing of cold‑sprayed Cu relaxes the severe plastic deformation structure produced by particle impact (dislocations, subgrains, residual stress) and so trades strength/hardness for improved bonding, ductility and conductivity. Whether you get only recovery or full recrystallization (and grain growth) depends on temperature and time; choose the regime to balance strength vs. toughness/conductivity.

What happens in the microstructure
- As‑deposited state: particles contain very high dislocation density, highly strained nanocrystalline/ultrafine regions at particle boundaries, large density of low‑angle boundaries, tensile/compressive residual stresses and some pores/particle–particle interfaces that are not fully metallurgically bonded.
- Recovery (moderate T, short time): dislocation annihilation and rearrangement into lower energy subgrain structures; reduction of internal stresses; partial elimination of low‑angle boundaries; limited diffusion across interfaces increases necking at contacts. No large grain growth.
- Recrystallization (higher moderate T or longer time): nucleation of strain‑free equiaxed grains, especially at particle boundaries and prior high‑strain zones; disappearance of much of the dislocation structure; conversion of subgrains to high‑angle grain boundaries.
- Grain growth (if overstated moderate T/time): coarsening of recrystallized grains, loss of ultrafine structure.

Observed with EBSD/TEM: lower dislocation density, increase in average grain size, reduction in fraction of low‑angle boundaries (after recovery → partial; after recrystallization → strong reduction), more continuous metallic bonding across interfaces.

Mechanical and functional property changes
- Hardness / strength: decreases. Recovery reduces hardness markedly; recrystallization produces larger drops. Typical Vickers hardness reductions reported on cold‑sprayed Cu are on the order of 10–50% depending on conditions. Tensile/ yield strength similarly fall as work hardening is removed.
- Ductility / toughness: increases—elongation increases because strain‑free grains and lower dislocation density allow plasticity to proceed.
- Adhesion/cohesion and fatigue: often improve because interfaces become better bonded and residual stresses relax, lowering crack‑initiation sites and particle pull‑out.
- Porosity / density: limited closure possible by diffusion and grain‑boundary migration; substantial densification is unlikely at moderate temperatures but some reduction of open porosity and better interparticle contact are common.
- Electrical/thermal conductivity: increases because of reduced electron scattering from dislocations and improved interparticle continuity.
- Wear/corrosion: wear resistance typically decreases with hardness loss; corrosion behavior may improve due to fewer localized galvanic sites and less internal stress, but depends on environment.

Typical temperature/time regimes (for pure Cu)
- Recovery-dominant: roughly 100–200°C (short times, minutes to an hour) — reduces residual stress and dislocation density with minimal grain growth.
- Recrystallization onset: ~200–350°C (depending on prior strain level and particle size) — nucleation and growth of strain‑free grains; stronger softening.
- Grain growth: more pronounced >350–400°C or long anneals at lower T.
Note: heavily deformed cold‑sprayed Cu can recrystallize at surprisingly low temperatures compared with undeformed Cu; exact numbers depend on deposit strain, thickness, and impurity content.

Practical guidance
- If goal is better conductivity/ductility and stronger interparticle bonding: use a moderate anneal that allows recovery and limited recrystallization (e.g., 200–300°C for tens of minutes to an hour) and monitor microstructure.
- If retaining as‑sprayed strength/hardness is critical: keep anneal below recovery/recrystallization thresholds (e.g., <150–200°C) or use very short anneals.
- Characterize with hardness testing, tensile or shear testing, EBSD/TEM for grain structure, residual stress measurement, and conductivity tests to identify the optimum balance.

Bottom line
Moderate annealing transforms the cold‑sprayed copper from a heavily strained, hard, but more brittle and imperfectly bonded deposit into a softer, more ductile, better‑bonded, and more conductive coating. The net effect depends on whether you stop at recovery (stress relief, modest softening) or allow recrystallization/grain growth (stronger softening but greater ductility and conductivity).

Short answer
Particle size controls both the as-atomized microstructure and the mechanics of impact during cold spray. Smaller gas‑atomized particles solidify much faster and therefore have finer/possibly metastable internal microstructures and higher strength; they also carry less kinetic energy and have a larger surface‑oxide/volume fraction. Larger particles cool slower, are softer/coarser, have greater impact energy (mass), and produce more intense local shear/adiabatic heating on impact. Those combined effects determine how much severe plastic deformation, dynamic recrystallization, oxide disruption/jetting and interparticle bonding occur, and thus the final spray microstructure and mechanical strength.

Detailed points

1) As‑atomized microstructure vs particle size
- Cooling rate rises as particle diameter falls, so small particles (few to a few tens of µm) solidify with much finer grains, higher dislocation and solute supersaturation, and a greater tendency to retain metastable phases or even amorphous structure in extreme cases. Coarser particles develop larger grains and more equilibrium phases.
- The yield strength of the powder particle before impact typically increases as size decreases (Hall–Petch and solute/dislocation effects), i.e. small particles are intrinsically harder to plastically deform on impact.
- Surface effects scale with size: an oxide shell thickness may not scale strongly with particle diameter, so oxide (and adsorbate) fraction and effective barrier to bonding are larger on smaller particles (higher surface area/volume).

2) Impact mechanics and deformation behavior
- Kinetic energy scales with particle mass (∝ r^3) at a given velocity. Larger particles therefore deliver much more energy per impact, promoting the severe plastic deformation, jetting and local adiabatic heating that create clean metallurgical interfaces.
- Small particles have lower impact energy and, because of their higher starting strength, may not reach the strain level or localized heating required for bonding; they can remain largely undeformed and produce poorly bonded, porous deposits if process conditions aren’t adjusted.
- Deformation mode depends on size: larger particles promote localized shear bands, adiabatic shear instabilities and dynamic recrystallization near the interface; smaller ones tend to deform more uniformly (if they deform at all), producing less of the intense surface disruption and interfacial mixing needed for strong metallic bonding.

3) Microstructural evolution in the deposit
- Wherever severe plastic deformation occurs (especially at interfaces produced by larger particles or sufficiently high impact velocity), dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement produce ultrafine/nanocrystalline zones and very high dislocation densities. These regions control hardness and strength of the coating.
- If particles are too small and bonding is poor, the deposit retains particle boundaries, oxide layers and porosity — lowering cohesive strength.
- If particles are large, you can get excellent bonding and an extensively refined interfacial microstructure, but also greater residual stresses and sometimes particle fracture or entrapped oxides in particulates.

4) Net effect on mechanical strength of the spray
- Strongest, most cohesive deposits are usually produced by particles in a size range that: (a) are large enough to provide sufficient impact energy to produce jetting/adiabatic shear and clean interfaces, and (b) are not so large that they produce defects from brittle fracture or inhomogeneous packing. That “sweet spot” depends on material and equipment but is often in the mid‑micron range for many metals.
- Using too-small powders tends to reduce deposition efficiency and interface quality (lower strength) unless compensating changes are made (higher gas pressure/temperature, higher velocities, preheating, annealing powder).
- Using very large particles can increase deposition efficiency and interfacial bonding but may increase surface roughness, trapped porosity and tensile residual stresses, which can reduce fatigue or adhesion performance.

5) Practical levers and tradeoffs
- To use fine powders: lower their initial strength by annealing or tailor gas temperature/pressure to raise particle velocity/temperature; consider in‑nozzle heating or using bimodal size distributions to fill voids and aid bonding.
- To use coarser powders: control particle size upper limit to avoid particle fracture and excessive roughness; optimize carrier gas and nozzle conditions to avoid excessive residual stress.
- For high‑strength alloys (age‑hardened, supersaturated), expect that small, hard powders will require higher velocities to deposit; powder microstructure tailoring (e.g., overaging/softening) is commonly used.

Summary
Particle size sets the starting microstructure and mechanical properties of each powder particle and also controls the impact energy and the nature of deformation during cold spray. Small particles → finer as‑atomized microstructure and higher initial strength but lower impact energy and higher relative oxide fraction (risk of poor bonding). Large particles → coarser, softer starting microstructure and much higher impact energy that favors jetting, dynamic recrystallization and strong bonds, but with risks of roughness, residual stress and defects. Optimal spray strength typically requires selecting a particle size (or size mix) and process parameters that balance these competing effects for the specific alloy.

Short answer
Rapid solidification in gas atomization (cooling rates typically 10^3–10^6 K/s, higher for the smallest droplets) produces much finer, more chemically uniform and often metastable powder microstructures than equilibrium solidification. The net effects are higher as‑atomized strength and hardness, altered precipitation/heat‑treat response, and sometimes reduced ductility or fracture toughness if brittle phases or high oxygen are present. The specifics depend strongly on particle size and alloy chemistry.

Detail — what rapid solidification changes in the powder
- Cooling-rate gradient with particle size: smaller droplets cool orders of magnitude faster, so microstructure varies with particle diameter (surface layer solidifies first; interior solidifies later).
- Grain/dendrite scale refinement: secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) and cell sizes are greatly reduced (sub‑µm to a few µm depending on alloy and size). SDAS scales roughly as (cooling rate)^−n (n ≈ 0.25–0.35), so higher cooling → much finer structure.
- Suppressed segregation and solute trapping: fast solidification reduces partitioning of solute to interdendritic regions, producing more homogeneous composition and extended solid solubility (solute trapping). This suppresses coarse interdendritic phases present in cast material.
- Metastable phases and amorphous/nanocrystalline structures: for good glass‑formers or very small droplets, you can get nanocrystalline or even amorphous powders; for conventional alloys you commonly get very fine cellular/dendritic and supersaturated solid solutions.
- Fine distribution of second phases: precipitates that do form are finer and more uniformly distributed (or may be absent as supersaturation).
- Defect structure and residual stresses: high dislocation density and residual thermal stresses can be present; also thin oxide/nitride surface films form on reactive alloys during atomization.

Consequences for mechanical properties
- Strength and hardness: increased by grain‑refinement (Hall–Petch), solid‑solution strengthening (solute trapping), and finer dispersoids — as‑atomized powders are typically harder/stronger than slowly solidified equivalents.
- Ductility/toughness: may be reduced if brittle metastable phases, coarse oxides, or excessive interstitials (O, N) form; however, very fine, homogeneous microstructures can also retain good ductility in some alloys.
- Heat‑treatment response: because of supersaturation and suppressed segregation, age‑hardening kinetics change (often faster precipitation, higher peak hardness possible). Homogenization treatments may be shortened or altered.
- Process performance effects:
  - Additive manufacturing (PBF/SLM): fine powders give more uniform melt behavior, faster solidification in the part, and finer as‑built microstructure; reduced feedstock segregation improves reproducibility. Elevated oxygen on small particles or oxide skins can reduce ductility or cause defects.
  - Cold spray: higher as‑atomized strength/hardness can improve wear resistance of deposits but extremely hard/brittle powders may fracture on impact, lowering deposition efficiency; oxide shells can hinder particle bonding.

Practical notes
- Particle‑size control is crucial: smaller particles = faster cooling → more refinement/metastability; but they also have higher surface area, more oxides and gas pickup, and tend to agglomerate.
- Alloy design/atomization conditions can be tuned to get desired balance: e.g., get supersaturated solid solution for later age hardening, or avoid glass formation if ductility is needed.
- Post‑atomization treatments (anneal/homogenize, passivation) are often used to relieve residual stress, reduce microsegregation slightly, or remove undesirable metastable phases/oxides.

Short version — successive particle impacts in cold spray act like high‑strain‑rate peening plus particle fragmentation. Their net effect on crack density, deposition efficiency and hardness of cermet coatings is set by the balance between beneficial plastic flow/peening and detrimental brittle fracture/erosion.

Mechanisms common to all three effects
- Each particle impact produces very high local strain rates and stresses (typical orders of magnitude 10^4–10^7 s−1), local adiabatic heating, jetting at interfaces and shock waves.  
- Ductile binder (Ni, Co) undergoes severe plastic deformation and work hardening, flows to fill gaps and produce mechanical interlocking/bonding.  
- Hard ceramic phases (WC, TiC, etc.) are brittle: they fracture/fragment under impact; fragments can increase packing density or create microcracks and stress concentrators.  
- Impacts generate near‑surface compressive residual stresses (peening) and subsurface tensile stresses; the spatial stress state and cumulative damage control whether cracks form or are healed.

Crack density — how it changes with successive impacts
- First few impacts: brittle ceramic particles commonly fracture, producing microcracks in particles and at particle–matrix interfaces. Crack density typically increases initially because fragmentation creates new crack surfaces and weak interfaces before significant plastically consolidated matrix forms.
